THE OWL AND THE SPIDER. In an old belfry tower, A dry. cosy bower, Dozed an owl by the hour. But the bell's sly old clapper Was a mischievous rapper, And soon waked the napper. "Mr. Owl, don't you mind him; With cobwebs bind him, And round and round wind him."

Thus spoke up a spider, Strip'd like an outrider; The owl sharply eyed her, And said, "If he cheat you, I'll not scold nor beat you, I'll just merely eat you." The owl saw her spin Her web, frail and thin, Round the bell, out and in. But, next Sabbath morning, Without word or warning, • The bell went a storming! With a cling and a clang, With a boom and a bang, The old clapper rang! The owl didn't chide her, Rebuke nor deride her, But he ate up that spider! Here is a moral, dear children, for you: Never promise a thing you're not able to do. ;7-St. Nicholas.

A MARRIAGE HYMN. " From henceforth no more twain, but one," Yet ever one through being twain, As self is ever lost and won Through love's own ceaseless loss and gain; And both their full perfection reach. Each growing the full self through each. Two in all worship, glad and high, All promises to praise and prayer, • Where two are gathered, there am I;"— Gone half the weight from all ye bear, Gained twice the force for all ye do— The ceaseless, sacred Church of two. One in all lowly ministry, One in all priestly sacrific?, Through love which makes all service free, And finds or makes all gifts of price, All love which made life rich before, . Through this great central love grown more. And so, together Journeying on To the Great Bridal of the Christ, When all the life His love has won To perfect love is sacrificed, And the New Song beyond the Sun Peals, "Hencefortis no more twain, but One." And in that perfect Marriage Day All earth's lost love shall live once more; All lack and loss shall pass away, And all find all not found before: Till all the worlds shall live and glow In that grelt love's great overflow. F—Good Words for February.

A story is told of a member of a certain American theolo- gical seminary who was so sensitive as to any suspicion of plagiarism that he never allowed himself to make the slight- est quotation without giving his authority. On one occa- sion, he commenced grace at breakfast thus: "Lord, we thank Thee that we have awakened from the sleep which a wi'iter in the Edinburgh Review has called the image of deeth! An Augusta man "gave himself away" in Boston the other day. He came to the city on business, and put up at one of the first-class hotels. The clerk gave his baggage and the key of his room to a porter. who conducted the Augusta gentleman to tbe elevator. Closing the door, they began to ascend, unperceived by the traveller. He eyed the four walls of the elevator a moment and exclaimed, "Take my baggage back to the office; you can't put me in a little room like this." FASHIONS IN BONNETS AND THE Laws OF HEALTH.—A lady may suffer from severe facial neuralgia on exposure to oeld ; but if the goddess of fashion decree that the bonnet shall be worn en the back of the head, she must suffer patiently till the reaction to poke bonnets arrives; then she will have a temporary respite from her agony till the next change again leaves the facial area exposed. She may have sensitive eyes, but no shade of head-dress shall protect her from the sun's piercing rays, unless bread-brimmed hats happen to be ala mode. If her skin is serstive and given to blister, there is a legion of c,lsmetics advertised—at prices which make a serious inroad on a lady's pin-money. To beautify the skin and clear the complexion, it is not essen- tial to wear a suitable head-dress; the modiste settles the form of the hat or bonnet, and if the cosmetic vendor is benefited thereby, why, there is no great objection to that. 1., not the lady of fashion one of the fat kine on which the le ,n k-ine can subsist ?)And theWire7igte plays into her fellow- tw hands.—Fashions and Physiology, in Good Words. RELIGION IN Russo.—After saying, "I regard the Rus- sian people as presenting a promising field for the diffusion of a more spiritual religion than they now possess," Mr. Lenedell makes the following remarks, which come with special weight from a witness for whom Russian ritual has evidently no attraction, and who condemns in strong terms the ignorance and spiritual apathy of the Russian parish priests :—" As for the uneducated Russians, the distances they will go, amounting to literally thousands of miles, for relizions purposes, manifests at least something in- tensely earnest about religious affairs. Never certainly, in any other country—have I met with such earnestness to get Scriptures and gcod books. This extends to both clergy and laity. When, on one occasion, my friend who edited the Rtssian Workman thought of giving it up, come of the priests sent their subscriptions again and imelored that it might be continued; and some of ;hose interested in the reigious societies at work in the empire have told me that in spite of the obstacles put in their way, they have far more opportunities of usefulness than they can use. I agree, therefore, with those who look upon Russia as a promising field for Christian effort."—Through Siberia by H. Lansdell. A BLIND MAN'S HOLIDAY.—" So my brother, a friend, and myself set out on foot. The first cwried a rifle, the second a bag of books for roe, and I an axe, bought on pur- pose for the expedition. I was not very vigorous: we reached the springs late at night, receiving a hearty wel- come. I went to bed, slept for twelve hours, and was fresh again; so I determined to go on to a cabin, five miles farther, which belonged to my uncle, and was sometimes occupied by his men when tending cattle on the hills. We took a day's food, and walked slowly, reaching the hut about three p.m. It was much out of repair, but I only wanted a Place to sleep in at night, and shelter in when it rained. Two miles beyond it was my uncle's house. There we went, and my auct promised to supply tie with food on condition that we sent for or fetched it." What a picture of life among the mountains, the glorious, free, wild life, so delightful to the young, if only they have eyes to see! But this young man had none, yet he seems to have done quite as well without them. "Our first few days were spent in reconnoitring our surroundings. The hat stood within a few feet of the brow of the mountain. ' If I threw a stone down I could hear it bounding down for ever so long. By- and-bye I learnt to clamber up and down this cliff, and found ten enormous trees growing there, one above the other, the upper one being only a few feet from the next down, the lowest about two hundred feet beneath. So I planned and proposed what backwoodsmen call a cataract,' and sallied forth, axe in hand, to attack my first tree, about four feet in diameter. My strength was below par; I got on slowly. The other two laughed at me, and suggested I should ask for help. But my brother was always out hunting, and he and the other lad took turns in fetching our food,ln read- ing to me of evenings. The weather was glorious, I soon drank in health at every pore. and was able to cut the whole ten trees three parts through in about a month. At last all was ready. The biggest tree, the one next our hut, was hewn through, except a very small bit, and prepared to fall. We were greatly excited; all the success of my plan de- pended upon the way the trees, beginning with the lowest, had been cut, so as to fall straight. I examined them one by one, then climbed beck to the topmost tree, and applied - my axe vigorously. Ten minutes more and I 13±s.ard brother cry out, 'Hurrah, it's going!' We all lea.,)ed aside lest we should be struck by the falling branches. dWhat a turmoil—tree after tree began to go, each pressibg upon each, till the whole of them went plunging down the moun- tain side. The topmost one finally found a resting place far below. Triumphant with succees, we three boys shouted and threw up our hats, and finally we brought our supper, and laid it out on the stump of the huge tree which had oompl,led our 'cataract.' "—" Francis Joseph Campbell," in Good Words. Certain Death to Rats and Mice by u,ing JACKSON'o LA.NC VERMIN KILLER. the most powerful killer .kno n. -- Mr. Ellis Lever, of Manchester, offers a premium of £5OO for the best approved system of electric lighting in collieries. The casing stones of the first and third pyramids at Gizeh, below the entrances, have been laid bare. They are of good

work and fine joints. Jean Crousouty, sub-librarian of the museum at Cracow,' has discovered what is believed to be the earliest book printed in Hungarian. It is a Legend of St. Paul, dated 1512. A pretty puzzle for Orientalists has turned up in the shape of an inscription in an unknown character, not Phce- nician, nor Cypriote, nor Lycian, nor Hamathite, which has been found on a contract tablet from Babylon, dated in the reign of Artaxerxes. The Etna Observatory, erected on a small mount near the crater, and so placed that a current of lava would probably divide in two and avoid it, has been completed. It is 2,943 metres above the sea; the Great St. Bernard Monastery is 2,491 and the St. Gothard 2,075 metres. The Courier of the Rhine reports the discovery at Steeten, on the Lahn, of a hitherto hidden cave, in which seven human skeletons have been found. At the opening of the cave a huge heap of bones of animals and other remains of primitive existence have been laid bare. Mr. Mongredien, author of "Free Trade and English Commerce " and "History of the Free Trade Movement in England," has in the press a new work, entitled "Pleas for Protection Examined," which Messrs. Cassell, Fetter, Gal- pin, and Co. will shortly publish for the Cobden Club. Mr. J. Stevenson has written an account in the New York Tribune of his researches among the pueblo Indians of New Mexico and Arizona, conducted on behalf of the Smithsonian Institute. He explored a number of rock-built towns, one of 'which he estimates to have contained a population of 100,000. Dwellings are excavated out of the rock for sixty miles along the face of a winding cliff. Mr. Stevenson has brought back a collection of many thousand objects of pot- tery. M. Meissonier, whose serious illness has already been re- corded, has completely recovered his health. During his sickness the painter made many sketches and designs, among the former of which was, says the Mordteur des Arts, a por- trait ot himself, sick, wrapped in an ample dressing-gown, and reeling on a large fauteuil. An amateur offered the painter 80,000 francs for this work, but Meissonier, who in- tended to give it to the Musee de Lyon, his native city, re- fused to sell the work. We (Athenceum) spoke last week of the disposition of Mr. Harrison Ainsworth's papers. It is said that amongst them is a large amount of correspondence with many men emin- ent in literature, which will probably form the basis of a memoir. A peculiar feature in Mr. Ainssvorth's library is a Large collection of books on the lives and exploits of noted criminals. The issue of sixpenny editions seems rapidly on the increase, and Messrs. Routledge are about to try the ex- periment with the late novelist's "Tower of London." Experiments have been made by M. Deck, the celebrated faiencier of Paris, with a view to replace M. Baudry's mural paintings at the Opera with copies on tiles, should it be found impracticable to use the electric light to illuminate the house. The paintings have already suffered from the gas. M. Legrain accurately copied one of the panels, and, after it was fired, the surface was treated with acid, in order to reduce the brilliance of the glaze. The success is said to be perfect, the copy having .the same ,tone and unreflective surface as the original painting. Just before his death Dean Stanley wrote for the Century Magazine an estimate of the life and influence of F. W. Robertson, in his opinion the greatest preacher of the 19th century. Unfortunately for the immediate publication of the article, the corrections and marginal additions were in the Dean's own handwriting, which to anyone except his amanuensis, and perhaps himself, was about as intelligible as the Mexican hieroglyphics. The article was sent back to England to be deciphered, and with what interecting re- sults will be seen in the February Century. A portrait of Robertson will accompany the article. The February number will also contain a new essay by Mr. R. W. Emer- son on "The Superlative," a plea for simplicity in literary style; and a long poem by Mr. Longfellow, entitled " Her- mes Trismegistus," dealing with the adventures of that semi-mythical personage. Herr Eeluard Strauss has been trying the experiment in Vienna of transmitting the sound of his orchestra by means of the telephone, and writes on the subject to a Vienna journal in the following terms :—" The experiment was bril- liantly and surprisingly successful. Four microphones, of Ader's system, were employed. Eight telephones were placed at a considerable distance from the orchestra, in the same house; which distance, however, was artificially lengthened, by means of cables, to four German miles. The tone of the whole orchestra was surprising ; the wind in- struments, it is true, dominate ; and even a stringed orches- tra sounds like a military bands The flute and clarionet, however, keep their tone and character unchanged. The harp alone bounds almost like a piano, the side-drum shriller than is poesible in nature. The voice retains its full quality of tone." Herr Strauss intends to give the public an oppor- tunity of taking part in these telephonic concerts. The material known as Spence's Metal has been applied with the greatest success to many ornamental purposes: Composed principally of iron pyrites, it has the properties of melting at a low temperature and cooling rapidly. These enable it to be caet in gelatine moulds, so that the most elaborate carving, with all the under cutting and fine work, ; can be reproduced in fac-simile swiftly and surely. A per- , fectly sharp casting can be obtained by pouring this metal at a temperature of 250cleg. F. into a gelatine mould which melts at 90deg. Chilled at once, the metal forms a hard 1 skin before the gelatine has time to melt. Afterwards the I heat of the metal melts the mould, but too late to injure the casting; and if both be allowed te cool together the mould can be used again. When taken out of the mould, the metal has much the appearance of black Wedgewood,; and is susceptible of the same amount of polish. Statues I and bas-reliefs of any size can be cast with accuracy, and the finest work, such as the plate of a steel engraving or the carving of a Chinese card.case, can be exactly repro- duced. Its capability of withstanding exposure to the wea- ther renders it very suitable for the decoration of architec- ture.—elcademy. Coen ic SOUTH AFRICA.—We have on former occasions referred to the mineral resources of Natal. It now appears that rich carboniferous deposits exist also in the Cape Colony. Two large companies have recently been formed in that colony for the development of its coalfields. Recent examinations by competent geologists have proved that the Stormberg range of mountains on the eastern frontier of the colony contains an almost boundless quantity of coal of ex- cellent qualfty, the careful development of which would make the colony independent of the supplies of coal now imported from England. For some years past the coal-mines at Molteno and Paardekraal have been worked with most successful results. As at present worked, the Molteno mine consists of a circular hill, from the summit of which a shaft has been sunk, while a heading has been driven from one side of the hill, opening up rich coal seams, which ap- parently pass right through the hill, and are estimated to contain at least 500,000 tons of coal. The Paardekraal mine, adjoining, covers an area of over 6,000 acres, with a main seam of coal measuring 2 feet 6 inches in thickness. A second fill, offering the same facilities for working as that already described, exists on this estate. The Molteno coal is already largely used in the town of Molten() both for household purposes and in some steam flour mills re- cently erected there. The Paardekraal coal is said to be in- ferior to the Molteno coal, especially as a steam-coal, while a third deposit of still finer quality is being opened up at Cyfergat, on aclosely adjoining farm, where another com- pany has beenformed to work th e mine. The Cyfergat coal was lately used in the manufacture of a large casting made from locally produced iron, and was pronounced equal to the best South Wales imported coal. All these mines will be in close connection with the new line of railway now being built to Molteno from East London. As besides coal, ironstone yielding a large percentage of metal is found in the neighbourhood of that town, a prosperous future seems to be in store for the district.—lron.

RE•COOKING OF MEAT.—There are the remains of a joint of underdone mutton in the house; one woman will cut this meat up into slices and put it into a saucepan, with the materials of making the hash, and boil all together till done. The result is that the meat is cooked twice, and eats like leather, and people say that they hate hash. Another woman will cut all the meat off the bone in nice slices, flour the meat, sprinkle with a little pepper and salt, and set aside. The bone she will then break into fragments, and boil it in water for two hours in a nice, clean saucepan. The vegetable or seasoning she will then fry in fat or but- ter till they are cooked fairly and nicely browned. She will then strain out all the fragments of bone (so that people can eat the hash without fracturing their teeth) from the stock, add th fried vegetables , and • lastly put in the meat. The whole will then be simmered for ten Minutes, so as just to warm the meat through, and carry the cooking of the underdone meat up to the proper point. Meanwhile some dipped toast will be made ready to set around the dish into which the hash is poured. Here, by attention to first prin- ciples, the remains of an underdone leg of roast mutton, in- stead of being spoiled for food and made disagreeable, are converted into a wholesome and delicious dish.

Charles Gerrish, a pauper, 70 years of age, was executed at Devizes, on Monday, for the murder of another pauper, named Coleman, in the Devizes Workhouse. At Wolverhampton, on Wednesday, Albert Perry, aged 12, was sent to prison for a month and to a reformatory for five years, for attempting to pull down a telegraph wire. Mr. Richard Brinsley Knowles, the only surviving son of Sheridan Knowles, died suddenly on Saturday morning, at his residence, North Bank, Regent's Park. Ile was 02 years of age. George Skillings, on Tuesday, pleaded guilty at the C3ntral Criminal Court, to feloniously assaulting girls at his wife's school at Leyton, and was sentenced to 18 months' impri- sonment. _

THE LAND QUESTION.
XVIII.

Every school boy knows that the United Kingdom con- I sists of Great Britain and Ireland, the Isle of Man, and the Channel Islands and it is also a matter of history that the latter are the only parts of the Dukedom of Normandy now belonging to the English Crown, to which they have been attached since the Conquest. They are five in number, Jusey, Guernsey, Alderney, Sark, and Rents, the three latter being small. When Philip Augustus, King of France, conquered Normandy from our King John, he met with a vigorous resistance from the inhabitants of these Islands, who were finally assisted by an English force, and since that time in recognition of their loyalty, although belonging to the British Crown, they have always enjoyed a species of Home Rule and the privilege of making their own laws. Like Normandy proper they were formerly largely subject to a feudal system, bat when they were separated from the Duchy most of the nobles who had property in the Islands threw in their lot with the French, and their manors in the Islands were confiscated by King John. There remained only four important manors in private hands which retained, and retain to this day, the privileges of primogeniture and other feudal rights. The rest of the land was and remains still subject to the old customary law of Normandy, which applied only to common people, and is very similar to the present land laws of Franco. The Right Hon. G. Shaw- Lefevre, M.P., in his very interesting article in the Fort- nightly Review of October, 1879, speaking of the land sys- tem of the Channel Islands, tells us that the island law aims at division of landed property, and is opposed to its accu- mulation. On the death of the owner of land, his property must be divided among the children in a certain proportion and there is no power of disposing of it by will if there be children. The eldest son has, however, a certain slight ad- vantage, he gets the principal house and two acres of land. The remainder is divided in the proportion of three-fifths equally among the daughters, but with a further provision that a daughter's share is not to be larger than a son's share. The widow, however, receives the income of one-third for her life, and as her right of dower to all landed property belonging to her husband at the time of marriage is inde- feasible, the necessity for marriage settlements is avoided. Till the year 1851 no land could be subjeet to a testamen- tary devise, but a law was then passed permitting the devise of land which has been Acquired by the testator provided he has no children, and in respect of inherited land, provided there be no descendants of the original purchaser. Entails are not permitted, and there are also a few unimportant pe- culiarities which need not be mentioned here. Suffice it to say that the whole system greatly favours the distribution and division of property. Practically the principle of corn- pnlsory heritage which prevails throughout a great part of the Continent of Europe, 'and under which land roust be ap- portioned among the children, prevails also in the Channel Islands, subject to a very slight advantage in favour of the eldest son.

Mr. Mitchell Henry, M.P., writing to a Dublin news- paper, protests against the hideous folly of the Parnellite obstruction, and asks the Irish people if they would, in a Parliament of their own, allow a small minority to trample on the rights and self-respect of the majority. It has been ascertained by means of chemical experiments made in Portsmouth dockyard, that xerotine siccative is in all essential particulars highly inflammable benzoline. The Admiralty are now considering the utility of experimenting upon a closed tank in the dockyard on a dock becoming dis- engaged, in order adequately to test its explosive qualities. At the Cornwall assizes, on Tuesday, Charles Luke, a gentleman of position, was sued by the father of Clara Harris, a young lady of 19, for loss of service occasioned by a breach of promise of marriage, aggravated by seduction. The defendant's father left £lOO,OOO divisible amongst his sons, and the plaintiff was manager of the estate. A ver- dict for £550 was accepted. Shortly before midnight on Saturday a slater of Chester- field, named Goddard, went home in a state of intoxication and kicked his wife in so brutal a manner that the poor woman, who fled to a neighbour's house for assistance, died in a short time from the injuries she had received. A coro- ner's jury on Monday returned a verdict of manslaughter in the case. At Wigan, on Monday, a collier named Jas. Dickenson was committed for trial on a charge of murdering Joseph Pemberton, another collier. The men quarrelled at a public house over a lark singing contest, and it is alleged that the prisoner enticed the deceased outside, and then kicked him and injured him so seriously that he died three days after- wards. THE HORNSEY RAILWAY ACCIDENT.—At an inquest held on Saturday by Dr. Danford Thomas into the deaths of the two persons killed in the Hornsey accident on Wednesday week, the jury were of Opinion that the driver of the Barnet train was guiity of great neglect of duty in driving his train so fast through the fog as to be unable to pull up in time to avert the accident. They also drew the attention of the Board of Trade to a rule on that subject in the Great Nor- thern Railway Code, which they considered not sufficiently definite. THE LEFROY REWARD.—Sir Wm. Harcourt has granted Mrs. Bickers, the landlady with whom Lefroy lodged, the sum of .E2O for the losses she has sustained in having to remove from her house at Stepney, in consequence of her other lodgers leaving her, and the expenses incurred in her removal. It seems an unpleasant notoriety has followed her to her new home, and she cannot let her rooms. The public believed that she had received a portion of the reward, but this is not the case, the solicitor's clerk having been paid floe £2OO, the whole of which he has kept. A copference of the promoters of the Land Nationalisation Society was held on Tuesday, at Westminster Palace Hotel. Mr. Alfred Russell Wallac,, F.R.G.S., presided, and con- tended that the entire interest in the land of the country, as distinguished from tenant-right, should p ,ss to the State by means of a general law which would secure all existing landowners and their heirs revenues equal to the annual value of the laud apart from tenant-right. A resolution to

this effect was adopted. THE BRADFORD FENIAN PLOT.—On Monday, at Bradford, James Fitzpatrick, an Irishman, was committed for six months for assaulting two policemen last July. John 'robin, who is awaiting his trial at the Leeds Assizes for complicity in the Fenian plot, was concerned in the same assault, and absconded to Middlesborough. Col. Pollard, presiding magistrate, said he was not in favour of magis- trates having the power to order flogging, but this was a case in which the prisoner ought to have 25 lashes. COMMITTAL OF MR. J. NICOL FLEMING.—On Wednesday afternoon Mr. J. Nicol Fleming was committed for trial on the charge of having on various occasions during 1874 and 1875 falsified the books of the City of Glasgow Bank, by making or causing to be made false entries, so as to conceal or misrepresent the true state of affairs from the share- holders and others. It is said that an application for bail will be made, and it is understood that the highest sum which can be fixed is £6OO.

In addition to this the process of transfer of land by regis- tration is simple and popular. Mr. Arthur Arnold, M.P., illustrates this in his book entitled "Free Land," as fol- lows : —"I had the pleasure of meeting one of the largest proprietors in the island (Jersey) ; his immense property, for such it seems to most Jerseymen, is 300 vergoes, more than 100 acres in extent. He told me that he thought his expenses for the purchase of that land (which cost £8,000) rather high, and he added that the amount was under Five Pounds. He said, and his statement was confirmed by others, that in the purchase of property worth £5OO all costs would not exceed One Pound. He showed me his deeds.' A Jerseyman has no fear that his parchments are the records of forgery, nor is his rest troubled as to their custody. He does not, like the less happy Englishman, leave his deeds' with his solicitor, with the knowledge that there will be costs attending upon every application concerning those documents. A Jerseyman's 'deeds' are worth threepence per 100 words, just so much and no more. He would have no objection to your throwing them on the fire, if you will take the trouble to call at the registrar's office and pay for new copies, which, upon his application, will be given to you readily and with much courtesy." What is the effect in these Islands of Primogeniture being so very limited in its operation, the prohibition of Entails, the subdivision of the land, and the inexpensive and expe- ditious mode of transfer. They believe in their own land system as very much preferable to ours, and contend that it is the cause of their thrifty, industrious, frugal habits, and the consequent wealth and prosperity of the Channel Islands. In Falle's History of Jersey we find the following eulogium of their special land system : "If the descent of property had been regulated here as in England, the island would long ago have become the property of a few powerful families, which would have left no intermediate class between the large landlord and the dependent rackrenter. It is to the land laws that we owe the substantial Jersey freeholders who are at once the boast and the protection of the country. . . . Under this sys- tem the country has flourished. Perhaps no population anywhere possesses collectively a greater aggregate of wealth, at the same time that there is scarcely any other place where a population of equal numbers could show so few very splendid fortunes. The system corrects itself. Where the shares are small the younger children do not think of farming them, but sell them to the elder brother for money or rents, and go into business. It is therefore so far from being correct that estates are reduced almost te nothing, that very few indeed could be found which are ma- terially reduced by partitions, and none whose relative agri- cultural produce is affected by them." The area of all five islands is not more than 50,000 acres, of which nearly one•third is irreclaimable. The population in 1871 was 90,56,3, or relatively about three times more numerous than that of the Isle of Wight. In Jersey the population is 57,000, of whom 30,000 reside in the town of §t. Helier, leaving 27,000 as the rural popu- lation. Its cultivated land does not exceed 20,000 acres, and there are 2,500 owners of land, with an average of about eight acres each. These for the most part cultivate their own property, and probably one-half of the heads of families in the rural districts are in this position. In the parish of St. Peter, which is a purely rural district, consisting of 3,030 acres, there is a population oe 2,150 or 530 families, and there are 404 persons registered as ownera of land or " rentes."

MISSION SERVICE IN A COALPIT.—On Wednesday noon the Rev. George Noel Storrs, vicar of Holy Trinity Church, Bridlington, who is conducting a special mission at Tanker- sley parish church, visited the Parkgate pit of the Wharn- cliiTe Silkstone Collieries, and de:ivered an impressive address to the miners underground before they were raised to the bank. About 300 men and boys are employed in the workings, so that there was a large and novel congregation to listen to the preacher's remarks. Mr. Gladstone on Tuesday received a large deputation from the Central and Associated Chambers of Agriculture on the subject of local taxation, and said most of the points raised had for some time past been receiving tho most care- ful and laborious attention of the Government, and the time was near at hand when their views on the matter would be submitted in a regular and practical manner. It was a sub- ject to which he had for some time past devoted close atten- tion, and would continue to do so for some time to come. THE LIBERATION SOCIETY.—A great meeting of support- ers of the Liberation Society was held on Tuesday night in the Free Trade Hall, Manchester, Mr. Hugh Mason, M.P., presiding. The Chairman, in his speech, said they did not I intend to press the question of disestablishment upon the Government in an impetuous or hasty manner. They could ' hide their time until public opinion continued to ripen upon it. Amongst the resolutions was one affirming that the ques- tion was sufficiently advanced in the public mind to entitle it the next Parliament to come within the sphere of prac- tical polities. EXTRORDINARY CONFESSION AT A SALVATION Artery MEETING.—Hannah Froggatt, a middle-aged woman, was charged before the Nottingham magistrates on Monday, on her own confession, with poisoning a female child, two veers old, entrusted to her to nurse at Sheffield, by repeated doses of laudanum. The prisoner attended the Salvation Army meeting on Sunday night, and on leaving gave herself up, in order, she said, to ease her mind. The crime is said to •have been committed at the time of the great flood. She was remanded for inquiries. ARMED BURGLAR.—Another London burglar who carried on his professim with the aid of a revolver has been cap- tured. Two policemen on duty at Claptoa, on Wednesday, saw two men attempting to break into a house. They attempted to arrest th 2 robbers, who ran away, and on being pursued threatened to shoot the officers. A third constable joined in the chase, and one of the burglars, Hy. Frauklen, tired at him, the ball grazing his arm and ripping up the sleeve from the cuff to the shoulder. The constable pluckily closed with the burglar and secured him,and his confederate was shortly afterwards arrested. THE RETFORD MURDER : SENTENCE OF DEATH.—At Not- tingham assizes on Tuesday, Herbert Snell, aged 17, was charged with the wilful murder of George Hardy, a farmer, at North Wheatley, near Retford, on Sunday evening, the 6th November. The deceased was found lying dead in the corn yard, with two stabs through his head, and a broken- pronged fork lying near him. Suspicion fell upon the prisoner, who had frequently quarrelled with his master, and on beim..' charged with the crime he admitted it. The jury returned a verdict of "Wilful murder," and Mr. Justice Hawkins sentenced the prisoner to death. The jury strongly recommended him to mercy. ANOTHER DREADFUL RAILWAY ACCIDENT IN NORTH LONDON.—The North London Railway has again been the scene of a lamentable accident. On Saturday night the draw- bar of a wagon which formed part of a long train of "empties " broke near Old Ford station. The bar was driven firmly into the ground for a part of its length, but not so far as to clear the axles of the following wagons. These dashed against the protrudilig bar, and were thrown off the line. Just at that moment, whilst the metals were blocked with a mass of debris, a passenger train came up on the other line from Broad-street, and dashed into the obstruction. The result was that several carriages were wrecked, and three women, a baby, and a man were taken out of the ruins dead. The baby was clasped to the breast of its dead mother. The fatalities were confined. to a telescoped third-class carriage in front of the train. The passengers in the other carriages escaped with comparatively slight injuries, and it was not found necessary to take any of them to the hospital. A Beard of Trade inquiry was held on Monday by Colonel Yolland, and a coroner's inquiry was also held, when a ver- dict of Accidental death" was returned.

Where the bulk of the farmers own the land they culti- vate, and stand in no fear of an increase of rent, or a notice to quit, forfeiting their improvements like our English farmers, we may expect good cultivation, and it is to be found in these Islands. Although the climate and soil are no better than many districts in the South of England, the amount of agricultural produce is wonderful. In Jersey alone upwards of 4,000 acres are planted with early pota- toes, at a cost of cultivation of ten of £4O an acre, and the produce is said to be worth £300,000 in good years. One farmer who was visited by Mr. Arthur Arnold, M.P., had spent £lB an acre on stable manure and guano in preparing for his "new" potatoes, and had a crop of 51 tons per acre. He had also got 50 bushels per acre of wheat by good culti- vation, though the average in Jersey is about 371 i bushels per acre. Mr. Thornton tells us that each peasant proprie- tor does all that ingenuity and labour can to turn every square foot of his little estate to the best account. Every scrap and corner of it, and what they are producing, and what they can be made to produce next year, or a dozen years hence, are constantly mapped in his mind's eye. This little bit of grass land will support a few apple trees. The apples before long will be ripening above the grass. Before his potatoes are out of the ground, beet or brocoli is set be- tween the rows. No leaf of this beet or brocoli will rot on the plant, but as soon as it has done its duty to its parent will be culled for the cow. The cow will supply milk and butter and cheese for the market. Cows and pigs and poultry are each kept in part as save ails, and all alike for the market." The prevalent idea in England is that small farming could not be successful for want of machinery, but in the Channel Islands the farmers hire a steam threshing machine, and if. two want it on the same day, it goes to the farm nearest to its then situation, and as to the men required to assist while the machine is ati;work, the farmers help one another. When farms are small there is not much land wasted on fences, and the practice in the Channel Islands, from whence we get the well-known Alderneys, is not to turn the cows into a big pasture field, as with us. No, a rope is fastened round the cow's horns, and secured by an ,iron spike driven into the ground, which enables the farmer , to manage without fences, and he contends that a cow sol tetnered will do as well upon one-fourth the quantity of grass which would be required if she roamed at large, and so destroyed a part of the herbage. When she has cropped her circle, she is moved. A larger etock, therefore, is kept in proportion to the acreage than on English farms. The farm houses and buildings are equally satisfactory under this system of small ownerships. Small but most comfortable farm houses are spread over the whole country, at short distances from one another. The walls are often completely hidden by rose trees, geraniums, and myrtles, which reach up to the ledge of the roof, and form an arch over the door. They are always substantially built of stone, and being generally of two storeys, contain plenty of accommodation. Except a few fisherman's huts there is not a house at all like the wretched cottages of many of our agri- cultural labourers described by the Bishop of Manchester and his colleagues. The people live well and dress well, and all who have visited the Islands concur in the all important statement that there is 'eery little pauperism. The Rev. F. B. Zincke, in an article in the Fortnightly Review for January, 1876, gives an interesting description of the Channel Islands, and writes as follows :—" The in- dustry, sagacity, thrift, and intelligence of their inhabitants are very remarkable, and may, I think, be traced directly to the wide diffusion among them of property in land. We have, within a few hours steaming of our own shore, living under the English Oren, a population more self-respecting, intelligent, enterprising, and generally well-to-do than any equal number on an equal space anywhere else in the United Kingdom. . . My belief is that they could not have attained to their present position if they had had our land laws."

The rent, too, ranges from LI per acre for poor land to £lO or £l2 for good land, being four times as high as in England. The population of these Islands is nearly three times as dense, relatively to acreage, as that of England and Wales, while the proportion of the population employed in agricul- ture is still larger, beity, estimated at one cultivator to every four acres in Jersey andGuerrsey. 2. At last, in 1793, a Relief Bill admit - thp hpatholics to the elective franchise was introduced a ein tne esover rnent, and after a warm debate was carried. %e tate,. s-ourse of the discussion Grattan made the following ItSt'ent of the case:—" The situation of the Roman Catho- sert4a reducible to four propositions. They are three- :ll2:ooatvu;flt:roeur people,paying their pro 0 "DO of r taxes; without any share in the repres_entation portion of near ; they pay your Church establishment with o (o)llteteah 0 ;ellfrei,buuttaionnuf:atehtue:fe. discharge the active and laoore husbandry and commerce, with- tlostryo,sa_ franchoe' es which are annexed to the fruits ff in- Coaut,tsis.ond they replenish your armies and navies without n' rank, 01 reward. Under time circumstanced

and under the further recommendation of total and entire oolitical separation from any foreign Prince or Pretender, they desire to be admitted to the franchise of the Constitu- tion." While supporting the Government Act Grattan com- plained of its imperfection. The admission of the Roman Catholics to Parliament was its necessary compliment, and by one bold measure the Ministers might .have set the ques- tion at rest for ever. The measure of 1793 conferred politi- cal power on the uneducated masses, while it retained the disqualification of the educated few. We pass over a few Sessions of the Irish Parliament in which Grattan, Ponsonby, and others endeavoured to reform the Constitution. But it was too late. The tide of corrup- tion had already set in, bearing all before it. The Irish rulers were to use Grattan's words, "a set of men possess- ing themselves of civil, military, and ecclesiastical authority, and using it with the fixed and malignant intention to cor- rupt the morals in order to undermine the freedom of the people." Ponsonby declared that at this time "there were one hundred and ten placemen in the House of Commons, and that one-eighth of the revenue of the country was di- vided between members of Parliament." Amidst this corrup- tion Grattan's voice was like the voice of one crying in the wilderness. One more effort, however. did Grattan make in this Parlia, ment to carry Catholic Emancipation. The excitement among the Catholics of the country was intense. Lord Fitz- william had warned the Gemernment that "to disappoint the hopes of the Catholics would be to raise a flame in the country that nothing but the force of arms could keep down." But the boon was denied. Grattan failed to carry his motion, and a sullen, menacing disloyalty overspread the land, creeping, in his own words, like "the mist at the heels of the countrymen." It was clear that the end and aim of the Government in Ireland was to perpetuate the power of a faction which was subservient to its policy, being always hostile to the country and the people, and with its aid to break down the national spirit and independence of the , nation. Its policy was to divide, and govern by division— to keep alive and foment religious dissensions—to promote the interests of a selfish minority while affecting to ignore its sordid views and to be unconscious of the hypocrisy that was covered but not concealed by the mask of an ardent zeal for religions interests; to bestow all State honours, patron- age, and protection on that small section of the country which Lord Stanley (the late Lord Derby) in one of his fit- ful moods was pleased to call "the remnant of an expiring faction." No wonder that against such a Government the people should indulge in hostile feelings. Everywhere in Ireland spread the spirit of discontent and. disloyalty. Higher and still higher surged the revolutionary tide. Daring the December of '96 and the early Months of '97, several dis- tricts of Ulster were proclaimed under the Insurrection Act. The terrible reign of martial law had commenced. General Lake was dragooning the people. Vainly Grattan uttered eloquent protests in behalf of Justice and Reform, and main- tained that the Government severities only increased the influence of the United Irishmen. At last, despairing of obtaining any good for Ireland from such a Government and from a Parliament so constituted, he announced his determi- nation to retire from political strife in these words :—" We have offered you our measure, you will reject it. We depre- cate yours, you will persevere. Having no hopes left to persuade or dissuade, and having discharged our duty, we shall trouble you no more, and after this day shall not at- tend the House of Commons." At the next General Elec- tion Grattan and Lord Henry Fitzgerald refused to allow themselves to be elected for Dublin. Curran, Arthur O'Conner, and Lord Edward Fitzgerald adopted a similar course. When Tone heard of this secession, he observed in his Journal—" I see those illustrious Patriots are at last forced to bolt out of the House of Commons and come amongst the people, as John Keogh advised Grattan to do long since." Arthur O'Conner and Lord Edward Fitzgerald speedily joined the United Irishmen, but Grattan, Curran, and Lord Henry Fitzgerald kept aloof from them. Accor- dingly while some like O'Connell blame them for seceding at all, others blame them because having taken this step they didn't go further and join the United Irishmen. But surely it is difficult to find any cause for blame. If they had. joined the United Irishmen they would probably have found them- selves in Newgate, as O'Conner and Lord Edward soon after did. Besides they were not Republicans, and abhorred French principals as earnestly as Lord Clare himself. Grattan had found it impossible to cope with the Government during this period of panic. He could not sympathise with the party who were appealing to arms, nor yet with those who had driven them to disloyalty, and so he took refuge in the Palace of the Silences.

LESSONS or THE STARS.—The distance between the farthest planet and the nearest star is twenty-one billions of miles. If we could travel as fast as light travels, we should gb round the world four hundred andeight times in a minute; and yet, travelling at the same rate, it would take us three years and seven mouths to get to that nearest star. The distance of Sirius is so great that it would require a journey of twenty-two years to reach it. There is another star, visible by the naked eye, so far away that we could not cover the distance in less than seventy-two years. Travel- ling at the same rate, it would take seven hundred thousand years to visit the group, remote and cloudlike, which Sir William Herschell discovered with his telescope. As these distant stars send their light down to us through the im- measurable space which intervenes, they serve to enlarge and rectify our ideas of magnitude, and to preserve us from un- due impressions of the greatness of near and present things. —From The Quiver for February. ARE EARLY MARRIAGES UNTHRIFTY P—My opponent declares that young people begin life in debt; try to live in the style their fathers did; do not consider ways and means, and laugh at the necessity for p-oviding for unforeseen ex- penses: therefore, early marriages are unthriftY. Does he not rather mean that such conduct is unthrifty ? If that is his opinion, I entirely agree with him, and, moreover, I maintain that people who could behave in such an improvi- dent manner under any circumstances would get into diffi- culties no matter what their position. Married people become nnited in thought, purpose, and feeling not through fellowship in pleasure and ease, but through fellowship in work, endeavour, and, it may be, suffering. Young people are unthrifty in the broadest sense when from motives of false prudence they fling away their chances of making their marriage a blessed union, -for they run the risk of wasting life and happinessior the sake of that which is most excel- lent when regarded as a means to something beyond, but which is worthless as an end ha itself—a good income.— Extract from "A Speech in the Family Parliament," in :Cassell's .Magazine for February. • How THE FLY WALKs.—The fly's apparatus for walking and holding on may be thus summed up :—On a rough sur- face the insect appears to use its claws 6nly ; on glass, or on a ceiling, three processes are brought into action—first, the "al mosc, infinite "number of hairs are pressed down on the ' smooth surface; a peculiar movement of the bristles then expels all the air from between or beneath the hair-like ' cushion; lastly, a fluid is poured out round the base of the entire hair-pad, and the expelled air is thus prevented from entering. A vacuum, is in this manner secured and main- tained so long as may be necessary. When the fly wishes to move, the 'flap, firmly pressed down on the glass, must be first raised, and this is accomplished by the hooked claws which lift up the edges of the tllin hair-pad, and thus let in the air and destroy the vaccuum. The movement of the claws in this process is very i:oculiar. Some notion of it may thus be gained :—Let a reader suppose that a sucker is fixed to the tip of his little finger, and that this sucker be- comes fastened to a table by atmospheric pressure; let him else imagine the tip of his thumb to be armed with a num- ber of fine hooks. He will be able to lift the edges of the little finger sucker by these thumb hooks, and thus the air will be admitted under the sucker. Somewhat after. this fashion does the fly loosen its foot from a surface of glass.— From " Recreative Natural History " in Cassell's Popular Educator for February. TirE r OUTRAGESVN JEWS Pis RUSSIA..—The Martsion Hous meeting to protest against the outrages on Jews in Russia was held on Wednesday afternoon under the presidency of the Lord Mayor of London. The attendance was so large that many members of Parliament and others who bad been specially invited were unable to enter the hall in which the meeting was held. Several letters of apology for inability to attend were read. The Archbishop of Canterbury sent Canon Farrar as his representative to express the horror with which he contemplated the disgrace brought on the Christian name by those shameful persecutions. The Bishop of Manchester stated that the outrages had aroused in his breast the liveliest feelings of pity and indignation, and he urged that the Goverr. ment of Russia owes it to the place it occupies in Christian Europe to extend the strong arm of its protection to the weak and helpless, and to repress with all the force at its com- mand acts of pillage and violence which one would have thought were only possible in some bygone age of barbarism. The speakers at the meeting included the Earl of Shaftes- bury, the Bishop of London, Cardinal Manning, Canon Farrar, Professor Bryce, and the Hon. Lyulph Stanley. Resolutions condemning the action of Russia to the Jews were passed. One of them' moved by Cardinal Manning, declared that "the laws of Russia relating to Jews tend to disgrace them in the eyes of the Christian population, and to expose Jeulsh subjects to the outbreaks of fanatical ignorance." The Lord Mayor was empowered to present the resolutions to Mr. Gladstone and Lord Granville, "in the hope that Her Majesty's Government may be able when an opportunity arises to exercise a friendly influence on the Russian Government."

TIIE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 4, 1882.

THE STATE OF IRELAND. The Right Hon. W. E. Forster, M.P., Chief Secretary for Ireland, arrived in London on Saturday from Dublin. A telegram from Paris contradicts a report that the Irish Land League funds are invested in the Union General. Mr. James Carey, of Currah House, Queen's County,was arrested on Wednesday, under the Protection Act, and seat te Naas Gaol. It is stated that on the acceptance of the resignation of :Sir. A. M. Sullivan, Dr. Kenny, now in Kilmainham, will be put forward for County Meath. A circular has been issued to the members of the Irish Parliamentary Party, asking them to meet at the offices in Westminster on the 6th February. Near Callan, county Kilkenny, on Saturday, a man named Neill, when walking home with his wife, suddenly att.cked and brutally murdered her. He was arrested, and on Monday committed for trial. A conditional order was granted by the Dublin Queen's Bench, on Wednesday, for the release of several members of the Ladies' Land League, imprisoned in default of finding bail to keep the peace. Large number of troops reached Ireland on Monday by special steamer from this country, and during the day there was almost a constant removal of soldiers thaough the streets of Dublin. Orders have been issued for a fresh distribution of the troops in Ireland. A novel notice has been posted on the walls of Mullagh and Kilrnurry. It consists of a threat of death to the far- mers who allow their children to get married under any cir- cumstances until the suspects are released. Young ladies are warned not to speak to police who have aided landlords in evicting tenants. Mr. Gladstone, writing to a correspondent who had ad- vised the release of the suspects, says that as they were im- prisoned because they had both the will and the power to do mischief to the cause of law and order, and as they refuse to give pledge for their good behaviour, the Government has no alternative but to carry out its painful duty. Some remarkable reductions of rent were made by the sub- commissioners sitting in Cork on Tuesday. In the case of one form on Lord Egmont's property, they reduced the rent from £B4 to £33, and in a number of other cases on this and other properties they made reductions of from 45 to 20 per cent.

IL is stated that with a view to mark its sense of the fora- aide and courage displayed by all ranks of the Royal Irish Constabulary during the protracted Land League campaign the Government intend to move for a substantial addition to the pay of this body of men when order is re-established in Ireland. A letter is published from Mr. Dillon, M.P., to Mr. Forster, refusing to avail himself of the offer of release from Kil- mainham on condition that he goes to the Continent. He declines, under all circumstances, to enter into any condi- tion with the Government, and concludes by requesting Mr. Forster to address to him no further communication on the subject. A Renter's Washington telegram reports that the House of Representatives, on Tuesday, adopted the resolution recently reported back from the Foreign Relations Committee, re- questing President Arthur to obtain a list of the American citizens now confined in English prisons. Some members spoke in condemnation of Mr. Robinson's proposal that the United States Government should demand their release. THE LOUGH MASH TRAGEDY.—The bodies of Lord Ardilaun's bailiff Hurdy and his nephew were discovered in the centre of Lough Mask by the use of dynamite cartridges, the explosion of which in the Lough brought up the bodies. A man named Kerrigan has been arrested. It is stated that the police were informed of the crime by an old woman,svho saw a number of men row out into the lake and drop into the water two large and heavy bags. In Kerrigan's house the police.have found traces of the dreadful crime, which, there is little reason to doubt, was committed within it. Import- ant information is in the hands of the police, and 15 arrests were made during Saturday and Sunday nights of persons living near where the murder was perpetrated. MR. HERBERT GLADSTONE ON THE SITUATION. -- Mr. Herbert Gladstone. M.P., writing from Dublin on the 25th of January to Mr. James Kitson, jun., president of the Leeds Liberal Association, says:—" I hope and believe that when Parliament meets it will be possible to show that there is a slight but distinct improvement in the state of the country. Rents have been coming in, and although the landlords are now beginning to show more energy in taking advantage of the help that the Government has all along offered them in enforcing their rights, outrages have to some extent decreased. Meanwhile our political opponents, while solemnly passing hollow resolutions declaring their intention to support the Government in restoring the rule of law, which has in some parts of Ireland been in abeyance since April, 1879, are doing everythin,g they can to discredit the Government and bring about it downfall." Archbishop Croke complains (in a letter to the Irish Times) that whilst the emigrant ships are filled with the flower of the' agricultural districts,—" virtuous and able- bodied 'young men and women who really are and should ne looked upon as their country's best wealth and pride,"—there are plenty of both men and women in the large towns whose removal to distant countries, "however discredieable it may be under some respects to the land of their birth," would not be regrettable, but who steadily refuse to emigrate, and "cling with the utmosttenacity to their wicked associations." The Archbishop is, however, of opinion that Ireland is big and fruitful enough to support all her children, and therefore he will never be a party to the systematic expatriation of any "useful portion of her people." Apart, however, from ,this consideration, he is emphatically opposed to emigration on "purely religious or spiritual grounds." Irishmen,he holds. "can, and do attend to their religious duties in Ireland better than elsewhere: and it must therefore be in the long run the best place for them to live in, as it is assuredly the safest place for them wherein to die."

_ DARESRURY PETTY SESSIONS. TIIESDAY.—Before Messrs. E. Greenall cud R. Pierpoint. ALLEGED ATTEMP rTO SHOOT A SOLICIT° E,.—T hOmas Cook, a wire drawer, was charged with having made use of threats towards Mr. Percy Davies, calculated to provoke a breach of the peace; and also with having unlawfully and wantonly fired a gun on the highway.—The complainant is a solicitor, practising in Warrington. On Sunday, the 15th January, he was walking with his brother, and accompanied by his dog, from Stockton Heath to Latchford, on the towing path of the canal. Near the footbridge at Wash-lane, he noticed a number of men, two of whom carried guns, and after he had proceeded about 75 yards he heard a gun dis- charged. Then he saw the shot strike the towing path and the water in the canal, about 12 yards ahead of him. He considered .he had had a narrow escape of being shot, ani he turned round, when a roar of laoghter came from the men, as if the shooting had been done for a joke. He re- turned to the men and asked for an explanation. One of the men said they had only been shooting at a rat across the canal, but that could not be the case as the shot would have gone in a direction directly at right angles to that which it did. Mr. Davies asked defendant if he had fired the gun, when he used most insulting and threatening language, saying he would split his (Mr. Davies) head. Not liking to risk his life, Mr. Davies told the defendant he would summons him and walked awly. The same afternoon P.C. Bowen took the defendant to the police station, and he then denied having been out with his gun, and said he had never seen Mr. Davies.—Complainant said he hid no wish , to press the case, but desired the defendant to be bound . over.—Defendant pleaded guilty to the charges, and said he . was only trying to shoot a few small birds. He was very sorry for what he had said to Mr. Davies.—He was bound L over to keep the peace for six months on the first charge; • , and on the second he was fined ss. and costs; total

£1 15s. ed. THE FOWL ROBBERY AT GRA.PfENRALL.—Wm. Bowers, ferryman at Thelwall, was brought up, on remand, charged with stealing a cock fowl, the property of Thomas Savage, from the Barry Arms, Grappenhall.—:The prisoner, on the 23rd January, went to the Barry Arms to borrow the prose- cutor's horse, but his request not being granted, be stayed in the inn the whole of the afternoon. He cut some hay for the prosecutor, who told him he might take away a few carrots. At 7 o'clock, as he was leaving the house with a parcel under his arm, the prosecutor met him, and being suspicious, examined the parcel, which was found to con- tain a cock with its head and feet cut off.—Mr. Moore, who appeared for the prisoner, said he bad been guilty of an in- discretion, hut not of felony, and explained that whilst the prisoner was cutting the hay for the prosecutor, the cock walked into the room, and he accidentally kicked it and broke one of its legs. In order to "put it out of its misery" he then killed it with his knife. He did not attempt to con- ceal what ha had done but at once walked into the house.— Prisoner was fined 10s. and 16s. costs.

ANOTHER. ALLEGED MISCARRIAGE OF JCSTICE. Since the release of the Staffordshire farmers, Clowes and Johnson, public attention has been called to the case of Amelia Jordan, ho four years ago was sentenced to 14 years penal servi- tude by Lord Justice Cockburn, at Lewes assizes, on a charge of stealing a box of jewels, valued at about £lOO, the pro- perty of the daughter of Colonel Lane, Broadoak, Boxhall, Sussex, in whose service she was as upper housemaid. It appears that Jordan who was about 20 years of age, and had borne an excellent Character, left her master's house on Wed- nesday evening, December sth, 1877, at half-past six, to go to church, leaving her young mistress, Miss Alice Lane in her bedroom. At about ten minutes to eight, a fire was dis- covered in this room, Miss Lane having iben gone out, and in the confusion the jewel box disappeared. It was shown that the box was on the table during the fire, for there was a mark on the white tablecloth, around which the smoke had left stains where the box had stood. Jordan was taxed with the matter next day, and taking umbrage at the implied charge, she left for her father's home in London. She was, however, arrested at Croydon, and brought back, having been searched before leaving Boxhill and auain at Croydon. She was charged with stealing some trifling articles, and .dis- charged by the jury at Lewes. Six weeks afterwards the jewels were found in the basin of the watercloset at C oydon station, and she was rearrested, and sentenced at Lewes assizes on March 8 following, as above mentioned. The evidence showed that she could not have bten connected with the firing of the room, and other circumstances have induced the inhabitants of Hastings and district to petition the Home Secretary to institute an inquiry into the case, as they believe Jordan has been the victim of a miscarriage of justice. The memorial bases its prayer upon the belief that all the facts of the case were not set clearly before the jury; that seven of the jury subsequently petitioned for a remis- sion of sentence • that the jewels were not discovered until six weeks after they disappeared; and that the prisoner was searched on the day of the robbery at Croydon station, where they were found; and upon other points in the prisoner's favour. •

FRANCE.—TRE NEW MINISTRY. 'lle Ministerial crisis in France has been terminated by the appointment of a new Ministry, with M. de Freycinat as President of the Council. The following is a list of the new Cabinet as now con- stituted :—M. de Freycinet, President of Council and Min- ister for Foreign Affairs ; M. Leon Say, Minister of Finance; M. Jules Ferry, Public Instruction ; M, Goblet, Interior and Public Worship: M. Humbert, Justice; General Billot, War; Admiral Jaureguiberry, Marine; M. Tirard, Commerce and Agriculture; M. Varrov, Public Works; M. Cochery, Post and Telegraphs. A Paris correspondent says great satis- faction is caused by the composition of the new Ministry, and nearly all the Parisian journals speak favourably of the new Cabinet. On the commencement of proceedings in the Chamber of Deputies on Monday, M. Gambetta took his seat among the members of the Left. M. Rouyicr, late Minister of Com- merce, brought in a bill for the prolongation for three I months of the existing treaties with foreign countries. M. Lebaudy afterwards read the report of the committee on Commercial Treaties, which recommended that the Govern- ment should be authorised to prolong existing treaties until March 31st, and that this prolongation might, if desired, be extended until May 15th in the case of those Powers which had already signed the treaties or which should sign them before March 31st. The Chamber then adopted the bill in the sense of the Committee's reports. PARts, Tuesday.—ln the Chamber of Deputies to-day M. de Freycinet read a declaration of the policy of the new Cabinet. After affirming that the Government would spare no effort to secure peace at home and abroad, and would up- hold the cause of liberty and progress, M. de Freycinet mentioned among the measures contemplated a bill for sanctioning the right of association whilst maintaining the rights of the State. The question of the revision of the constitution would be postponed until the expiration of the present Legislature. The Premier announced also the in- troduction of Judical and military reforms, including the reduction of term of compulsory service in the army to three years. Nothing woula be neglected in order to arrive at a definite solution of the customs tariffs. The House after- wards adopted a bill authorising the prolongation of the

• treaties of commerce. FAILURE OF THE UNION GENERALE.—A telegram from the capital on Monday evening says that the jfessayer de Paris announces that at the instance of the Board of Ad- ministration of the Union Generale, and in accordance with a petition presented by itself to the President of the Tribu- nal, a judical administrator of its affairs has been ap- pointed in the person of M. Hal. The Frangais says that the Union Generale, in presence of the claims lodged against it and in conformity with legal advice' thought it right to suspend its payments until the general meeting on Friday. The Corporation of Lyons Stockbrokers has been officially declared bankrupt. The suspension is due to a rupture with the Vienna Laende Bank, the Austrian Syndicate having refused an advance of seventy millions required by the Union Generale to meet engagements at the end of the month. An inquiry has been instituted by the authorities into the affairs of the bank. The cash reserve is only re- presented by 50,000 of its own shares, in which the company had been speculating, and these, of course, are depreciated. All the ready money appears to have been swept away, and a verification of the accounts shows a deficit 96,000,0001., although at a recent meeting the chairman announced that the company possessed securities of the value of 57,000,000. BURSTING OF A RESERVOIR AT CALMS.—A reservoir in Calais, containing upwards of 110,000 gallons, burst on Monday evening. The flood completely submerged and destroyed three houses, one of which was used as a school. Thirty seven bodies were recovered. GE RMATI" Y.—MONETARY FAILURES. The banker Roes, of Frankfort-on-the-Main, has shot himself on account of his losses. From Cologne comes the report of the fall of the banking house of Solf, which it is .said, has caused the Middle German Credit Bank a loss of £50,000. From Hamburg we learn of the :insolvency of Herr Warburg, with liabilities to the amount of £lOO,OOO. There have also been several failures at Brestau, including one for £30,000. At Munich likewise there have been bankruptcies owing to an interim settlement. The stock of the Petro- leum Industry Company at Oelheim, has been seized by the officers of the law for the benefit of the creditors.

SOUTH AMERICA. WASHINGTON, Monday.—Chilian peace conditions em- brace the absolute •cession by Peru of the Tarapaca district, together with the payment of a war indemnity of twenty millions of dollars by instalments spreading over 16 years, during which tittle Chili will occupy Arica. Chili is also to have the Lobos Island guano deposits. RUSSIA.—THE CZAR AND THE JEWS. VIENNA, Wednesday.—The Neue Freie Presse to-day states that a communication from Baron Gunzburg, the Russian banker, has been received at Cracow, according to which the Emperor Alexander does not approve the pro- posals made by the Commission of Inquiry into the causes of the anti-Semitic agitation, which were in favour of re- stricting the domiciliary proprietary rights of Jews, and has directed that the Israelite community shall be represented at the future deliberations of the Commission. GREAT GALE IN RUSSIA.—SUPPOSED LOSS OF 600 LIVES.

A St. Petersburg correspondent telegraphs :—A. terrible disaster has occurred at Astrakhan. The fishermen there are in the habit of going out in large parties to fish at the mouth of the Volga. Last week 600 of them were so en- gaged when a terrific gale caused the ice to break up, and it is feared that all have perished. The storm also passed over Moscow, where much damage was done. Many large trees were uprooted, and the roof of the new exhibition building was blown off. AUSTRIA.—THE SOUTHERN PROVINCES IN REVOLT. The Austrian and Hungarian Delegations held a special session on Saturday, at which Count Kalnoky, Minister of Foreign Affairs, introduced a bill for the extraordinary war credit of 8,000,000 florins for the suppression of the insur- rectionary movement in the south of the Monarchy. The bill was referred to a Committee. Committees are being formed in Bulgaria to promote a general South Slavonic in- surrection. The possibility of a war between Austria and Russia is spoken of in Bulgaria. Meanwhile the Austrian Government is making an immense effort to crush the in- surrection offhand. A contract has been signed with the Austrian Lloyd's Company for the transport of 30,000 men to South Dalmatian ports. Nine large steamers are con- tinually employed, and 65,000 men will soon be ranged against the insurgents. THE UNITED STATES. Mr. Murray, the Governor of Utah Territory, in his mes- sage to the Legislature, calls upon that body to carry out the Federal enactment against polygamy. A large building formerly occupied by the World news- paper, in New York, was destroyed by fire on Tuesday night. Several lives were lost, and the damage to property is estimated at 500,000 dollars. Mr. Scoville, the counsel for Guiteau, has formally per- sented to the Supreme Court a petition for a new trial. The convict has issued a long address to the American people, in which he asks for money to contest the case. A Washing- ton telegram says that the execution will take place on June 30th. Mr. Blaine has published in the Washington Post an ex- planation of his remarkable policy in South America. It is an adroit attempt to excite the national feeling against Eng- land, on the ground that our commercial interests will re- ceive an enormous impulse through the victory of Chili. He complains that Chili had been " backed" by England, whose "ceaseless activity" in spreading her commercial power he admires, but he does not wish to see that power advanced at the expense of the United States. i ,

WARRINGTON. PETTY SESSIONS. WEDNESDAX.—Before Mr. George Artingstall (chairman) and Mr. Houghton. FOOTPATH OBSTRUCTION.—A young man named Alfred Holt was charged with obstructing the footpath on the high- way at Riston, by riding a bicycle thereon, on the 21st inst.—He was ordered to pay costs, Gs. Gd. A P ÜBLIC-HOUSE ATTAC KED .—William Callan and Wm. Harrison, youths, were charged with having, on the 23'd January, at Rixtoii, unlawfully damaged the palings, gate, and stable door of the Red Lion Inn, to the amount of ss. —Mr. Moore, jun., appeared for the landlady of the inn, Mrs. Charlotte Petford, and stated that on the date named a dancing party was held in the house. The defendant Har- rison wished to enter the room, but the landlady refused to allow him, and he went away. In a short time he returned with four other Youths. They broke the palings, upset the water tub, smashed the stable door, and threw stones and brick bats on the roof of the house. When Mrs. Petford remonstrated with them they threatened her, and sent stones at a man named Gregson, who was helping in the bar. The defendants were the ringleaders, and caused great annoyance to the complainant.—Evidence was given in support of this statement, and the Bench fined the defen- dants 10s. and costs each. THEFT OF A GUN.—John Millington, who had been con- victed several times previously, was charged with stealing a single-barrelled gun, the property of William Moorcroft, farm labourer, Cuerdley.—The prisoner placed the weapon in the barn on the 7th ult., and next day he discovered it had been abstracted. The following day the prisoner sold the gun to James Houghton, toolmaker, Upton, near Wid- nes; and he was apprehendPd on Sunday last by P.C. Rogers.—He was committed to take his trial at the next Liverpool sessions. A DELAYED OflDEll.—Thornas Dutton was summoned by Adam Roberts to show cause why he should n,t be com- mitted to prison in default of paying £5 193., the costs of an order made upon hjm on the 3rd December, 1879.—Mr. Riley, of St. Helens, appeared for the defendant, and stated the order was only served upon the defendant a week ago.— Under these circumstances the Bench ordered the defendant to pay the amount in monthly instalments of 103.

At the Leeds Assizes, on Wednesday, the Grand Jury re- turned a true bill against Kate Dover, charged with the murder of Mr. Skinner, by poisoning, at Sheffield. The trial was fixed for Monday next. The bill against a manu- facturer named Mercer for the manslaughter of his house- keeper at Sheffield was ignored. -
