Mr. ASHMEAD BARTLETT, M.P., at a meeting of the South Warwickshire Conservative Association, on Wednesday, condemned the Irish policy of the Government, maintaining that the principle of confiscation without compensation was undiluted communism. The Handsworth Conservative Association held their annual dinner on Wednesday night. Colonel King Harman spoke of Mr. Gladstone's policy as one of spoliation and plunder, and said Ireland was now literally seething with rebellion, murder, robbery, and mutilation being wide- spread. The ARCHBISHOP of Yortx, presiding on Tuesday at the opening of a new wing of the York Certified Industrial Society's School, spoke of the admirable objects of such insti- tutions in rescuing neglected boys from dishonest habits, and by teaching them some useful trade enabling them to become excellent members of society. Messrs. HIBBERT and STANLEY addressed their constituents at Oldham, o'4 Tuesday night. Mr..Hibbert spoke of the difficulties the Government had to contend with, and said the two difficulties now staring them in the face were Mr. Bradlaugh and obstruction. He advocated a reform of pro- cedure, and supported Mr. Bradlaugh's admission. Mr. Stanley defended the action of the Government in respect to Ireland. , The Right Hon. ROBERT BOURKE addressing his con- stituents at King's Lynn, on Wednesday, referred to his mis- sion in the East, and said if the recent decree of the Sultan is maintained, order might be restored to the finances of Turkey. Speaking of Ireland and its present unhappy state, he could not avoid the conclusion that the legislation of the last twenty years had thoroughly demoralised the people. Legislation ought to have proceeded upon generous and constitutional principles. The Government had wilfully blinded itself to the object of the Land Leaguers, who de- manded nothing less than separation. With regard to foreign affairs, the Government policy in Natal and India had lowered England among the nations. Mr. LABOUCHERE, M.P., and Mr. BRADLAUGIT were present on Wednesday night at the annual dinner of the Northamp- ton Radical Union. Mr. Labouckere, in responding for the House of Commons, remarked that in drinking the toast Northampton was grateful for very little, seeing that the House had behaved in a bad and scandalous manner towards the town. Mr. Bradlaugh said it was possible they might soon have another fight. The Tory party spoke of a disso- lution as though they could force it, and whenever it came he meant fighting right through with every trust and conti-

dence. Earl LITTON, addressing a large Conservative meeting in Manchester, on Wednesday evening, said Lord Hartington, in a speech at Sheffield some months ago, accused him of urging upon the late Government a policy embracing the annexation or military occupation of Afghanistan. His mound for that assertion was a minute writteta by him in September, 1878 ; but that minute was very explicit, and only pointed out the military importance, in view of the in• cessant advance of Russia, of a small portion of Afghanistan. Lord Hartington had, therefore, entirely misrepresented the minute. Referring to the criticism of Mr. Bright and Lord Hartington on the means adopted by his Administration in dealing with the taxes of India, he said he thought the only Administration that strained every nerve to render the salt tax and other taxes impossible was the Administration over which he presided. They, in fact, sought to undermine the whole fabric of the Indian customs tariff, of which very little would remain when these duties were gone. That was their policy, and they made no secret of it, and he should always reckon the measures they took as the best of their administration. Mn. MUNDELL& ON COERCION.—At the Sheffield Liberal Club, on Tuesday morning, an interview took place between Mr. Mundella, M.P., and a deputation from the Sheffield branch df the National Land League, which protested against the coercive policy of the Government, and asked him to use his influence for the release of the Irish suspects. Mr. Mundella, in reply, defended the expression he had used in a speech, when he characterised the obstruction as a con- test with wild beasts. He had always denounced ob- struction as destructive to all liberty, for when the business of the country could no longer be carried on by party government it meant anarchy and despotism. As to coer- cive measures, he had frequently said force was no remedy, but the Liberal Government had proposed a remedy. Was the Land Act no remedy? Yes, and the best and noblest men of Ireland thought so. The Liberal Government would not have resorted to coercion if there had been any other alternative. It became a matter of necessity to stop with a strong hand the murders and the nightly burning in Ireland. That state of affairs in Ireland was the result of a rash and hasty leadership, and he believed the Liberal Government were the best friends of Ireland. When the tranquillity of Ireland justified the step, coercion would be abandoned and the Irish suspects released. The Tories, by trying to spread dissatisfaction with Liberal legislation, were using the Irish for their own purposes. He was not going to be deterred by threat or intimidation, nor should he swerve one Itair from the right line of doing justice to Ireland, and of trying to secure for her tranquillity and prosperity. SIR CHARLES DUKE AND HIS CONSTITUENTS —DISGRACE- FUL PROCEEDINGS—Sir Charles Dilke and Mr. Firth ad- dressed their constituents at the Vestry Hall, Chelsea, on Tuesday evening, and although every precautiou was taken to prevent, if possible, such disgraceful scenes as occurted at the Tower Hamlets meeting last week, a very large rough element got into the hall, and interrupted the proceedings almost a 4 soon as they commenced. The precincts of the hall appear to have been crowded by a big force of roughs- whose yells, screams, and hootings interrupted the right hon. b tronet at intervals, and at last, possession having been ob- tained of one part of the building, a body of roughs, armed with short staves, dashed into the room, and, breaking down the barriers and smashing the chairs, stormed the platform, which, after a severe struggle, they succeeded in clearing. A considerable force of police was stationed on the premises, and they managed very quickly to eject the rioters who appeared to be under very good organisation, and cleared out the hall. It was understood that only a few arrests were made, among them being a Roman Catholic priest, who is credited with having given the signal to the romths, and under whose guidance they seemed to act. The disturbing element having been ejected, the friends of order returned to the late scene of riot, and Sir Charles Dilke delivered his speech, dwelling mainly upon foreign affairs. He said the Government looked with satisfaction upon our ppsition in Egypt and our relations with France. In this connection he hoped and believed, notwithstandiag the present state of affairs, that a satisfactory commercial treaty would be con- cluded with France; but the Government would make no treaty which did not give the advantages of the old one. He supported Mr. Gladstone's policy in Ireland, and endorsed what had been said by Messrs. Bright and Chamberlain There were further interruptions.

TRADE NOTES. STRIKE IN THE Inox TRADE.—At Stockton, Darlington, and Hartlepool the irorsworkers on Wednesday struck for the advance they claim of 7-1- per cent. The standing Com- mittee of the Board of Arbitration sent out a resolution stating that the Board would not consider the dispute, and could not by its rules till the men returned to work. Several thousand men have struck, and they seem resolute in their action, having adopted a resolution at a great meeting at Stockton to keep out till the advance is given. WAGES IN TIIE LANCASHIRE COTTON TRADE.—At an adjourned representative meeting of operative cotton spin- ners' associations of North and North-East Lancashire, held at Church, near Accrington, on Sunday, when 10 districts were represented, a resolution was adopted declaring that the present state of the trade warranted an application for an advance of wages, especially as the districts represented are among the lowest paid in Lancashire. It was further resolved that, owing to the unsatisfactory state of the wages question' employers be solicited to adopt payment by indicator or length of yarn spun, instead of by weight. THE LINeASHIRE COAL TRADE.—ThQ coal trade of this district remains in a depressed condition owing to the con- tinued absence of demand for house-fire purposes, and large quantities of the better qualities of round coal are still going into stock. The colder weather of the last few days, and the gradual working out of stocks, has brought about some little improvement, but requirements are still so limited that the bulk of the collieries are kept on short time. Other classes of round coal for iron making and steam purposes are generally in tolerably good demand, but supplies of these con- tinue plentiful. Prices generally show a want of firmness, and concessions are made to secure orders, but the anticipa-

tions of a reduction in list rates with the close of the month have not been realised. The Manchester firms are maintain- lugcases o oml,yh emr eo dr ees;aisteedly,lisatosdhsahvoewbseaenn seeanstieerutte.odßur' yy; their full rate, and in other districts it is only in excep- tionalmoves off slack, also, except in the better qualities, is fairly plentiful, and as a rule prices are only maintained at late rates. The average prices at the pit mouth are about as under :—Best coal Os to Os 61 ; seconds, 7s to 7s Gd; common house coal 5s Oct to 6s 3d; steam and forge coals from 55 upwards; burp?, 4s Gd to 5s 05; good slack, 3s 95 to 4s 3d; and common, Zs to 3s 3,1 per ton. Shipping con- tinues quiet. TIIE LANCASHIRE IRON TRADE.—The somewhat depressed tone which has prevailed in the iron trade of this district during the last week or so has been rather intensified during the last few days by the unsettled state of the money mit.- ket. Buyers have shown an increased disinclination to place out further orders at present, and for prompt deliveries there has in some cases been a slight giving way in prices. The present depression, however, is regarded as only temporary, and there is generally a sufficiently healthy basis to the trade of this district which prevents any anxiety with regard to the future, or any real 'pressure to sell for forward delivery at under current rates. Quotations for Lancashire pig iron remain at 525. Gd., less 2 for forge and foundry qualities; inquiries are not coming forward at this figure, but makers are kept well employed with deliveries under centracts. Some outside brands of pig iron are easier by 61. per ton as c3m- pared with last week, and second-hand lots are offered at low figures. Finished iron makers, who are generally kept very busy, still quote £7 2s 6d for bars delivered into the Man- chester district, but merchants in want of specifications for expiring contracts are offering at under makers' prices. The engineering branches of trade continue well employed, and the erection of new cotton mills is bringing a good deal of local work into the hands of both founders and machinists.

ECCLESTON HILL MISSION Room, ST. HELENS.— 0/1 Sunday, the Salvation Railway Servants conducted religious services in the above Mission Room. They are a body of working men from Liverpool—their headquarters—and other places where they have organised branches. Mr. C. M. Irlam. a railway engine driver, is their recognised leader, and after a hard week's labour they go in various parts of Lancashire, Cheshire, and Wales, upon the Sabbath, trying to do good. There was a small attendance at the Sunday morning service, but in the afternoon the school room was nicely filled. Mr. Irlam conducted the latter service, assisted by Messrs. Woodcock and Hall. In the evening a religious experience meeting was held. The school room, in spite of the bleak and miserable weather, was well filled, and Mr Irlam again led the meeting. Short addresses were given by Messrs. Woodcock and Hall. The day's work was brought to a close by a prayer meeting conducted by Mr. Irlam.

would thus be reduced to the lowest possible point. On the whole, his address, though extremely Radical in its tone. was very well received. Mr. Arch is a man who speaks with great force, and his delivery tells how deeply he feel, the wrongs to which the agricultural labourers of this coun- try have had to submit for a number of years. I understand that the political lectures to which the people of Widnes have thus the opportunity of listening during the course of twelve months are provided at the expense of the esteemed president of the Association—Mr. E. K. Muspratt. There is said to be "a tide in the affairs of men, which, taken at the flood, leads on to fortune!" This aphorism of the Bard of Avon is generally acknowledged to have a firm basis of truth, and if this be so, the Runcorn Board of Com- missioners have missed their "tide," so far as letting Water- loo House is concerned. This massive building appears to be a sort of white elephant on the hands of the Board, and a short time ago Mr. Craig, the master of the Runcorn Col- legiate School, made an offer to take it upon lease, but though I understand the rent proferred was a very fair one, it was refused. Within the past few days the Commissioners ' seem to have reconsidered their determination, for the master of the Collegiate School has been told that he could have the building. However, owing to the lukewarm manner in which his proposals had been received, Mr. Craig, before being informed of this changed action on the part of the Commissioners, had taken his present premises for another year. I believe that it ii eon suggested by some of the Commissioners that it wruld be a wise course to make Waterloo House into public buildings for the town, and if this could be done without any very large expense to the ratepgyers, it would be a very commendakle course to adopt. Young " Argus " has been attempting a history of "our own times," in which he deals with local matters of vital importance. The History is not a comprehensive one, but is sufficient to show how we are governed. Mr. Argus, jun., is troubled about the Borough Bench, which, for his sake, and for the sake of justice, I trust will not be far off, not- withstanding the efforts that have been made to debar the people from the enjoyment of that boon. Here it is: Once upon a time, not very far removed from the present, and in an age when the common people were neither in reality nor supposition subjected to the dominations of the squire of the parish, who, in other benighted ages, sometimes called "the goode olde tymes," exercised his powerful and oftentimes tyrannical prerogative in all matters civil, religious, and even domestic—matters imperial being at that time too high for the plebian intellect, and consequently out of the ques- tion—there was situated a village in the south-western portion of Lancashire, named St. Helens. The name, as everyone must see, is eminently respectable, and if anyone is in doubt about the matter he has only to refer to a file of one of the local newspapers, when all doubts respecting such respectability will he removed, an authority on such matters from an adjoining city having spoken it. The papers, of course, duly reported that interesting information at the time it was uttered. The village, through a variety of causes—principally coal, chemic, and crown and plate glass—sprang up like a piece of fungi until it reached the size and dimensions which enabled it to be dignified by the appellation of a town. This transformation naturally was accompanied by many disagreeablenesses, which rendered the town, as many candid but by no means disloyal towns- people—influential residents—said, unfit to live in. Some of those who could afford it resided in sylvan retreats out- side, and these were gentlemen who were mainly instrumen- tal in making the town what it was. The town, although it was entitled to many, and had obtained some, municipal privileges, was in many respecta similar to what it was in the good old times. The spirit of the autocrat had not been damped by any manifestations of inte ligent democracy, and the one or two families which had for years conducted the affairs of the community with almost absolute sway found worthy representatives to guard zealously :their power, in their progeny. These Bismarckian Proclivities were not unnoticed by the burgesses, who, while they were sometimes apathetic in matters concerning the government of the borough—which fact had not been lost sight of by the aforesaid rulers—they were, nevertheless, a peeple not to be "sat upon," to use a common expression. Whenever a glaring injustice was perpetrated the irate inhabitants would at the polling booth administer a severe castigation to the offender; but oftentimes, owing to the power of the cand-- date's influence, aided by powerful cash, an equally offerd- ing delinquent would rise superior to the struggle and return as a "dog to its vomit" to cajole his constituents. Others sent to guard the interests of the people would sink into contemptible sycophancy, and worship the golden image of authority, on which they had been warned to look with eyes only of stoical indifference. The consequence was that the government of the community was managed by the families aforementioned, regardless of the wishes of the ratepayers. Some of the more faithful and independent representatives on the matter of dealing out justice to the inhabitants advocated the formation of a bench of magis- trates who wece better acquainted with the people and their dispositions than the county magnates, who lived at a dis- tance, knew not the people, and whose only qualification for the position was, not that which made the King of Israel immortal, but the possession of filthy lucre—" siller and gowd." For years this agitation continued, and met with strenuous opposition from the big wigs and their parasites, some of whom went so far as to insult the townspeople by asserting there were none to be found in the borough worthy the honour of sitting upon the bench to deal out justice to their fellow men. So much for the respectability of the town and its people. Apparently all the respectability is concentrated in the name. What's in a name P Respecta- bility. At time went ow the people desired a change, and this was nearly affected, when the great men, seeing their power slipping from their fingers, stopped the coming boon, in the hope that it might never come. This was done through an insolent meddling in the proceedings by the men whose co-workers had neglected their duties as magis- trates, and caused the people to cry out for justice. As a crowning piece of assumption a scion of one of the despotic families was placed on the roll of magistrates in preference to many of the townsmen who, by virtue of their citizen- ship, experience, and ability, were eminently qualified for the position. This was the straw which broke the camel's back of patience ; but whether the manliness of the towns- people is going to assert itself in an unmistakeable manner remains yet to be seen. FLACCUS.

CHEMICAL LEC GEE AT WIDNES. —On Saturday even- ing Mr. H. Wade-Deacon gave a lecture on "Soda ash, refined alkali, and soda crystals," under the auspices of the Widnes Science and Art Classes. Mr. F. H. Gossage presided, and there was a fair attendance of students. WIDENING OF A WIDNES Lllki E OF RF`LWAY.-I'ho contract for widening the London and North-Western line from Widnes to Speke has been let to Mr. James Evans, contractor, of Walsall and Wolverhampton, who is at present engaged in constructing the new line from Sutton Coldfield to Birmingham, for the same company.

THE PROPOSRD COUNTY COURT FOR WIDNES.—NO decision has yet been arrived at in this matter, notwith- standing the efforts put forth by Mr. W. T. Husband and his supporters. Within the last few days the following correspondence has taken place upon the question : Widnes, 24th January, 1882. To the Right Honble. Sir Richard Assheton Cross, M.P. Sir,—Nothing has been heard yet in reference to the petition which you were kind enough to present in this matter. lam being continually asked about it. I regret to give you further trouble in the matter. I should be glad if you could further our wishes. —I am, sir, your obedient servant, W. T. HUSBAND.—The following reply has been received from Sir R. A. Cross : "Eccles Riggs, Broughton-in-Furness, 27th January, 1882. Dear sir,—Your letter of the 24th inst. only reached me on my return home last night. I have this day written again to the Lord Chancellor's secretary.—Faithfully yours, R. A. CROSS. W. T. HUSBAND, Esq."

LANCASHIRE INJEPENDENT COLLEGE.—Mr. W. Bennett M.A., of this college, has just taken a very distinguished position in the Theological Tripos, at Cambridge. Net only is he in the first class, but all the three prizes viz., the Hebrew prize, the Evans prize, and the Scholfield Greek Testament prize are awarded to him, and he is first in Hebrew. Mr. Bennett studied first at the City of London School, and after taking various prizes and a 'scholarship there, applied for admiesion to I ancashire Independent College. Thrcugh the arrangement between that college and Owen's College he had the advantage of the lectures at Owen's College, and graduated M.A. in Mathematics, in the University of London. After attending the Theological classes at Lancashire College for two sessions, he went to St. John's College, Cambridge. He returns this week to Man- chester, and will complete his course at the Lancashire Independent College next midsummer. WIDNES GASES.—Writing to the editor of the Liverpool ifercury Mr. J. H. Allott, of Warrington, says:—" I am glad to see a line in your paper about tlaees gases, but Liverpool side does not alone suffer; they are very much felt in and near Warrington, and between Walton and Runcorn, and when much of the nuisance is known to be preventable, it is the more to be complained of. I knew Widnes well several years ago, when you might suffer by the gases from the works, but not much from the sul- phuretted hydrogen spoken of. Now, this is an ever present smell when I go there, and opposite Knight's Old Bone Works there is a most offensive evolution of this, caused by acid and waste drain tge running off together. This has existed for years. Widnes is a lost place and not much cared for, and although a century of earth on the waste banks would render them nearly inocuous—as witness Messrs. Crosfield's here—nothing is done ; indeed the Central Station waste heap at Widnes is, I am told, yet hot —that is, on fire—and the smell is strong enough, and the , drainage from the waste there and on to Ditton, and about some of the works towards Ditton' is most offensive. We hear a good deal about inspection of alkali works, but I believe Widnes must be left to its own sweet will, or the inspector lacks a nese, though his technical knowledge would, if he walked about the district, tell him things were not as they should be. I speak with some little knowledge of the I matter by reason of my early training under a now deceased, but honoured professor. One worof more. Why do I not see this vat residue, waste, used by the London and North- Western Railway Company for their embankments? I see they have none in theirs, and I say they are wise—a worse thing could not be used."

div.head: EXAMINER SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 4, 1882.
div.p: THE EXAMINER SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 4, 1882.

WIDNES PARISH CHURCH SCHOOL ENTERTAINMENTS.— The seventh entertainment of the series took place on Tuesday evening, under the presidency of the vicar (the Rev. J. Wright-Williams.) There was a very interesting programme.

THE CASE OF JOHN HARRISON, RUNCORN FERRYMAN. —We are requested to state that the fund on behalf of " Old Johnnie Harrison," amounts to £36 35. Vtd., for which the secretary and treasurer desire to express their thanks to the contributors.

Mn. B. J. M.LtnEiv AT RUNCORN.—Mr. Malden gave a lecture, illustrated with with dioramic views, in the Public Hall, Huncorn, on Wednesday evening. There was a good attendance. The proceeds will be devoted to the reduction of the debt on Weston Wesleyan day schools. HALTON Pia is CHURCH MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY.—A meeting in connection with this society was held on Tuesday evening, when Mr. Haddock read an ex- cellent paper, entitled "The life and character of General Grant." Mr. T. Miller occupied the chair, and there was a fair attendance of members.

ST. JOHN'S BAND or HOPE, RIINCORN.—" The Drunk- ards and Abstainers of the Bible" was the subject of a lecture delivered on Thursday night by the Rev. J. I. Jones of Brecon, before a large audience at the St. John's school- room, Runcorn. Mr. W. B. Gibson occupied the chair.

PROMOTION OF A WIDNES romcEmA.N.—P.C. Strick- land, who has now been connected with the Widnes police force several years, has been made a sergeant. It is gratify- ing to see that Superintendent Barker is determined some of the old officers shall be encouraged in the discharge of their duty, by receiving promotion. Strickland is the second officer who has had his services in the force acknowledged since the advent of Mr. Barker in the district. The super- intendent's courteous treatment of the men is the subject of general comment amongst them. BOLD HEATH ScnooLs.—The annual tea party in aid of the above schools took place on Thursday evening, when there was a crowded attendance. The tea was followed by a miscellaneous entertainment, to which some of the best known vocalists contributed. The Rev. G. Bond, vicar of Farnworth, occupied the chair. Mr. W. Tipping, of Bold Hall, had promised to be present, but was prevented by ill- ness from coming.

SUDDEN DEATH OF A WIDNES INFANT.—On Sunday morning, Edward Williams, aged 14 weeks, the son of Richard Taylor Williams, a joiner, living in Anne-street, West, was found dead in bed by its mother. The little one was put to bed at half-past twelve on Sunday morning, whPn its parents retired, and it appeared in its usual health, but it was found dead at five o'clock. On Thursday, an inquest was held in the case, by Mr. C. E. Driffield, county coroner, at the Market Gate Hotel, and a verdict was returned to the effect that deceased died from convulsions.

HALTON MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY.—On Mon- day evening last Mr. Smith, of Runcorn, read a paper to the members of the above society, on "The tongue." Mr. A. E. Davies, in the absence of the president, occupied the chair. Mr. Smith, in the course of his paper, spoke of the tongue under tha following heads—the lying tongue, the flattering tongue, the conceited tongue, the tongue in the pulpit, and the tongue of exaggeration. At the close the following gentlemen made a few remarks :—Messrs. T. Miller, R. Hughes, S. Barrow, and G. Pennington; and the essayist was thanked by the members for his clever and interesting essay. FREEMASONRY IN WIDNES.—The annual festival of thi " Equity " Lodge of Ancient, 'Free, and Accepted Masons, was held at Widnes, on Thursday, at the Masonic Rooms, Alforde Chambers. There was a fair gathering of brethren from Widnes and neighbouring lodges. The, lodge was opened by Brother Carlile, W.M. Brother James White, P.M., then installed Brother Jonas Foster as W.M. for the ensuing twelve months, and invested the following officers: —Brother Kyle, S.W.; Brother McTear, J.W.; Brother Copland, treasurer; Brother Purver, secretary; Brother Pankhurst, S.D. ; Brother Matthews, J.D. ; Brother Robin- son, I.G. ; Brother Wood, S.S.; Brother Hough, J.S.; Bro. Watson, organist; Brother Kennion, tyler. The annual banquet was subsequently held at Brother Fewiler's Central Hotel.

HALTON PARISH Cnuncn Cnorn.—On Tuesday even- ing last the members of this choir, numbering 25, were kindly invited to supper by the churchwardens, Messrs. Joseph Stokes (Rock Savage) and Joseph Wallworth Bag- uley (Stockham), at their own personal expense, as a mark of appreciation of their services as well as from a deep in- terest they take in the welfare of the church in which they hold office with such zealous attention. The supper was held at Mrs. Ormson's, Norton Arms Hotel, where there was a splendid spread, Mr. Baguley presided, supported by the Vicar (Rev. J. Lockwood) and Mr. Ex-Churchwardeia Wright. A letter was read from Mr. Stokes expressive of deep regret at his unavoidable absence through indisposition. After supper the usual toasts were honoured, and songs were given by Mr. Lambert and Master Rogers. WIDNES NONCONFORMIST SUNDAY SCITOOLS.—DISSOLV - ING VIEWS EXIIIEITIONS.—Last autumn a committee representative of these schools was formed to provide for the scholars a useful and amusing entertainment, by exhibitions of dissolving views with illustrative lectures. Apparatus and slides were hired from the Sunday School Union, who have latterly added these to the many and important aids they have rendered to the Sunday school cause. The sub- jects chosen were " Life in the East," with which chrome- tropes and miscellaneous views made up about 140 slides. During the past ten days these views have been exhibited in most of the schools, and have been a complete success, though pressing engagements prevented several schools from parti- cipating. On Monday week the views were shown at Lacey- street Wesleyan School, where the Rev. J. H. Cummings gave the lectures, and Mr. J. Hargreaves was exhibitor. On the following evening, at Simm's Cross Congregational Church; lecturers, the Rev. T. Peters, and Mr. T. J. Peters; exhibitor, Mr. W. Doming. On Wednesday and Thursday at Albert-road 'Wesleyan Church, lecturer, Mr. F. Lawrin- son ; exhibitor, Mr. Hargreaves. On Saturday at Moor-lane Welsh Congregational Church, lecturer, Rev. D. Davies ; exhibitor, Mr. Hargreaves. On Monday last at Hutchinson- street Primitive Methodist Church, and Tuesday at Simm's Cross Primitive Methodist Church, at both of which places Mr. H. G. Seddon was lecturer, and Mr. A. W. Coxon, ex- hibitor. The views and apparatus being of the best and most improved manufacture gave entire satisfaction on all hands. AS the Sunday School Union are not alining at pecuniary profit, the committee were enabled to fix the prices for admission very low, but the schools will each be able to hand a small sum to its treasurer (after payment of expenses) as the financial result. WELSH METHODISTS AT WIDNES. The Welsh Methodists are a body who claim to be amongst the earliest Dissenters who established themselves in Widnes. Their advent into the town dates about a quarter of a century back, when, of course, the population was very sparce. As the works spread on every hand, the Welsh community naturally increased, and they determined to start a place of worship where they could listen to the tidings of "the wonderful works of God in their own tongue." A Mr. Cooper placed at their disposal a room which was used during the weekdays for sail making, and for some time this continued to be their only place of worship. Principally through the efforts of Mr. Edward Roberts, the requisite funds were ultimately raised, and a Welsh Methonist chapel erected in Cromwell-street, which it was at that time supposed would ultimately become one of the leading thoroughfares of the town. This hope was, however, doomed to disappointment, and the building was eventually surrounded by a class of property of a somewhat indifferent description. Under these circumstances, it has been decided to erect a new chapel, and subscriptions have been promised towards the building fund by a number of the leading manufacturers. Several lectures have also been given, the proceeds of which have been banded over to the committee. The total cost of the proposed structure will be about £1,200, and as the congregation is mostly composed of those who have to earn their bread by the sweat of their brows, a considerable amount of outside help will be re- quired. The sanction of the North Wales Chapel Building Committee has to be obtained, and it is said to be contrary to their custom to make any grant unlgss they are satisfied that the movement is really taking a practical shape. On Monday evening, a concert in aid of the building fund, was held in the Lacey-street schoolroom, Widnes. Mr. Benjamin Brown presided, and the artistes who took part came from Liverpool. Birkenhead, and Abergele, and were all natives of the principality. The glees and part songs were given by the members of the Birkenhead Glee Union. Miss Maggie Evans acted as accompanist and performed her part in an admirable manner. The glees " Oh, we will o'er the downs," and Bishop's "Now by day's retiring lamp," "The sailor's chorus," and "Ye mariners of England" were beautifully given. Miss Maggie Evans gave a pianoforte solo—a selection of Welsh airs—in a manner that showed her per- fect mastery of the instrument. Miss Annie Jones, of Abergele, was very successful in the song Somebody," and afterwards sang " Yr aderyn pur," in which she was heartily applauded. Mr. Wyatt Evans gave a Welsh song " Glyndwr " and was followed by Miss Annie Williams, whose rich contralto voice was heard to great advantage in the song "The better land," for which she was encored. A humorous song entitled "Perverted proverbs" was very successfully sung by Mr. Llewelyn Wynne. Mr. Wyatt Evans' song "The Wolf" was also encored. Miss Annie Williams won another success in the Welsh song " Deignrvn ar fedd fy mam," and Mr. W. Evans rendered "Y Bachien deur." Miss Williams was heartily applauded in "Jeanette and Jeanette "; and Mr. L. Wynne caused much amuse- ment in the song" Muddle Puddle porter."—A vote of thanks was given to the artistes for their services, on the motion of H. W. Roberts, of Liverpool, seconded by the Rev. J. Tessy- man ; and after a similar compliment had been paid to the Chairman, on the proposition of the Rey. I'. Hughes, seconded by the Rey. T. H. Carver, the proceedings termin- ated.

OAKLAND-STREET WESLEYAN MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT CLASS, WIDNES.—The weekly meeting of this class took place on Wednesday, when a paper on the Book of jenesis was read by Mr. T. Hughes, who sketched the history of the Bible, and said that Christianity claimed that it was in- spired, that its revelations were wonderful, its claims marvellous, and its study grand beyond human compre- hension. It contained the will and mind of God to His in- telligent creatures. He then spoke of the great events depicted in the book of Genesis—the creation and fall of man, the lives of the patriarchs, the flood, the Tower of Babel, I,:c. A discussion afterwards took place on some of the leading points of the paper, the subject on which there was the greatest difference of opinion being the universality of the flood.

THE WIDNES LOCAL BOARD AND THE CHESHIRE LINES CO3IIkIITTEE.—In the Chancery Division, on Thursday,Vice- Chancellor Sir C. Hall heard the case of Tebay v. the Man- chesler, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire Railway and the Widnes Local Board. This was a motion for an injunction to pre- vent the defendants from infringing the rights of the plain- tiff.—Mr. Pearson. Q.C., who appeared for the plaintiff, said that since the matter was before hfs Lordship the previous week the motion had been amended, and the Cheshire Lines Committee brought before the Court. The Widnes Local Board were also made parties, as they were doing the acts complained of upon land belonging to the Cheshite Lines Committee and sold by plaintiff for the purpose of the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire Railway. Taking all circumstances, however, into consideration, it would be better that the motion should be allowed to stand over again, the interim order against the Widnes Local Board being con- tinned, and the same undertaking being given by the railway company and the Cheshire Lines Committee as was given last week.—The Vice-Chancellor asked if the plaintiff, con- sidering the Cheshire Lines Committee were not doing any- thing, was not reasonably and sufficient assured as regarded this and the time for bringing on the motion to which plain- ' tiff could object.—Mr. Pearson said he was satisfied with that, and, of course, his Lordship would know what to do if they fouud, when the motion came on, anything had been done that was objectionable.—The motion was then ordered to stand over fora week.

NEW LANCASHIRE MAGISTRATES: APPOINTMENT OF Sr. HELENS GENTLEMAN.—On Saturday morning, the Right Hon. John Bright instructed the Sealkeeper of Lan- cashire to put the following gentlemen en the commission of the peace for the county. :—Mr. Arthur Earle, Childwall, Liverpool ; Mr. J. C. Gamble, Cowley Hill, St. Helens ; Mr. Joseph Hartley, Brook House, Glazebury, Manchester; Mr. James H. Sch6tield, North View, Whitworth ; and Mr. Thomas Smithson, Facit, Rochdale. THE BISHOP OF LIVERPOOL AND THE LIDERATION Socirry.—ln the form of a pamphlet of sixteen pages, there has just been republished two letters addressed to the Right Rev. J. C. Ryle, D.D., Bishop of Liverpool, by "A Luc shire Liberationist," in reply to an attack his lordship made in his charges at Liverpool and Wigan on the object and operations of the Liberation Society. The writer treats of the condition of the Church of England in Liverpool, the Old Nonconformists, and the approach of Disestablishment, and then states the argument in favour of that step, refers to the false al arms in which opponents of the measures in- dulge, treats of free religion in America, quotes the opinions of John Wesley, Andrew Fuller, and Robert Hall, on Church and State, and replies to the charge of Liberationists of making unscrupulous statements, and, in conclusion, makes an appeal in the interests of spiritual religion. INTERNATIONAL ARBITRATION AND PEACE ASSOCIATION. —The first report of the Committee of the International Arbi- tration and Peace Association has just been issued, and con- gratulates the members on the satisfactory progress that has been accomplished. It states that the scheme of procedure, embracing the constitution, the principles and policy cf the association, has been finally adopted and approved by the members; and that the disastrous war between Chili and Peru ; the war in the Transvaal : the cession of the Dulcigno to Montenegro; the rectification on the frontiers between Greece and Turkey; and the war between France and Tunis, have one and all occupied the serious attention of the Com- mittee, and much useful work was accomplished in the in- terests of peace in these international difficulties. The settlement by arbitration of internal difficulties between the United States and France; between Nicaragua and France; and between Chili and Columbia is mentioned ; and the report concludes with an earnest appeal for support on the grounds that amongst all the nations of Europe there is an earnest longing for the deliverance from the Curse of war, and from the gigantic preparations for war, which are weighing down the nations, and crushing them beneath their burden. The founders of the association, it is stated, are firmly convinced that the only hope for peace, and for relief fr,..1 the oppressive military system, rests in the adoption of a system of arbit- ration, and the establishment of an international tribunal. to which governments may safely refer their national' differences.

SAD DEATH OF AN OLD WOMAN AT WARRINGTON.— At the Golden Ball, Winwick-street, on Monday, Mr. C. E. Driffielcl, coroner, held an inquest touching the death of an old woman named Mary Clare, which occurred under the following circumstances :—Hannah Clare' widow, 22, Hay- dock-street, said: Deceased was my late husband's mother, widow of James Clare farmlabourer, who died many years ago, and she has li-zed with me for some years, and in may present house for 10 or 11 years, she being 73 years old. On Sunday, the f2nd January, deceased was as -sual, but she has not gone out much since winter. She got her tea and supper, and went upstairs about a quarter-past 10, fol- lowing my children up, and she went into her own room. In 10 or 15 minutes I heard the deceased scream, and then my boy John and I made upstairs. Deceased was in her night clothes only, which were on fire about the shoulders, and John, who was in her room, was attempting to put out the flames. Taking up a flannel petticoat I smothered the fire with it. Lasked how she did it, and she said she caught the •:.andle with her hand, and asked me to take her down. I did so, placed her on a chair, and applied Oil, Sze., and called in Mrs. Birchall. I sent, too, for deceased's daughter and grand-daughter, and they got Dr. Cannell the same night. He brought oil stuff, which he applied, and we got her to bed. Her burns were on the right arm and shoulder. The doctor came each day up to Thursday night. The deceased was sensible, but she was going lower, and the burns seemed more angry. About three o'clock on Friday morning, the 27th January, she died. I do not remember seeing the candle on going up to deceased, who was in the habit of setting it in the window, and from what she naid she had probably knocked it down with her hand from there. She had seemed bright until that night.—Mrs. Birchall and the boy were called, and after being briefly interrogated by the coroner, the jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death."

PRIZE DISTRII3L LION AT WYCIT.FFE SCAOOL. —A large number of the scholars of Wycliffe Sunday School, some of whom were accompanied by their parents, attended the annual prize distribution in Wycliffe Hall, on Monday evening. The distribution was made by the Rev. John Yonge, assisted by Mr. W. Wallington, superintendent. In opening the proceedings. the Rev. J. Yonge remarked, that this year there were not so many prizes to be given as there were in previous years. It had been customary to give two classes of prizes. A first class prize represented 100 atten- dances at Sunday school out of a possible 104 in the year; while a second class prize was given to those who made a smaller number of attendances. But this year, for reasons which appeared satisfactory to the teachers, it was decided to give only first class prizes, so that those who received prizes would have the gratification of knowing that they were all first class people in this particular respect. The prizes, which consisted of handsomely, bound books, were then dis- tributed. During the evening the following programme was gone through :—Recitations : Harry Edwards, "There is light ;" Nellie Wilcocks, " Little by *little ;" Fredk. Butter- worth, "People will talk ;" Fred. Griffiths, "The Welsh boy's prayer ;" Oswald Barker, "Mrs. Candle's curtain lec- ture ;" Mary Hayes, "The dying mother's counsel ;" Emily Wilcocks, Emily Ainsworth, Alfred Podmore, and John Shaw, "Jesus and the children ;" Lizzie Ditchfield, " Knock- ing at the gate of heaven ;" Mr. C. H. Mills, "A brave little boy ;" songs by Mary Podmore, " Sweet Sabbath bells ;" and Emily Ainsworth, "Little sister's gone to sleep ;'' and hymns by the choir. Mr. Thomas Ford acted as accompanist. Mr. Wallington, in a short address, referred to the removal of Mr, Rigby, and urged the children to be prompt and re- gular in their attendance at the Sunday school. The recita- tions were well delivered, but in most cases there was Tom for improvement in regard to attention to the punctuation. In one or two instances where this drawback was not apparent, the delivery of the pieces was admirable. The entertainment closed with a vote of thanks to the reciters and singers, which was accorded on the proposition of Mr. W. Roberts, seconded by Mr. J. S. Garland. CHRIST CHURCH, LATCHFORD : ANS UAL TF t MEET. 'rm.—About 200 persons were present at the annual parochial tea party and entertainment, held in connection with Christ Church, Latchford, on Tuesday, in the school- room, Wash-lane. The vicar, the Rev. B. B. Prescott, pre- sided over the meeting held subsequently, and there were also present—the Rev. James Prescott, the Rev. F. Slater, the Rev. W. Yates, Alderman Harrison, and Mr. John White. The Chairman expressed his thankfulness for the many blessings they enjoyed in the parish, and his gratitude to those who by their self-denial and by the service they rendered showed that they took an interest in the affairs if the church and in the schools, and to those who during the past year had given offerings to the church and to the schools. He was also thankful for the blessings which attended the mission which had recently been held in the parish.—The Rev. W. Yates afterwards addressed the meeting. During the evening the following programme was gone through : , Glee," Gaily through the Greenwood," the choir; dialogue, "In the lane" (in three parts), Fanny Dickins and Eva I Leather; songs, " The Midshipmite " and " Philip the Falconer," Mr. Edward Reynolds; violin solo, Mr. John . Reynolds; song, " Sailing " (chorus sung by choir), Mr. George Monks; song, "Moods and tenses," Mr. Joseph I Harrison ; trio, "The Bells of St. Michael's Tower," Mrs. Monks, and Messrs. Monks and Dinwiddie; four part song, "Beware," Messrs. Monks, Lake, Starkie, and Dinwiddie ; I song, "Two Spoons," Mr. Fry, • reading, "A Night with a Baby," Mr. Joseph Harrison; glee, "Softly fall the Shades of Evening," the choir. Mrs. John Reynolds and Mr. Fry , accompanied on the piano.—Mr. John White proposed a vote I of thanks to the Chairman, and Alderman Harrison seconded I the motion, which was carried. The Vicar having briefly I replied, an enjoyable entertainment was brought to a close by the singing of the National Anthem.
UNITED METHODIST FREE CHURCH. RUNCORN. SALE OF WORK.

On Tuesday afternoon, an interesting sale of work was opened at the schoolroom of the United Methodist Free Church, Ellesmere-street, Runcorn, by Mr. J. R. Frith. There is a debt of about £370 on the chapel belonging to the denomination, and for some time there has been a floating circuit deficit amounting to nearly £3O annually. Notwith- standing these facts, many.of the friends have repeatedly expressed a wish that the pews, which are scarcely up to the times, should be removed, and replaced by others of more modern construction. It has long been considered that a bazaar should be held with the object of wiping off the £370 of debt, and it was determined that the friends should be , asked to get together materials for a bazaar, or sale of work on a small scale, so that the incubus of the circuit debt might become a thing of the past. The necessary prepara- tions were carried out by Mesdames Gandy, Cordon, White, Rayner, Holford, Newall, Billington, Stubbs, Niel, Shaw, 0. Jones, Clarke, Jones (Captain), E. Jones, Timperley, Carr, Curzon, Winding, and Paul; and Misses Jones, White, Ash- brooks, Clough, Royle, Norcott, and Shaw. The room had been decOrated for the occasion in a very fair manner by Mr. Richard Moore, assisted by Miss Dun- bavand and Miss E. Royle. The general arrangement of the stalls had been planned by Mr. Edward Gandy. Mr. F. Clarke, of Duke's-field, had succeeded in obtaining a mag- nificent " Christmas tree," about twenty feet in height, from Delamere Forest, and this was laden with a profusion of articles for disposal. No. 1 stall was superintended by Mrs. Timperley, Mrs. Cordon, Mrs. R ivner, and Miss Ashbrooke. No. 2 by Mesdames E. Gandy, Newall, J. Holford, and E. Jones; and the refreshment stall was in charge of Mesdames White, Jones, and Willding. Mrs. Shaw, Mrs. Carr, and Miss Royle had the management of the Christmas tree; and the Misses Shaw and Norcott dealt with the mysteries asso- ciated with a tub containing bran, in the midst of which were articles the constant disclosure of which caused much laughter, at the expense of Ihe speculators in bran-tub stock. Though the two stalls devoted to the useful and ornamental articles were not, of course, filled with any rich display of goods, in the case of an effort which is preliminary to the bazaar proper, many commendations were elicited by the utilitarian character of the things offered for sale. Too often the articles offered on such occasions are "things of beauty," which fail to prove "a joy for ever," as the idea so often comes into the mind of the purchaser that he has paid far too dearly for his whistle, as the philosophical Franklin would have put it. The goods were of a very useful charac- ter, and many of them commanded a ready sale. - About half-past two o'clock the formal proceedings con- nected with the opening were begun.

After devotional exercises, • . The Rev. J. BILLINGTOti congratulated the ladies, and all who had taken part in the preparations for that sale of work. The beginnings of it were truly small, and in a certain sense, the end reached was not very large, though it was ?ouch larger than they had expected it would be. The ap- pearanca of the schoolroom was such as to give anyone in- terested in the church and its affairs much gladness. The principal portion of the work had, as usual, been done by the ladies, whose help had proved remarkably convenient. It was to the credit of their fair friends that however much the gentlemen despised, or professed to despise them, or whateveituncomplimentary terms they might ungallantly use towards them, they never asked for their help, whether in the smallest matter of the routine of their daily life, or in church work, but they gave them their assistance right heartily. (Applause.) Though no word of thankfulness had, perhaps, been spoken to many of the friends who had shown the church much kindness on that occasion, he wished each one of them to understand that they were very grateful, and they should: be sorry that any misunderstand- ing should occur owing to their gratitude not having found vocal utterance. (Applause.) He had much pleasure in introducing to them Mr. 3. R. Frith, who had kindly cm- sented to open the sale of work. Mr. FRITH, who was warmly received, said that, from his knowledge of tha Ellesmere-street society, he was able to say that it had always had willing workers in connection with it. When he looked at the building in which they were at that moment, he could not but feel impressed with. the idea that if their religious societies generally had the same willing workers amongst them which there were in connection with the Methodist Free Church in Ellesmere- street, when that school-room was erected, they would have fewer debts, and they would sooner have them wiped off when they happened to exist. (Applause.) When he looked round that building, and remembered that the man who carried the hod, the bricklayer who laid the bricks, the car- penter who put on the roof, and the slater who slated it, all did their work without expectation of reward, beyond that which God would give them in that great and final day when every good deed should be brought into remembrance, ha felt constrained to say that 'the structure was one of the finest monuments to the power of individual effort which they had had in Runcorn. (Loud applause.) He wished there were more places built in a similar way. When he remembered how they had laboured in the particular matter to which Ile referred, he felt convinced that God would prosper them. They had shown by their actions that they I were willing to put forth effort in the work which God had committed to their care ; and he felt sure that He would not let them go on struggling, year after year, without the blessed reward of seeing the members of their own families, with whom they were so intimately connected, "brought to '- a knowledge of the truth as it was in Christ Jesus." He trusted that the efforts they were putting forth would be crowned with success. They might, at times, feel some- what disheartene4 owing to the difficulties they had to meet; but he would remind them that each individual had special difficulties with which to contend. In like manner there was no society of Christian men which had not diffi- culties to encounter ; but after all they were enabled to say, . "Thanks be unto God, who giveth us the victory ;" for He gave them power to overcome all their obstacles. They had not the battle to fight alone, but they went forward, Strong in the strength which God supplies,

Through His redeeming Son, _ _ and with the knowledge that they could amidst all their trials, shout aloud, " Victory, victory, through the blood of the Lamb." He trusted that they would be given strength to go on in the good work in which they were engaged, and that the object of removing the circuit debt would be fully accomplished by that sale of work. He felt sure that it would be; and when he looked round and saw the product of the three months' labour in which the ladies had been engaged he felt sure that the baz tar %which it was intended to hold twelve months hence, would be a groat success. (Hear, bear.) Let them be encouraged to go on with their labour, remembering that it was not the great things of life which were the means of doing the mos,t good, but often- times the infinitely little matters—" the common task "—in which they plodded on, day by day, adding little by little to what had been accomplished in the past, until, at last, the Master said, "Well done" inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me." In conclusion, he said he hoped that their asso- ciation together on that occasion might prove a source of spiritual blessing to them all. He had much pleasure in declaring the sale of work open, and he hoped they would all do their best to make it a success. (Loud applause.) The practical business of the sale then commenced. The total receipts amounted to £49 55. ld., and about £lO worth of articles yet remain unsold.

div.head: WESLEYAN TEMPERANCE SOCIETY.
div.p: WESLEYAN TEMPERANCE SOCIETY.
RUNCORN BRANCH.

On Monday evening the annual meeting of the Runcorn circuit branch of the Wesleyan Methodist Temperance Society was held in the Public Hall. Mr. John Simpson presided, and there were also upon the platform the Revs. J. Nowell (superintendent), George Hack, J. Colwell (of Manchester), Messrs. S. B. Beckett and J. D. Jones. After devotional exercises, The CHAIRMAN said he believed the cause of temperance to be the most important that could occupy their attention. Most, if not all of them, were aware that in the Wesleyan Temperance Society there were two pledges. Every .one did not think it necessary to take the total abstinence pledge, although all Christian people felt it requisite that every one should be temperate, so that one of the pledges was that by which persons engaged to promote temperance. Some considered that the friends of this society took very much safer ground if they advised everyone to be a total abstainer; and he said most decidedly that this was the ground he took himself. He felt that, as a Christian man, he was standing on safer &round, and in a safer position, if he was a pledged total abstainer. (Applause). It was not everyone that understood the great temptations which drink held out, and on this ground he considered it better that those who stood should take heed lest they fell. When they looked around, and saw the number of Christian men and women who had fallen through drink, they must come to the con- clusion that it was safer they should abstain. They must allow that if they could get people to be total abstainers, they put them in a very different position from what they occupied if they only engaged not to take too mnch. 11e did not believe there were any people in the habit of taking wine, beer, or spirits, who were not sometimes placed in circumstances where it seemed easier to take a little more than not to take one single drop in addition to that they had already had. In this way many were led on to take too much, who, at first, had not the slightest intention of so doing. Indeed such persons, if spoken to upon the subject, would be the first to exclaim "Is thy servant a dog that he should ever take too much, or be 'overseen' by drink." He, however, certainly felt gratified that the temperance question occupied such a different position to-day as com- pared with what it did years ago. He quoted from an article which appeared in the Times recently, and observed that a change must have passed over the public sentiment to permit such opinions to appear in that journal. He after- wards read a report of a speech on the liquor traffic made at Liverpool, the other evening, by the Dean of Bangor, and then urged all present, whatever else they might do, not to be persuaded to take strong drink as a beverage. He be- lieved that hundreds and thousands by taking drink under the orders of a medical man, had been led on and on until they had lost themselves completely. He could assure them that however great the self denial might be, however great the suffering they might experience in through giving up drink; however unpleasant tha. circumstances n which they might be placed, these things were not worth a moment's consideration when they considered the safe ground on which they would be placed by becoming total abstainers. They must also not forget , the influence which such action

on their part might have upon others, and that they might be the means, by their example, of saving others from be- coming victims to the curse of drink. In conclusion, he observed that the society was progressing in a very satis- factory manner. (Applause.) The Rev. GEORGE HACK, who was warmly received, said he was a total abstainer for his own safety, •that as a tee- totaller he had more power as a minister of the Gospel with his people. In reply to some who, in his last circuit, tried to get him to take liquor, he said he was in this happy posi- tion that, owing to being an abstainer, the teetotallers thought all the better of him, and they who were trying to constrain him to break his pledge thought none the worse of him. .Under these circumstances he got the respect of both parties—(laughter)—and he could assure them it was of the utmost importance for a minister to have the respect of his people. He was convinced that it was hecoming more than ever the conviction of physiologists that alcohol was of no value to a healthy man. Speaking at Exeter Hall, Sir Henry Thompson, a very eminent physician, bald that for the purpose of health, alcohol was not necessary, although he admitted that in some forms of disease it might be of value as a medicine; and Dr. Richardson, a celebrated physiologist, remarked that in former years he was of opinion that alcohpl enabled a man to bear physical and mental fatigue, and lifted up the mind into a greater activity, but his views had changed. He (Dr. Richardson) was asked to study the action of alcohol in connection with other chemicals, and he began to ask it what it would do? After a long series of analyses and experiments, he found that it did not warm the body; that it did not give muscular strength ; that whilst it expedited the heart's action, it re- duced its strength ; and so with the nervous system, which more quickly wore out with this agent than without it ; while it did not increase the strength or the tissues .of. the body. Ttaus he found alcohol

to be an agent which gave no strength, reduced the tone of the blood vessels and heart,. reduced the nervous power, built up no tissues, and could be of no use to him, or any ether animal, except under the exceptional circumstances of some diseases. He found that if a man took into his body Goz. of alcohol per day, it caused the heart to beat 18,000 times more than it ought; with 40z., 12,000 times; and with 3oz. per day, 10,0)0 times oftener than it ought. Dr. Richardson also said that he never did more varied work, or did it with greater facility, or freedom from anxiety and wrong, than he had during the whole of the time he had abstained from taking stimulants. The testimony as to the value of temperance came from men in all positions of life —from men like John Bright, Canon Farrar, and Mr. Wilber- force ; from travellers like Livingstone and Stanley; from literary men, from soldiers, and from sailors, who, as total abstainers, had gone to the ice-bound north or the tropical south. Speaking personally, he might say that during the last four winters he had, for the space of eight or twelve weeks, talked away, day after day, and night after night, at special evangelistic work, and, as the other reverend gentle- man on the platform well knew, there was no labour half an exhausting. Surely it was not too much to ask fiom those who were professors of the religion of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, and who longed to do their fellows good, that they should renounce the use of intoxicating drinks, and contribute their quota of influence and effort to rid the country of this terrible curse. Talk of British interests! Tnere was nothing which was so damaging to them as the drinking customs of society to-day. He was told that for every 117 of the population there was a public-house, and under such circumstances he had to cry, alas for the prac- tical living out of our Christianity! Canon Farrar said that this was the simoon, withering and blighting all that was best and fairest in this highly favoured land. It was the drink which was the principal cause of the filling of the lunatic asylums of the c:untry. Drink was the one gigantic obstacle in the way of civilisation and Christianity. The contagion from this traffic had followed our missionaries into foreign lands, and had proved itself a blot upon the peerless name of Christianity, whilst at home it frustrated their efforts to extend the triumphs of the Gospel, and tilled our prisons and penitentiaries. Indeed, it was nearly im- possible to exaggerate the awful effects of the drinking system. He had many times thought that notwithstanding the wonderful advance which had been made in regard to the cause of temperance, they were still far from seeing the accomplishments of their hopes. They had achieved this and that victory, but still the frequenters of the public-house seemed to be as numerous as ever, and the drunkards as great a number as many years ago. The influence of the intoxicating cup appeared to be as widespread in its ramifi- cations as ever, and he did not think that any Act of Parlia- ment would be very powerful in regard to making a sober Great Britain. Ile believed that if ever they were to have what they had been hoping and praying for, it must be as the result of the whole church getting on to her knees, and beseeching God in relation to this matter. They had weeks of special prayer in respect to evangelistic work, and why should they not have about this, for was it not indeed the obstacle in the way of the progress of their labours ? He might say with Gerald Massey :

"Oh! who would not a champion be, In this the lordlier chivalry? Uprouse ye now, brave brother band, With honest heart and working hand. We are but few, toil-tried, but true, And hearts beat high to dare and do; On there 13 those that ache to see The day dawn of our victory Eyes full of heart-break with us plead, And watchers weep, and martyrs bleed; W-rk, brothers, work! Wok, hand and brain, We'll win the golden age again, And love's miilenial morn shall rise In happy hearts and ble,sed eyes; We will, we will, brave champions be, In this, the lordlier chivalry," • (Loud applause.) The Rev. J. COLWELL commented upon the great neces- sity which existed for such a society as the one with which they were associated, as there were many cases which would never be met by the more simple Bands of Hope. They were able to 'feel that they had a real practical foe to fight against, and were not engaged in "beating the air." He referred to the great obstacle which existed to material progress in the drinking customs of society. A sovereign spent on alcohol was about the very worst invest- ment they could make. Let them spend their money on bread or clothing, instead of on intoxicating drink, and then they would soon find a difference in the social condition of Nvorkinc.r,rnen, for there was nothing which interfered so much with the material prosperity of England as the wasting of se many millions in drinking. Everyone who studied the political tendency of the present age, must come to the con- viction that it was towards democracy. Very soon it would not matter so much what the leading statesmen thought or said, but it would matter a gteat deal what the mass of the people thought and did. What he wished to ask those present was whether they were prepared to put political power and influence into the hands of a drunken mob, who could be turned blue, red, yellow, green, or any colour, or no colour at all, by a pint of beer or a noggin of rum? (Laugh- ter and applause.) If they wished to make the political future of England safe, they must keep intoxicating drink out of the brains of the British workingman. In concluding, the speaker drew the attention of the audience to the fact that whilst the people of this country were spending 81d. per head with the object of evangelising the world, they were spending £4 10s. per head on strong drink. On the motion of Mr. BECKETT, seconded by Mr. J. D. JONES, a vote of thanks was passed to the speakers; and a similar compliment having been paid to the Chairman, on the proposition of the Rev. J. NowELL, seconded by the Rev. GEO. HACK, the proceedings terminated.

div.head: LYMM.
div.p: LYMM.

CHURCH BAZAAR AT Ot7GIITRINGTON.—OR Monday last, a bazaar was held in the St. Peter's schools, and was very well patronised. At intervals, Mr. Oliver G. Smith played some excellent selections on the piano. The proceeds are to be devoted to the school fund.

LYMM Missiox HALL.—Mr. Linley, of Burton Stafford- shire, who has been holding revival services in the above hall, completed his series of sermons on Thursday night. During his stay at Lymm, Mr. Linley has been the means of converting many of the working class, and his meetings have been attended by crowded and attentive audiences. His visit will be long remembered by all who have heard him.

div.head: LYMM LOCAL BOARD.
div.p: LYMM LOCAL BOARD.

The meetirg of this Board was held on Thursday evening. Present: Messrs. Cameron (chairman), Rogers, Taylor, Gibbon, Appleton, Hall, Simpson, Ridgway (clerk), Mullard (deputy clerk), Dr. Fox (medical officer).

div.head: MEDICAL OFFICER'S ANNUAL REPORT.
div.p: THE MEDICAL OFFICER'S ANNUAL REPORT.

Dr. Fax presented his annual report, which stated that for, the year 1881, Lymtn had the lowest death rate of all the I sanitary districts, urban or rural, in the Mid-Cheshire com- bination. (Hear, hear.) It was surpassed in regard to the zvmotic class of diseases, however, by Nantwich and Sand- bach, which had only one, whereas Lymm had two deaths referred to scarlet fever, and one to diarrhcea. The pi esent population of Lymm, as shown by the census, was 4,665, I being an advance of 124 upon the previous census; but the actual addition to the population in that period, as deter- mined by the annual difference between births and deaths, was 676. 552 persons had therefore in ten years passed from Lymm to add to the populations of other districts. The actual rate of increase in Lymm was thus 2.7 per cent in the decennial period, but the rate of natural increase was 14.9 per cent, which was slightly in advance of the rate of incre Ise for all Cheshireovhich was 14.6. During the past year there were registered 144 births, and 52 deaths, showing a birth rate of 31, and a death rate of 111, which was -the lowest annual death rate he had ever recorded in an urban dis- trict. The mortality had been very equally distributed in the four quarters of the year, the death rate having never exceeded 12. The zymotic death rate exhibited an equally gratify- ing reduction from an average of 3.74 to 0.62. The fresh out- breaks of scarlet fever was in May last occurring simultaneous- ly in Higher-lane, Sandy-lane, and Rush Green. Connection could not be traced between these cases and those in the ad jacant township o f Millington. It was impossible without an appeal to coercive measures, to affect a removal to the hospital at IVarrington. However the result had proved that the steps taken were as adequate to prevent a more ex- tended outbreak as if the hospital had been brought into use. The report concluded with explaining the object of erection of hospitals, which it stated was to protect the public and not the patient. The CHAIRMAN congratulated the Board on the healthy state of the district, and on the motion of Mr. HALL seconded by Mr. ROGERS, it was decided that the medical officer's re- port be printed. _ RESIGNATION OF MR. BOLT.
The CHAIRMAN said he had received- the following ?ocn- Inunication ;—" Manchester, Jan. 19th 1882.—Dear Sire"'

Bearing in mind cur last meeting and what has come to my knowledge of having taken place in the offices of the Board this week, I do not feel myself justified in remaining a member any longer, so that you will please accept my resignation. '.!..ours faithfully F. Holt." On the motion of the CHAIRMAN, seconded by Mr. APPLETON, the resignation was accepted.
DANGEROUS DITCHES.

Mr. HALL proposed that prompt measures be taken for filling up the ditches at Rush Green and Statham, which he stated had caused frequent accidents. The matter was referred to the Roads Committee. THE GAS WORKS IMPROVEMENTS. On the motion of Mr. HALL, seconded by Mr. ROGERS, it was decided that a statement be prepared of the expenditure of the monies voted for the improvements at the Gas Works.

THE CROSS. It was decided that the stocks which had recently been removed from the Cross should be repaired and replaced. This concluded the business, and the Chairman remarked that the members had conducted themselves very well, and done the business in the way they ought to do.

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.

Earl Spencer on Thursday received a deputation with reference to the restrictions imposed upon the removal of diseased cattle. They urged that the local authority should have power to declare an area of not less than a quarter of a mile infected, and that an inspector should be appointed to see that the restrictions were carried out. Earl Spencer, in reply said Contagious Diseases (Animals) Act had been very successful, and be hoped to meet the views of the deputation, and stamp out the disease.

Mr.. Mundella on Thursday received a deputati3n of Catholics, who asked him to use his influence with the Go- vernment in favour of making it compulsory for Boards of Guardians to provide Catholic priests in workhouses. Mr. Mundella, in reply, said he did not think the House of Com- mons would for a moment entertain such a proposal. He was now in communication with Mr. Dodson on the subject of the education of children at present In workhouses as to the advisability of placing them in schools outside workhouses.

THE ST. HELENS KICKING C LSE.—Yesterday, the magis- trates, on the application of Superintendent . Johnston, estreated the recognisances of Joseph Barrow and Joseph Henshall, who became bond for ti.e appearance of Owen Braidy and James WEvery on Decernbe.r 23rd, the two last— named flaying been remanded on a charge of violently assaulting and kicking Joseph Finney, on the night of Dec,tuber 12th oil Prescot-ro,a. The amounts in each case were mitigated from --C2O to £lO.

div.head: MEETING OF THE CABINET.
div.p: MEETING OF THE CABINET.
The Cabinet met at two o'clock yesterday, and broke up at a quarter to six. All the members were present. PROPOSED EASTER VOLUNTEER REVIEW.

A meeting of the :National Rifle Association was held yesterday afternoon, at Pall Mall, Lord Rauelagh in the chair. It was agreed that it uould be desirable to hold Easter Monday Review, and a committee of commanding officers was appointed to select and report up6n a suitable locality for the event.

div.head: GOVERNMENT OF NATAL.
div.p: GOVERNMENT OF NATAL.
Last night's Ga:ctte announced the appointment of Sir Hy. Ernest Bulwer as Governor and Commander-in-Chief of Natal and Special Commissioner for Zulu affairs.
RELIEF FOR THE PERSECUTED JEWS.

The Mansion House fund for the relief of the persecuted Jews in Russia amounted last evening to over ...x.:25,000, in- cluding donations received' during the day of £l,OOO from Lady Louisa Goldsmid, £l,OOO from Messrs. Stern Bros., and £l,OOO from another subscriber.

div.head: HORNSEY RAILWAY ACCIDENT.
div.p: THE HORNSEY RAILWAY ACCIDENT.
Mrs. Harriet Chowles, the lady who was injured in the Hornsey railway collision, died yesterday morning in the Royal Free Hospital: This makes the third death.
MR. A. M. SULLIVAN AND THE CHILTERN HUNDREDS.
Mr. Gladstone yesterday signed the warrant conferring the office of steward of the Chiltern Hundreds on Mr. A. M. Sullivan.
THE PRESTON ELECTION.

Mr. Henry Cecil Raikes was on Thursday elected one of the Parliamentary representatives of Preston, in the room of Sir John biker, recently appointed a Lord Justice of Appeal. Mr. Raikes polled 6,045 votes. No fewer than 4,212 were recorded for Mr. Simpson, of Liverpool, who stood as an " independent" candidate. SAD DROWNING CASE AT WINSFORD.

The people of Winsford were yesterday morning much excited by the report of a sad drowning case in the river Weaver, a short distance below the the town bridge. Shortly after midnight, as a sailtnaker named Dooley was returning from work along the river bank he heard a splash in the water, immediately followed by loud cries for help. Running to the spot he saw a man struggling in deep water, but could render no assistance. The cries of the drowning man awoke the people on a canal boat lying near, but no help conld be given him before he sank for the last time. Grapnels were obtained, and in about a quarter of an hour the body was brought to the surface. On examination it was found to be that of Mr. John Stanier, who held a post of some responsibility in the Wharton Railway and River Salt Company, Limited. It was thought that the deceased was proceeding to the works of his employers, and that, the moon being overcast, he fell from the river wall, which at this point is high. He was well known and respected in Winsford.

div.head: BRIBERY SENTENCES.
div.p: THE BRIBERY SENTENCES.

The Press Association learns that the Committee which recently communicated with the Home Secretary asking for a remission of the sentences in the bribery cases at Maccles- field, Deal, and Sandwich has now dissolved, and the move- ment is not likely to be carried any further. The last meeting of the Committee was held on Thursday afternoon at the Westminster Palace Hotel, and it was resolved, after much deliberation, that they considered it unadvisable to take any further steps to procure the release of the remainder of the bribery prisoners.

div.head: STRANGE DEATH OF A CHILD.
div.p: STRANGE DEATH OF A CHILD.

An inquest was held at Sheffield, on Thursday, on the body of John Thomas Hadfield, aged four years, son of a pattern-maker. He had surreptitiously obtained possession of a bottle containing two wine glasses of neat brandy, which was in the bedroom window, and had drunk it. He became unconscious and died. T;)..e Coroner said it was a most sin- gular case. He did not think the child would have drunk so much brandy voluntarily. A verdict of "Died from drinking brandy" was returned.

div.head: REPRESENTATION OF WESTMINSTER.
div.p: THE REPRESENTATION OF WESTMINSTER.

Last night's Globe said :—" We understand that it is the intention of Sir Charles Russell, Bart., in consequences of his continued ill health, to immediately make application for the stewardship of the Chiltern Hundreds, thus creating a vacancy in the representation of Westminster. In this event, we believe it is understood that the Conservative party will forward a requisition to Lord Alder- non Percy, the second son of the Duke of Northumberland, requesting him to become their candidate."

div.head: STATE OF IRELAND.
div.p: THE STATE OF IRELAND.

The Sub Commissioners sitting at Belfast, yesterday, de- livered judgment in the cases which had been heard during the week. There were two estates only interested, one owned by Mr. Hamill, J.lt!, and the other by the sisters of Mr. Biggar, M.P., the latter property having been managed by Mr. Biggar himself. The Hamill tenants' rents were reduced on an average by 15 per cent., and the rents on the Biggar property by 40 per cent. A land bailiff, named Madden, in the employ of Mr. Donnell, on returning home from Westport market, yester- day, was attacked by a party of men, and so brutally beaten that his life is dispaired of. "UNITED IRELAND" SEIZED IN LIVERPOOL.

The police yesterday seized 20,000 copies of United Ire- land in the printing works of Messrs. Matthews, Brothers, Thomas-street, Liverpool, where the machines had been at work all night and up till noon yesterday. The paper was dated "Paris, Saturday, February 4th, 1882," and was "registered for transmission abroad." The cartoon repre- sents Mr. Gladstone and Mr. Forster in conversation about the female prisoners, Mr. Forster informing " Bill " that his "resources of civilisation are exhausted," and he "must in- vent more." The Land League Funn shows receipts for the week amounting to £7,850. The seized edition was carted away to Hatton-garden. This is the second time United Ireland has been printed in Livrpool, but the edition printed six weeks ago in the same offices got safely away. SIR WM. HARCOURT AND MINERS.

On Thursday, a 'deputation from the Miners' Association Of Great Britain, accompanied by local representatives from nearly all the mining districts of the country, waited upon the Home Secretary, urging upon him a variety of altera- tions in the Mines Regulation Act and the Employers' Liability Act, which they believed would tend to the security of workmen and the better working of mines.—Sir Wm. Harcourt said it seemed to him that many of the points raised could be settled without legislation by the powerful organisation which the miners themselves had at hand. With reference to the Employers' Liability Act, be did not think Parliament would be disposed to reopen that question at present, but he promised that he would consuit the mining inspectors upon the whole question, in order to see if any, and what changes ware necessary.
