LIBERALISM AT EARLESTO\VN.

SPEECH BY MR. BRIGGS, M.P. A crowded meeting in connection with the South-West Lancashire Liberal Association was held in the Viaduct Institute, Earlestown, on Monday evening. The chair was occupied by Lieut.-Col. McCorquodale, who was warmly applauded on making his appearance, There were also present Mr. W. E. Briggs, M.P., who met with a flattering reception, Mr. Richard Pilkington (Mayor of St. Helens, and Messrs. J. E. Johnson Ferguson, W..R. Kennedy (Li'eer m , - pool), B. Walker, C. F. Bosom worth, A. Sinclair (St. Hetens, e!s: John Squires, A. McCorquodale, P. M. Campbell, H. isel Squires (Conway), J. Howard, E. L. Pilkiregtore, McCorquodale, Sze. The proceedings were opened wetse Oas song "The Pilot of the State," the chorus Of wialcerwas heartily sung by the audience. The CITAIRMAN, in addressing the meeting, reviewed the political history of the country for several years back. He remembered, he said, attending a meeting in that very hall when the late Government were in power, 'see the purpose of , protesting against Lord Beaconsfield's foreign policy. Eng- land at that time was in great trouble. 'Trade was depressed, uncertainty prevailed with regard to almost everything, and people looked anxiously slay by day in the morning papers to see what fresh startling news there was. It was shortly before that period the announcement was made that we had acquired the island of Cyprus (laughter), about which a great deal of fuss was made. Indeed, it was just as if the Conservative Government had found out a way of paying off the National Debt without requiring the public to put their hands in their pockets,or that perpetualmotion had been discovered. (Laughter, and hear, hear.) It transpired after- wards, howeever, what we had got when the annual bills be- gan to come in from Cyprus, and when it was realised that there was no harbour there in which to place her Majesty's ships. The next important event that followed this achieve- ment was the transport of Sepoys from India to Malta. When I the troops reachei the latter place, they did not like it, and the Maltese, very soon getting tired of their visitors, the Sepoye were taken to our new possession Cyprus. (Loud laughter.) The Indians even did not like the climate of that place, or, indeed, anything about the island; and that reminded him (the speaker) of the Scotch boy who, upon , making his way through a hedge towards an apple tree, was I discovered by the owner of the orchard. (Hear, hear). " Where are you going?" asked the owner; "I'm going back again," said the boy. (Loud laughter). So much for the Sepoys yet it might be as well to state that this little trick, or whatever it could be called, cost John Bull £750,000 or thereabouts, which went out of the pockets of the British taxpayer. The parade, it was thought, would frighten Russia, but whether that had been accomplished he could not tell; the general opinion appeared to have been that England was more laughed at than anything else. (Hear, hear.) About the same time the seeds had been sown for trouble in South , Africa, and they brought forward terrible confusion. This country, it would be recollected, took a large territory there called the Transvaal, and did what it had no right to do. (Hear, hear.) As to the subsequent proceedings it must be admitted that our arms and honour had been tarnished for a time, and when the present Government came into office they sent over a numerous army in order to crush the Boers. But when that army arrived they found the inhabitants of the Transvaal willing to come to fair and reasonable terms. So that to avenge the disaster of our troops after that, and under the circumstances, would not have been a manly act, or consistent with Christian principles. (Hear, hear.) Terms were accordingly come to, and a large portion of the British Army returned home—(applause) ;—afterwards, when the Transvaal people were unwilling to ratify their engagement, Mr. Gladstone distinctly announced that they would be obliged to fulfil the arrangement they had entered into, and that he would not for one moment allow any change. (Loud applause.) The action the Government took on that oc- casion evoked the admiration of men in high positions in I America, France, Belgium, and other countries. (Renewed applause.) With regard to the war in Afghanistan, that terrible event was prompted by the Tory Ministry, and it was only when Mr. Gladstone and his Cabinet took the reins of power that they put an end to the terrible havoc, blood- shed, and desolation that bad been raging. (Loud applause.) All these things, of course, paralysed trade in this country; manufactures suffered thereby; wages were lowered, and people worked on short time. Then the day of reckoning came. Parliament had to be dissolved, the Tory Govern- ment apeealed to the country, and the verdict of the coun- try was• eluilty." (Loud applause.) Mr. Gladstone bad been in office for nearly two years, and we were now at peace with the whole world. (Hear' hear.) The reason for that was because the present Prime Minister treated foreign nations as he would they should treat this empire. (Hear, hear.) Ceerfidence had been restored to the country, and trade was improving, and, to give an instance, there were several works in Earlestown at present on overtime. The last month's exports were shown in the returns to he over the value of the corresponding month of last year by £4,800.000---(10ud applause)—and this was not all that the Liberals had done for the couutry. Mr. Gladstone, when he was Chancellor of the Exchequer, originated third-class rail- way fares, which now amounted to £250,000 per week— (hear, hear)—the duties on food and drink, such as tea and coffee—(kear, hear,)—Were reduced largely; and, lastly. I there was given to the people a free Press, by which they were made aware day by day of the course of events and the action of the Government. (Applause.) With regard to Ireland, be (the speaker) hoped, and verily believed, that the Land Bill passed last session would be productive of a very great deal of good. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Already its working had been satisfactory, and a great number of arrangements had been made between landlord and tenant without the cases coming into court. (Hear, hear:) It could not be expected that the injustice of two or three cen- turies could be wiped out suddenly,but abetter state of things would gradually be seen. (Applause.) So far as his own opinion of Paddy was concerned,if he would now only throw away the thillelah and ask no one to tread upon the tail of his coat, and apply himself to that most ancient occupation designed by God for man, that was, the tilling of the soil, he had no doubt they would s2e very much better days in Ireland. Now that a change in the land laws of Ireland had been effected, the people of this country considered that the time had arrived fot a change in the land laws oi Engllnd and Scotland. (Rear, hear.) But the tenure of land in these latter countries was differenc to the Irish system, although there was no disguising the fact that in some parts of this kingdom mealy landlords had caused great hardship to their tenants. According to our present laws, if a landed 'proprietor died and left no will, or if the land was entailed, the property went to the eldest son, to the exclusion of the widow and children. ("Shame.") It was contemplated to effect a change in this law—(applause)_dld it was very very much wanted. He (the speaker) held that land, like every other property, ehoeld be liable for a man's debts— , (hear, hear)—and that as a poor mau's goods could be seized for a debt, so should lend be treated under similar circum- stances. (Hear, hear.) At present this was not so with en- tailed property. The eldest son, who acquired it from his father, could 'do what he liked, but the land was not to be interfered with, because he was merely living upon it as an occupier. In drawing his remarks to a close, Colonel Mc- Corquodale touched briefly upon the inequality of the fran- chise in counties as compared with large towns, and expressed his confidence in the present Administration, not only to chane-e this, but to grant county boards whereby people inhabiting country districts would very rightly have a voice in the expenditure of their own money to pay for roads and other improvements. (Hear, hear, and ap- plause.) Then there were the new arrangements in regard . to the Army, which, he believed, bad so far worked remark- ably well. One thing was clear, that crime and disorder had 1 perceptibly diminished in the Army since the abolition by the present Government of flogging. (Applause.) Mr. Briggs would deal with obstruction in the House of Com- mons, but he (the speaker) would only say this, in conclu- sion—it was said that Lord Randolph Churchill—(laughter) —had spoken 1345 times last session. ("Oh.") In the coming session they would all no doubt be satisfied if 310 of these speeches were taken away, leaving the remaining five to Lord Randolph Churchill to deliver, as being just as many as the House would listen to. (Applause.) -Mr RICEIARD PILRINGTON said be had the honour to move the first resolution, which was, "That this meeting cordially approves the conduct of the Government, both in their home and foreign policy, and rejoices that the country will have under their rule a period for the development of , her home and foreign trade; and believes that the highest interests of the great empire are safe in their hands." He was sure that it must be a great gratification to them that they had in power the present Government. He was sure the present contentment, the present security and confi- dence the people felt in the Government were a great I change, and a very great difference, to the confidence and security they had he ore the dismissal, or the "very happy despatch" of the Government of the late Lord Beaconsfield. They knew to their cost that during the period of Lord Beaconsfield's government they did not know what to expect. Perhaps during the first one or two years of that terrible six years Lord Beaconsfield's Government kept very quiet, because, perhaps, they were a little frightened as to how fir they should-go. 'thinking they had got the length of the foot of the people of England, it was surprising to look back and see how far they really did go. They really did not know what to expect ; and the late Government dill things which had been unheard of for centuries, or at least 50 or 60 years. Troops were moved about, which was very illegal to do, without the consent of Parliament. The reserves were called out, and many thousands of men engeged in their quiet employments were called from those employments recklessly, just for the vanity of a Minister or Cabinet, because they wanted to pose before the world in the same manner as a Bismarck, who had the absolute ear of his sovereign. (Cheers.) What suffering could be greater than that of those people taken from those occupations, not for fighting, but simply for brag, and to come back and find their situations not open to them. Instead of Lord Salisbury they had now Earl Granville as foreign secretary. He thought Lord Salisbury was pretty well found out when he went to Constantinople. Everybody thought he was a strong, able man, and would speak the will of England, and when he had spoken that will, it would be carried out. The Go- vernment however, did not support him, and in his opinion, when a thing was ordered to be done, it ought to he insisted upon and, if necessary, by force. Lord Salisbury spoke in a 'downright and most determined manner, but the Government did not support him, and nothing was done. The Turks did just what they chose. A simple illustration of the manner in which they did their business was to be found in the proceedings of the Conference at Berlin. Lord Salisbury and Lord Beaconsfield were to go there and up- hold the honour of England, to say that England would not be bullied and treated as if it were nobody; and what did they do? They went to Berlin to insist upon the Treaty of

San Stefano being al* "'ed. And what did they do? They made a secret treaty with the very power they went to bully —Russia—as to v a Alai was to be done; and before they went they had actual) . , ate settled with Russia. He asked tleem if they called etat English, straightforward, or becoming for an Englis it noble. But there war a higher intellect that made Lord, esallswury do what it wished. At Berlin Salis- bury let ' stese French suppose that they could take Tunis, and that V As..'s nut the first time the Conservative Government mad sraresents ef property that did not belong to them. They g3' A Trance Tunis, and took Cyprus just to show that s'itile they gave other people that which did not belong to f tham, they would just take a little themselves. (Laughter.) VContrast that policy with the policy of the present Govern- ment. The present Government, in foreign policy, had not 'attempted very grand things ; had not begun to make the people of England think that they were going in for the grand tEairs of the late Government. The present Govern- ment told the Porte that it must give a portion of the terri- tory esf Dulcigno to the Montenegrins, and notwithstanding \ the little artifices on the part of the Porte, the territory was handed over to the Montenegrins. But the Conservative statesmen were either too dishonest or too lazy to insist upon the cession being made. Take the Greek question. Greece was most undoubtedly deserted at Berlin, but fortunately they got it put upon paper that certain teeritory should be 'iven to them. Although that was the case, the Conserva- tive Government would not move haed or foot to see that , Greece got it. But after the present Government came into power, they set to work and got for Greece what it was en- titled to. (Cheers.) There could be seen two modest I triumphs of Earl Granville. Such a policy as that was far 1, more worthy the honour of a great country like England ' than the dishonest, flaring tricks that tarnished the states- manship of Lord Beaconsfield. (Hear, hear.) The present Government kept us out of that Afghanistan scrape. The late Ameer wee perfectly friendly with us, but Loid Beacons- field and Lord (Lytton said they wanted to have a resident at Cabul, and the way of sending him in a sort of peaceful way was to send him to the frontier with three or four thousand soldiers. Of course, the Ameer did not like a lots of soldiers coming in amongst him and his people. Thelate Government did not see it in that light, and they made war upon the Ameer, upset his territory, got into Cabul, and made the greatest possible disorganisation and the greatest possible misery on the Afghans. The late Government said they wanted a friendly and a strong Afghanistan. Supposing a man entered another man's house, punched the man's head and made him senseless, so that he could not recover ' fer twelve months; upset his house, and smeshed his crockery, and on reporting the matter to his chief, said "I merely wished to make him strong and friendly." (Laugh- ter.) That was the way the late Government did all through. Mr. Pilkington pointed out that the late Government made a mistake of a great many millions in their estimate of the Afghan War, and said that when the present Government came into office, General Roberts looked upon Ayoub Khan as a pretender and Herat was evacuated. But he would venture to say that if the Conservatives had remained in power, we should now not only be holding Cabul against its people, but garrisoning Candahar and Herat, and spending money on the possibility of a war with Russia. He asked them if there could be the slightest possible question as to which Government was the best Government, or if there was the slightest possible wish that the late Goverament should take the reins of power again. (No.) It was absurd to compare the individual members of the two Governments. The Conservatives had not got a man amongst them—(loud cheers); if they put the whole lot of them together and they multiplied them by a hundred they could not come up to Gladstone. (Renewed cheers.) Take Sir Stafford Northcote ; he was not as good as the last man in the Cabinet. The only thing he had got left—his morals having been corrupted—was his pious opinion, and that was not worth much. (Laughter.) As for iir Richard Cross, and Mr. Smith they might do pretty well. He hal mentioned the two best men, and he did not believe they had another man amongst them who was worthy the position of a statesman. (A voice: Lowther.) Take the coming man, Lord Randolph Churchill—(laughter)—ancl "Jimmy Lowther." (Renewed laughter.) If the English people gave to those men the keeping of their interests, the peeple would be greater fools than he took them to be. (Cheers.) It was of the greatest importance that they kept in power the splendid array of statesmen who now constitute , the Cabinet, with the greatest leader; the greatest statesman; the noblest, the most honest and the greatest Englishman that he firmly believed ever lived. (Applause.) Mr. W. R. KENNEDY, in seconding the resolution, re- marked that it was necessary in an epoch like this, when the Government had ,in their hands measures of the utmost im- portance that they should put forward their best efforts to make the still small voice of policital reason heard among the din and shriekings of those who earned much for party, much for Toryism, and nothing for the people of England. (Cheers.) The Liberal Government had been in power for two years and what was the state of things? It was patent that we had peace abroad, that trade, which was frightened from us by the mere rumours of war, had returned, and was, flourishing, that not only were the Afghans again a free people unfettered by foreign control, but that . also in Afghanistan, where we had to deal with a more difficult and complicated problem, which had not only secured peace, but England had been able to teach the world a lesson which he believed had borne fruits even in this heur, in the conduct of international politics, that there was something better than what was called national honour, and that was, national honesty. (Cheers.) Turning tee home administration, they , had had to do the hest they could with the leavings of the Conservative Government. (Laughter.) It was the duty Of the Government to deal with the question of Ireland, and he firmly believed this difficulty had been dealt with firmly, wisely, and he hoped, successfully. (Hear, hear, and cheers.) There were those who declared that the present condition of Ireland was the outcome of the Liberal administration, but euch was not the case. The trouble did not begin with their term of office, but it had, so to speak, grown almost to its head before a change of Ministry took place. (Hear, hear.) The speaker, in dealing witti the Bradlaugh question, ex- pressed a hope that those rusty hinges of formalism which would exclude Mr. Bradlaugh from the House of Commons would soon be unbarred, and that whatever a man's religious opinions might be they should not be a bar to the exercise of , his civic rights. (Cheers.) He urged them to support those ' at the head of the Government so that they might carry to a successful end the ship of state freighted, as it would be, with reforms Which would make this country happy and prosperous. (Cheers.) Mr. BRIGGS, M.P., on rising to support the resolution, was most cordially received. He said he quite agreed with the preceding speakers that the policy that had been pur- sued by her Majesty's Government since they came into office merited all the encomiums that had been passed upon them that night. (Hear, hear.) Where they saw turbu- lence and riot, and military disturbences to tradee they new saw the peaceful avocations of trade pursuing their legitimate course; and they saw all those heated passions which were generated by military enterprise gradually sub- siding, and that friendliness which formerly existed between this country and other countries on its borders, was begin- Ling to aesume under the sway of Mr. Gladstone, Lord , Hartington, and John Bright—(cheers)—ite normal and legitimate condition. But there were questions which were looming in the immediate future to which he should like to ask their attention. .When they were considering what the policy of their side was, it was as Well to glance at , what their opponents thought about them. (Hear, hear.) They were aware that they had lately had an election in the North Riding of Yorkshire. He was sorry, as he supposed most of those present were, that it did not turn out quite as 1 successfully as.they anticipated, but they had no reason to , be discouraged—(hear, hear)—far from it. He thought ' when they considered that it was the first election under the ' Ballot Act that had taken place there, that there had been ' a secession of Whig bigwigs, or big Whig wigs—he did not know how to put it—(laughter)—it was not altogether a lamentable conclusion that Mr. Rowlandson, their gallrnt candidate had been defeated only by a small number of votes. The tenant farmers had shown that they were deter- mined to have a voice and a port in matters which con- cerned them so intimately and se deeply. However, ' they had to lament, as the Conservatives would say, adefeat. The little boys in London, when Parliament meets, would have to holloa, as they did on the sth of November," Holloa, bolloa, here's another guy." Mr. Guy lDawnay would take his seat is the House of Commons in the place of Mr. Rowlandson. But how did they think it would be when there was an extended suffrage? Did not his audience think that , there were a great many people in the North Riding of Yorkshire at this present moment who were tingling with indignation to the ends of their fingers because they could not help Mr. Rowlandson just a little? (Hear, hear.) When the next election came he hoped there would then be an ex- tended suffrage—(loud applause)—and when every house- holder in the county who was at present unjustly debarred bad an opportunity of throwing in his voice into the political scale, they would see who would be at the head of the poll —whether it would be Mr. Row landson or Mr. Guy Dawnay. (Hear, bear.) These remarks applied, to a great extent, to the district in which he was speaking. (Hear, bear.) If it would not be asking a rude question, he should very much like to know how many there were in the room who had not votes '? (A voice, "Nearly all of them." Laughter.) It was from no want, then, of proper qualification that they had not votes. They were just as intelligent, as well informed, and , as capable a forming a just and proper opinion as to the current political questions of the day as many of the voters in those benighted wards in Liverpool that returned Con- servative councillors— (laughter and applause) —and yet they were unjustly debarred from exercising that which ought to be the right of every Englishman. He counselled them, however, to have patießce, for this matter of necessity came last, and when this boon was conferred upon them here would have to be a redistribution of seats, and an immediate appeal to the country. (Hear, hear.) Apart from foreign politics, there were many measures of domestic reform which intimately affected all present. There were the bankruptcy laws. There was the reform of the patent laws. (Hear, hear.) There was the removing of the last vestiges of the difference between the Established Church and those various Dissenting bodies who had done and were doing so much good to the religious life of this country —(cheers) ; and there was a proper readjustment of the licensing laws. (Applause.) He would impress upon them —ardent Liberals or Radicals though he hoped they were— (cheers)—the necessity of exercising moderation with regard to this last subject, and others. It was impossible that there should be a thorough and radical reform of the licensing laws of this country unless there was something in the nature of compensation given to those eneaged in the trade. They had entered into it under Parliamentary sanction, and they had pursued it hemmed in by a variety of restrictive measures which no doubt were necessary, and which many people told them needed further amendment in the same direction. Each restriction that had been imposed upon them had been he considered an additional proof that the Legis- lature recognised that these men were earning their liveli-

hood and were pursuing their trade under legislative sanction. Therefore he, thought when they had a measure—and he hoped they might have one—which would give munici- palities the right of buying up, if necessary, all or some of the public-houses in any town, such a measure ought also to secure compensation to those engaged in the trade. (Hear, hear.) The previous speaker had referred to the obstruction in the House of Commons, and he .(the speaker) was one of the unfortunate individuals who had suffered from its effects. He remembered getting up one Monday morning, and not going to bed until the Wednesday night— (laughter)—which the working men preeent would consider was putting in rather a great amount of overtime. (Renewed laughter.) The house presented a most extraordinary sight upon that occasion. There were respectable members of Par- liament, who had never been out of their beds after 12 o'clock at night for the past 20 years, sitting in the grey light of the early morning with crumpled white vests and with their white cravats anyhow—(laughter)— looking with an up-all-nightish kind of air, and wondering what the people in the House of Commons restaurant could give them for breakfast. (Laughter.) Apart from joking, it was really a very serious question. (Hear, hear.) They met in London to do business, but they were made by an insignificant number of men, who represented an insignificant number of voters, to play the fool. (" Shame.") Were they willing that this state of things should continue. ("No.") Were they willing that such men as Mr. Biggar should be allowed to read Blue-books for hours and hours, and when the Speaker told him he was reading in such a tone that he not be heard, have him reply, "Well Mr. Speaker, I will move a little nearer," and have him go on hour after hour in similar fashion? Or did they wish that the business should be stopped by the man who was supposed to represent the aristocracy of England, Lord Randolph Churchill (laughter), whose father was in the enjoyment of an hereditary pension. Did the electors wish that the business of the nation should be stopped by men like these? If not, then they must give a hearty and unanimocs support to Mr. Gladstone, and those who followed him. (Hear, hear, and applause.) The electors . must tell him that they recognised the gravity of what had taken place, but that when they sent members to do their work, and had devoted a large portion of their time to the consideration of the business of one portion of the empire, they had a legitimate claim, which they meant to the assert, that some part of the coming session should be devoted to the consideration of affairs with which the constituents were intimately and nearly concerned. (Cheers.) He did not hesitate to say that during the coming session, while giving i perfect freedom to minorities to express their grievances, • the Government would put a stop to the system of obstruc- • tion to which men like James Lowther and Guy Dawnay were likely to give their assistance. Speaking of Guy . Dawnay reminded him, he said, of another contested • election that he was glad to say was now going on—he meant that at Preston. Mr. Cecil Raikes was not likely to get so easily into the House of Commons as he thought. He supposed Mr. Raikes was of opinion that he would have nothing to do but walk to the door of the House of Commons, and then walk up to the table and take his seat for Preston. Bat he was very likely to be subjected to severe handling before he got there. (Laughter.) He thought that in Mr. Simpson—(cheers)— Mr. Raikes was very likely to find an opponent who would leave no joint of the Conservative harness undiscovered and unexplored. Why? Because he knew where those joints were. (Laughter.) Mr. Simpson told them that at the General Election before the last one he "stumped" South- West Lancashire against the Right Hon. W. E. Gladstone, and he thought his present position was the very best re- pentance in sackcloth and ashes that ever he knew. Bat someone challenged him and said, "Mr. Simpson, you were paid by the great Constitutional Conservative Patriotic Party. What did you get ?" Mr. Simpson said this, "I stamped South-West Lancashire against the Right Hon. W. E. Gladstone. My agreement with the Conservatives was that I should have travelling expenses and £5 for each lec- ture I gave. I did the travelling, I gave the lectures, but I never got paid"—(loud laughter) ;—so that he thought they would agree with him that Mr. Simpson, of Liverpool, did not owe much to the Conservative Party. (Hear, hear.) Well, but his opponent, he understood, was so confident of victory that he went off to London just an hour before Mr. Simpson arrived. (Laughter.) He hoped this was a very good omen. There were some people who said that "the wicked flee when no man pursheth." (Loud laughter.) Mr Raikes apparently fled before he knew that Mr. Simpson pursued. (Laughter.) But this was what Mr. Raikes thought about the programme that they, unfortunate Liberals, had got to propose to the country, and this was what he thought—at least professed to think—that they had the courage, not to say the impudence, to propose to those who, he supposed, were endowed with the same liberal allot- ment of brains as Mr. Cecil Raikes himself possessed. In a speech he made at Preston before he thought Mr. Simpson, of Liverpool, was going to be on his track be said, "The great Radical Prime Minister of France was defeated in Parliament yesterday, and lead had to resign. (This was in reference to M. Gambette.) Such accidents sometimes oc- curred to great Radical Prime Ministers, and were always possible to the party (the Liberals) that based its strength upon the Radical programme, which, as he ventured to think, was a programme appealing to the worst qualities of a man as against the better." If he had said appealing to the best qualities as against the bitter beer—(laughter)— he (Mr. Briggs) would have agreed with him. Then he went on to say that the Liberal programme, the programme of the Queen's advisers, the programme of the party which was in power, and which, thank God, controlled the des- tinies ot the emplre—(cheers)—had to appeal to the na- tural cupidity of those who were not rich, to the not un- natural envy of those who were not privileged, to the timidity of the coward, and to the economy of the miser. If he (Mr. Briggs) were a Nonconformist minister—which he was not—he could make an excellent text out of those few sentences of Mr. Raikes'3. When he talked about ap- pealing to the natural cupidity of those who were not rich he wished to know what Mr. Raikes meant. (Hear, hear.) Did he mean to tell them that working men, who had to struggle for their daily bread, who worked harder than ever Mr. Raikes did, even when he was paid £1,500 a year for doing it, had not as much right to vote and to exercise a voice in the choosing of a man who should represent them as Mr. Raikes himself? (Cheers.) He wanted to know when he talked about "appealing to the natural cupidity of those who were not rich" would he go back upon the times when men like Cobden and John Bright appealed to the na- tural cupidity of those who were not rich, when a man went , into his cottage at night, after a bard day's toil, and eaW his , little folks there without their supper, when he could not earn enough to pay the high price of the flour and corn, which was gold in the pockets of those who were naturally rich? (Laughter and cheers.) He thought even Mr. Raikes him- self, if he were contesting Preston at that time, would feel very much inclined to appeal to the natural cupidity of those who were starving, whilst the natural richness of those who owned the land and who held the possession in their pockets were maintaining a system which preserved what Mr. Raikes called their natural cupidity. (Laughter and cheers.) Before be left this subject be should like to say that be recognised in Mr. Raikes a man who knew a great deal about the procedure of the House of Commons, and he was a man whose voice could be of great service it he chose to make it 80 in the discussions which were likely to take place upon Parliamentary procedure. But a man's voice was always within his own power, just as a man's thoughts were, and Mr. Raikes must take care lest he should allow himself to join hand in hand and be hand and glove with those who would rather seek to obstruct than to amend. ' There was not the slightest doubt that Mr. Raikes must know that Parliamentary procedure was in such a condition that it was necessary that it must be to a great extent amended if it was to be in accordance with the fresh burdens which had lately been placed upon it. Formerly Members spoke seldom; business was not pressing. Now everything in the country was discussed, the light of pub- licity was thrown upon it by the gentlemen of the Press. and; in fact, matters excited public interest both inside and out of it that never did before. The old cumbersome pro- cedure would need amendment: and it was time they ad- dressed themselves to it. No man would wish to stop the YOiCe of the minority, but there must be some way of bring- ing adebate to a conclusion. (Hear, hear.) There was now, but it was a bad one. If he were to go on talking they would say "Shut up"—(langhter),—and he would shut up like a knife and sit down. (Laughter.) But they might call for half an hour to some of' the gentlemen in the Horne of , Commons to shut up, and they would not do it, because some of them could not afford to do it. After alluding to the system of asking questions, and the course of a bill through Parliament, the hon. gentleman said when they got to the end of the seven stages they had to face the heredi- tary House of Lords. He had not the slightest doubt those present would not mind this hereditary House if all its members were of the type of Lord Dalhousie and Lord Derby. (Cheers.) But unfortunately they were not, and he thought, whatever they thought about the amelioration of the procedure of the House of Commons, they ought to consider that still greater queetion—the reformation of the House of Lords. (Cheers.) In conclusion, Mr. Briggs re- ferred to the Bradlaugh question, and said Mr. Bradlaugh's opinions outside the House were one thing, and his consti- tutional duty to this country and to his constituents was another. (Hear, hear.) The constituents had a right to I elect Mr. Bradlaugh. They knew every point of his charac- ter, public and private, and it was a wicked and wrong thing for Parliament to stand between that constituency and the man that they had chosen to represent them. (Cheers.) They ought first to get rid of this great constitutional ques- tion, as to whether a great constituency had not the right to be represented by those whom they pleased. (Hear, hear.) Be urged them to attend to the register, and to co- operate, remarking that if they did this he had not the, slightest doubt they would receive in Parliament that repre- sentation which was their due ; and that they would con- tinue as an association to flourish for many years, to the detriment of the party to which they, as. Liberals, believed the want of progress, and many of the disasters which had i occurred to this country, had been due n the past. (Cheers.) Mr: C. PresEeGcoel moved a vote 0.1 thanks to Mr. Briggs. He was sure they wonld all .back him up in Parliament in every thing that he had mentioned, and that they could do nothing better than to cordially thank Mr. Briggs for the trouble he had taken in coining down to .address them. Mr. A. MCCORQUODALE secandsd the motion, which was carried with enthusiasm Mr. BRIGGS briefly acknowledged the compliment, and proposed a vote of thanks to the the chairman. Mr. BOSWORTH seconded, and . . . THE EXAMINER, 9 SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 4 1882 • WARRINGTON CHAMBER OF COMMERCE. The fifth annual meeting of the Warrington Chamber Of Commerce was held on Mo:-.day, at the Lion Hotel. The president (Alderman J. Davies), occupied the chair, and there were also present: Alderman J. R. Pickmere (mayor), Councillors C. Broadbent, J. Fairclough, F. Monks, Colonel McCorquodale, Messrs. H. Bleckly, T. Jolley, William Long, John Dun, R. A. Naylor, Jas. Smethurst, and Carson.

The report was as follows:—On presenting this fifth annual report, it may be interesting and satisfactory to know what has been accomplished by the chamber since the inau- gural address of its first president was delivered in August, 1876. In July, 1877, at the request of the chamber, the several railway companies reduced the passenger fares be- tween Warrington, and Liverpool, and Manchester. In IS7B, a sub-committee of your council, acting in conjunc- tion with the Corporation, assisted in promoting and pro- tecting the interests of manufacturers, on the Warrington Waterworks Company applying for further powers, and the Corporation, on the earnest solicitation of your council, granted permission to lay pipes for the conveyance of water from the river for manufacturing purposes. In the same year this council was affiliated to, and is now one of the Associated Chambees of Commerce of the United Kingdom, and your appointed delegates have uniformly attended the various sessions in London and the provinces ever since. In 1879, a well-furnished room was provided for the convenience, of of members, where they can inspect the current commercial periodicals and papers issued by the Government, Parlia- ment, the Association, and others who find chambers of com- merce the proper medium for conveying information to commercial localities. The members are invited to avail themselves of this convenience. In 1880 the Employers' Liability Act was passed, and the "council is pleased to think that valuable suggestions from this chamber form a part of that important legislation; and in the same year a moral support was given to the Warrington Corporation in I, obtaining amendments in the Liverpool Corporation Water- works Act, 1880, which will prevent obstacles to improve the navigation of the river, and may afford improved water I supply to Warrington. As you well know, the parliamentary session of 18E1 was peculiar for its barrenness, but there was a wide field for chambers of commerce to give information to the Government and Parliatnene on pending measures, which will, we trust, bear good fruit in the session of 1882. The extension of the powers of the Railway Commissioners has been promoted, and the memorial from this chamber to the select Parliamentary Committee on railway rates was considered by the Board of Trade so important as to be printed at length in the appendices to the parliamentary report. Your council would continue to urge that each chamber of commerce should have a locus stanch i before Par-- , liament and railway commissioners in the interest of their local manufacturers and trading community. The Anglo- French Commercial Treaty.—The Foreign office and Board of Trade have communicated valuable official information to this chamber, and your council was one of the earliest to convey to those departments the suggestion that if the con- templated new treaty cannot be negociated on the basis of terms that will be considerably better for this country than under the existing treaty now about to expire, the Govern- ment be memorialized to abandon all negociations whatever. Rivers GAservancy and Floods Prevention Bill.—Although the promotion of this measure is more immediately the work of a municipal corporation, yet the local manufacturing in- terests are seriously affected by the floods, and we would ex- press ens satisfaction that the Corporation, through their Rivers Committee, was ably represented in the deputation to the Local Government Board in support of this Bill. Your council look forward to this Bill being carried also as a measure of materially improving the navigation of the river, and they appointed a sub-committee who acted in concert with the Rivers Committee with this object in view. On the 4th and sth October last, the Associated Chambers met at Plymouth, and your delegates were the President, Alder- man Joseph Davies, Mr. Artingstall, and Mr. Bleckly, who expressed the instructions of your chamber, and their report was printed in the local newspapers. We cannot clole this report without urging upon the members the desirability of extending the usefulness of the Warrington Chamber of Commerce, and inviting others to become members. It indeed has a mission in promoting the interests of our local manu- factures and free and improved trade in the widest sense, assisting in obtaining lower foreign tariffs, securing cheaper and improved railway, river and canal carriage, simplifying laws affecting bankruptcy and bills of sale even to making the latter altogether illegal, assisting the Corporation in developing the natural advantages and conveniences which Warrington presents to the trade manufacturers which have grown so satisfactorily during the last few years. All this can be achieved by a little cost, as is shown by referring to the annexed statement of receipts and payments. A sub- scription of one guinea a year will suffice—a very trifle when it is considered what has been, and can be, done by the combined work of a local chamber of commerce, and which would never have been or can be achieved by in- dividual or divided action. The financial statement showed that after paying all ex- panses there was a balance in the bank of £2 19s. 3d. The PRESIDENT said, speaking generally, Chambers of Commerce had an excellent mission in promoting trade and commerce in the localities where they happened to be ,tuated. In Warrington we had an excellent Corporation —(hear, bear)—whose duty it was to look after the police, sanitary arrangements, the making of good streets, and the progress of education—(hear, bear)—and, if it confined itself to municipal objects, it would have quite enough to do. The Board of Guardians had to assist the poor, and to exercise economy whilst spending the ratepayers money with that object. He mentioned these two bodies to show that the Chamber of Commerce had a mission peculiar to itself—that of watching the interests of trade and com- merce. Chambers of Commerce in England had been in- creasing in influence and in usefulness; and since the forma- tion of the Associated Chambers in London, they had made their influence much further felt than in their own localities. The Warrington Chamber could be a useful local institution by giving great moral support to any scheme the Council might undertake to promote the trade of the neighbourhood. In one or two cases this had been done. The trade of the town had been encouraged by low rates; but during the last few years these had increased. A suggestion, however, from that chamber to the Corporation, at the right time, might Induce the Corporation to make greater exertions to reduce the rates, and thus encourage manufacturers to settle in the town. There was no doubt that Chambers of Com- merce were giving great assistance to Government at the present in bringing in that vexed question of bankruptcy; and were exercising some influence upon what they ex- pected would be a good bankruptcy bill. The Associated Chambers had elected a special committee for the purpose of getting a universal wire guage. In Warrington the wire trade was a most important one, and was therefore especially interested in the question, which it was intended to bring before the Board of Trade. The Associated Chambers of Commerce considered it very desirable, when an extension of powers, either of a municipal or a commercial character, was applied for, that the inquiry should be held in the im- mediate neighbourhood, and not in London as at present. A great deal of expense would in that way be avoided. (Hear, heir.) The last time Warrington made an applica- tion to Parliament, the cost was something like £1,500 or £2000; and he was inclined to think Parliament would adopt the suggestion made by the Chambers. Referring to the report, the President said they were pleased to think that the information given to Parliament by that Chamber, one or two of its members, had been the means eosfpcecaivaslilny by one insertion of one or two useful clauses in the Employers' Liability Act. He took that opportunity of thanking Mr. McMinnies for the ready manner in which he had presented any memorials they wished to present Parliament or to the Board of Trade. It was stated that the cost of carrying out the work contemplated by the Rivers Conservancy and Floods Prevention Bill, would be about £1,500,000 ; and with the expenditure of another million and a half, it was supposed that free navigation from Liverpool to Manchester could be obtained. They coald well understand that it would be to the interest of the Warrington Chamber of Commerce, that they should impress upon Manchester and the neigh- bouring towns that while they were doing the small work of preventing floods the greater work of providing naviga- tion coald be done by the expenditure of a little more money. (Hear, hear.) After speaking of the advantages to be gained by the Chamber, if it a-ere incorporated, Mr. Davis said he had been inviting one or two legal gentlemen to join the Chamber, and he had received a letter from Mr. Robert Davies, in which he said he should be very glad to do so. (Hear, hear.) He (the president) was quite satisfied the Chamber was useful to Warrington, because he felt there were individual interests which could be better promoted by it than in an individual capacity. It was often deplored that the trade and manufactures of Crewe were not carried on at Warrington. If there had been a Chamber of Com- merce in these days, be was satisfied that the trade of IVarrington would have been so promoted, that all the manufactures they now saw at Crewe would not have gone away from Warrington. (Hear, bear.) He begged to move the adoption of the report. Councillor C. BROADBENT seconded the proposition. He thoug,ht those gentlemen who had been connected with the Chamber from the first hid no reason to regret its inaugura- tion. They bad never been ambitious to make a great noise or a great fuss in the town, but they believed that a Chamber Of that kind, round which business men and manufactures could gather, and, by their united action, tend to promote the eood of the trade of the town, or to get rid of any dis- abilities or grievances which might exist, was a good thing. If they had had any doubt as to the desirability of such a Chamber, it would be removed by the very excellent report which had been presented; or, if any further doubt remained, by the speech of the president. There was no doubt the Chamber had already done good, and would do so in the future. Its advantages and power of usefulness were very much increased by being associated with the other Chambers of the country. (Hear, hear.) They had, for- tunately, been very ably represented at the various meetings of the associated Chambers, and the voice of Warrington had been heard, and, united with the voices of the other Chambers, had had good effect. He thought the growth of the Warrington Chamber, being somewhat slow, was better than if it had developed all at once; but he should like to see a larger number of business men of Warrington connected with it. Be did not think it necessary or desirable that it should be confined entirely to the manufacturers, but that it should embrace those who were in any way, directly or indirectly, connected with the trade of the town. It would be well if they could induce some of the larger tradesmen of the town to join the Chamber, because the interests of trade in all its branches were so intimately connected that

the more representative the Chamber was the greater would be its influence and the greater its usefulness. (Hear, hear.) Mr. BLECIELY remarked that though the accounts of the Chamber were small, it was not languishing for want of funds, which were sufficient for the purposes in which they were engaged. The President had not in his speech referrel to the Bills of Sale Act, which was one of the most pernici- ous and unjust which had been passed. It led to more oppression and injustice than probably any other Act of Par- liament on the same subject they were acquainted with. (Hear, bear.) The associated chambers had brought it pro- minently before the legislature, which, baying large matters to deal with, did not trouble itself very much with little matters like the Bills of Sale Act, which perpetrated a great amount of injury among small people. (Hear, bear.) He thought it would be better to abolish the Act altogether. (Hear, hear.) If bills of sale were made they ought to be made public in:the most complete manner. (Hears hear.) During the last session a Parliamentary Committee had sat a long time, and examined a great number of witnesses with regard to the conveyance of goods. Mr. MclVlinnies was good enough to send him the evidence, which formed a large quarto volume, and it showed that in many parts of the country railway companies had exercised a great amount of arbitrary power, and had levied rates which their Act of Parliament did. not justify. Of course, the railways had their explanation to give of these things, and they' were bound to bear what they had to say. A perusal of the evidence produced the impression that the railway compan- ies had in different parts of the country charged rates in excess of those which they were authorised to charge, and be thought they ought to be treated as frauds. There had recently been passed an Act by which contracts entered into by a man, when he had not full freedom of contract, could be annulled. Now certainly no man was free to make a contract with a railway company, because he was obliged to send his goods by them, and seeing that Parliament Cad re- cognised that a contract in that way might be put aside, there was no reason why it should not intervene and tell the companies they would take away some of the excessive power which had been put into their hands, and used to the injury of the country. Mr. Bleckly mentioned some of the anomalies of railway rates, and said be would not for a moment seek to take away some of the companies rights without compensating them. The passenger tax pressed heavily upon them, and it would be well if the companies could give something to the public and receive an advantage from the Treasury in its place. English manufacturers had to compete against all the world, and they ought to be placed in a fair and right position, and that position Parliament ought to acquire for the trade interests of the country. (Hear, hear.) No machinery could be put in operation, which would more efficiently bring about that result, than the Associated Chambers of Commerce. It was a subject on their programme of work for this session, and he was quite sure they would press it upon the Govern- ment. The question of the wire gauge would have to go before the Board of Trade, and Mr. Chamberlain, who had been in the wire and screw trade, knew whether the gauge would be a good thing or not. He (Mr. Bleckly) was told that it would be a troublesome thing, double the number of gauges, and bring them to such a degree of fineness as to involve the wirema.kers in great trouble. He thought they might leave that in the bands of the gentleman who would have to deal with it. The Warrington Chamber had taken great interest in the bankruptcy laws, which, it was admitted, lost us some £15,000,000 a year, and put a premium on fraud and dishonesty, and should be put an end to. Mr. Chamberlain had taken up the question with energy, and it was likly he would succeed, if the procedure of Parliament was put upon a more manageable basis than it was at present —if they should be able to stop people talking a long time, which at all meetings was an injurious thing, and he thought he had occupied their time sufficiently long upon these subjects. (Applause.) Mr. DUN said he approved of what had been said with regard to bankruptcy. .It had been announced that it was the intention of the present eminent organiser who ruled over the post office to introduce this year a measure which had been attempted to be passed some years ago, namely, the extension of the Post Office Savings Bank. At present the limit of the savings bank deposit was £3O in one year, and a total amount of £3OO. It was proposed to extend the £3O to £lOO, and the total amount to £3oo—at all events, a con- siderable extension. The country was filled with private banks and joint stock banks, whose mission it was to acquire information of the manufactures of the country, and apply the deposits they collected—after retaining such a suns of money as would enable them to meet their liability—in fostering the trade of the country, by advances, and in other ways; and if the Government was in any way put into com- petition with those banks, the funds of which at present were so usefully employed, the trade of the country must inevitably suffer, because the funds, instead of being em- ployed on the spot, went into the hanpls of the Income Tax Commissioners, who used them for the purpose of dealing in consols. It was all very well for Mr. Gladstone or any other Chancellor of the Exchequer to have a large amount of money for the purpose of great financial payments, but if it were to be done to the disadvantage of the trade of the country, then he thought the thing should be opposed. (Hear, hear.) There was really too much tendency for the Government in the present day to get hold of this, and that, and the other thing. (Hear, hear.) Let them always remember that the commercial supremacy of this country had been built up upon individual exertions (hear, hear); and that if the foundation of individual and in- dependent exertions amongst a free and unfettered competi- tion was withdrawn, we should become a bureaucratic country, and be content to lose what we otherwise should retain; notwithstanding foreign competition, our great commercial supremacy. (Hear, bear). He would ask the Chamber to consider, and, after due deliberation, memorialise, at the proper time, against the extension of the powers of savings banks. (Hear, hear, and applause). Mr. Wm. LONG expressed his surprise that the Chamber had not a greater number of subscribers in a manufacturing centre like Warrington, and, referring to railway rates, said he had had brought prominently before him, by a personal friend in Liverpool, a local " plateway scheme," which he thought would very successfully compete with railways. The promoters showed that the carriage of goods from Liver- pool to Manchester was now considerably more than it was before the introduction of railways, and the prospectus, assuming the figures to be correct, showed that goods under the system could be carried from Manchester to Liverpool at a nett cost of 25, sd. per ton, the carriage at present being about 11s, per ton. The report was adopted. The election of president, &c., was then proceeeded with, the following being the result :—President, Alderman Davies; vice-president, Mr. C. Broadbent; council, Messrs. Gebrge Artingstall, Henry Bleckly, Thomas Draper' Joseph Davies, Thomas Jolley, Samuel Rigby, George McCorquo- dale, Charles Broadbent, John Dun, Win. Long, Sylvanus Reynolds John Rylands, Fred. Monks, the Mayor (Alder- man Pick;nere), and J. G. McMinnies, M.P. The two last named are ex-officio members. At the conclusion of the business the members sat down to an excellent lunch, provided by4the president and vice- president. "Success to Warrington Chamber of Commerce" was proposed by the President. Mr. Bleckly gave the toast "The health of the President and Vice-President," whith was responded to by Alderman Davies and Mr. Broadbent. The latter gentleman spoke of the good work the Chamber had performed, and referred in flattering terms to Mr. Bleckly's and the President's services. The health of Mr. Artingstall and Mr. Bleckly was proposed by the Mayor. Mr. Artingstall responded, and said he should be glad at all times to promote the interests not only of the Chamber of Commerce, but of the town and trade of Warrington. Mr. ; Bleckly also responded. In the course of his remarks he said there was exported from Warrington very little short of 150,000 tons of iron-per year, and he could recollect that within a few years there was not a ton made in the town. He con- cluded by proposing "The Mayor and Corporation," to which the Mayor responded. to I citis

NEWTON AND EARLESTOWN. NEWTON PETTY SESSIONS.—At these sessions on Saturday, before Col. McCorquodale and Messrs. Gillespie, Houghton, and Pearson, Thomas Howard and James Thompson were each charged with committing a breach of the peace. by fighting at Golborne on the previous Friday night. The Bench °dismissed the charge against Thompson, and a warrant was issued against Howard who failed to appear.— Thomas O'Neil and Michael Fitzgerald, charged with com- mitting a breach of the peace on the highway at Newton, on the previous Saturday afternoon, were each bound over to keep the peace for six months in the sum of £5, each to pay his own expenses.—Margaret Lever was charged with having, on the 23rd January, at Earlestown, made use of threats towards Mary Shemin. A cross summons had been taken out by the defendant in this case charging Shemin with a similar offence. Defendants were each bound over to keep the peace for six months in the sum of £5 each.— Alfred Hughes and Patrick Donoghue were charged with being drunk and disorderly on the highway at Newton, on Sunday the 15th of January. The Bench fined each of the defendants 10s. and costs, or in default 14 days' imprison- ment.—Thomas Manning, Martin Lune, Henry Charnock, Robert Nutrnan, James Critcheley, and Hugh Williams were each fined ss. and costs for drunkenness. NEWTON POLLING DISTRICT CONSERVATIVE ASSOCIATION. —The annual meeting of this associatiou took place on Monday evening at the Newton Town Hall. Mr. Pearson, president of the association, occupied the chair. Tne ac- counts for the past year were passed and a new committee was appointed. Mr. Pearson was re-elected president of the Association, and the vice-presidents, Messrs. Comber and Gillespie, were also re-appointed. The trustees who have held office during the past year were re-elected, and Messrs. John Dixon and W. Melling were again chosen as secretary and treasurer respectively.—The Chairman, in addressing the meeting, spoke of the condition of the association, which he constdered very satisfactory, and in conclusion thanked , them for the honour they had done him by re-electing himn as their president. Mr. Comber also made a few remarks and the proceedings terminated. ASHTON RECREATION SOCIETY.—On Monday evening the annual meeting of this society took place at the Public Hall, Ashton, Mr. W. Bardinan occupied the chair. The b_,lance- sheet showed that the total amount of the receipts was £lO9 Os. Bd. Of this £0 2s. id. was from donations. The honorary subscriptions amounted to £l7 10s., and the or- dinary subscriptions to £4O 18s. The total expenditure was £lO3 3s. 3d. Of this amount £27 s. 'ld. had been spent in constructing a new pavilion, and £lO in laying down a new bowling green. The accounts were unanimously passed.— Mr. Moubert was re-elected president for the ensuing year, and the following other appointments and re-appointments , were made, viz., hon. treasurer, Mr. Valiant; secretaries, Messrs. W. Ross and J. Hill ; captain of bowling club, W. France; sub-captain J. Corless ; captain of cricket club, R. Williams; sub-captain, T. Holdbrook. The former com- mittee, with one or two additional members, was re-elected.

div.head: FOOTBALL.
div.p: FOOTBALL.

RUNCORN SECOND TEAM V. NORTRWICII FIRST TEA:II. A well-contested game was played between these teams at Northwich, on Saturday, and eventually the home team won by 1 goal, 1 poster (disputed), 4 minor points, to Runcorn 2 touchdowns. Mason and Riley played well for the visitors, as did Capper and Forster for Northwich.

RUNCORN TRUE BLUES T. ST. JOHN'S WARRINGTON.— On Saturday last, these teams met on the ground of the latter, in the presence of a moderate number of spectators. Each club was well represented and the play was good. Up
to half-time the Blues had the score in their favour, one try,

one touchdown. After the change of ends, however, the home team pressed the visitors severely and claimed a try, but the Blues disputed, on the ground that Matthews slipr)ed over the ball, and E. Leicester touched it dead first. The ball then dropped out at the twenty-five, and soon the Blues placed the leather behind the goal, but was not improved on; and when no time was called the score was as follows

Blues: Two tries, three minor points. St. John's: One dis- puted try, one minor point. The teams were as follows : True Blues, F. Gaiter, full back; T. Johnson. H. Hankinson, E. Leicester, three-quarter backs; J. Jones, J. Marlow, half; T. Bratt, E. Rawlinson, E. Orme, W. Worthington, J. Ridg- way, H. Russell, J. Howard, J. Snowball, J. Huline, sub- forwards. St. John's: Full back, F. Crank; J. Matthews, A. Robinson; three-quarters, S. Bolton, J. Dumbell ; for- wards Potts, Unsworth, Forster, Ridmore, Fogg, Waywell, Chambers, Baines, Whitfield, Gregory. NORTHWICII (RUGBY) V. RUNCORN (A TEAM).—A match between these teams took place in the Park, Castle-North- wich, on Saturday last. A law and respectable company of spectators assembled to watch-the game. Runcorn made an impetuous attack at the commencement andthe ball was driven into the hands of Johnson, the Northwich back, who returned it by a kick into the Runcorn quarters. The home team followed up the advantage and compelled their opponents to touch down. Next followed a series of splendid runs by Capper and Dutton, but the Runcorn men tackled well, and, keeping the ball well before them they gradually gained ground, and at last obliged Northwich in turn to touch down. From the kick-out Runcorn showed some very good running and passing, but a careless pass at last lost them much ground, and F. Thompson and Dutton ran the ball into dangerous proximity to their goal-line, but the home team only succeeded in obtaining a touch in goal. After changing ends Northwich had the ground in their favour, and soon showed their superiority. Walker took the ball neatly from a scrimmage, and, passing it to Capper, the latter secured the first try, which was quickly converted into a goal by Burgess. Shortly afterwards Runcorn again touched down in self-defence, but Northwich was not to be denied, and Johnson, bringing the ball from the vicinity of his goal-line in fine style into the centre of the field, Capper once more showed himself unapproachable land secured a second try, of the legality of which, however, some of the I Runcorn men professed to be dissatisfied. Eventually the referee was understood to allow it, and the kick for goal re- sulted in a poster. During the last five minutes of play Dutton again showed "in possession," and, by as fine a run as took place during the game, secured a third try. The kick for the goal by Burgess, which was successful, brought the game to a close in favour of Northwich by two goals and a poster to nil. The spectators impartially applauded throughout the game, the points which seemed to most ex- cite their admiratson being the running of Messrs. Capper, Dutton, and Johnson, and the smart collaring of the Run- corn team.

RUNCORN v. CREWE.—The return match between these clubs was played at Runcorn, on Saturday. Bate started the ball for Runcorn, which was well returned up to half- way flag. For some time play was of a very even character; the visitors began to work gradually into the home-team twenty-five, when Roach and Gatley together relieved their lines, forcing the leather back in the Crewe territory. Cowap repeatedly tried to get away, but the tackling of the Run- corn backs was excellent, H. Hughes frequently indulging in short points, which proved of good service to his side. The home team forwards worked well together, and Roach got a smart run across the field, not, however, gaining much headway, the ball going into touch on the throw-out. Wright. made a good attempt to get forward, but was held, scrim- mage being formed. The leather getting loose, the visitors worked up into Runcorn quarters, when Hickton grounded the ball across the line, the place kick, however, proving a failure, On the drcp out, play ensued on neutral ground, each side holding their own. With the ball here, half-time was called. On changing ends, Critchley started the ball, Larkin nicely returning. Redtails working up into Crewe quarters, H. Hughes, getting hold, got close up to the line, when he unselfishly passed to Bro fdy behind him, and that player nicely grounded the leather across the line, Bate landing the ball across the bar. The ball being again sent into play, Crewe following up well, play ensued in the home twenty-five. But not long did it remain so. Larkin making a good run, nicely clearing his lines, and following well up, Crewe was compelled to touch down. Dropping out again, C. Pownall returned well up into neutral ground, Critchley and Cowap working with spirit and making frequent attempts to get off with the leather, but Andrews and Hughes, the home team half-backs, had them set, frustrating all their endeavours to get away. Some good play was then shown on both sides, the ball being taken up to the Crewe lines, where it was held some time, the visitors eventually touching down again. The ball again being put into play, it was forced up to the Runcorn goal-line, but the home team for- wards, with Wright, Bennett, and Cox to the front, cleared the danger, workings up past the half-way post, and Broady, getting hold, got up into the visitors' twenty-five, when the ball was kicked across the line, Harvey touching down a third time. The ball being started, was held in neutral ground some time, when H. Hughes got hold, and got in close proximity to the visitors' line. Here he unluckly slipped, having earlier in the game sprained his ancle, but still holding on to the ball a scrimmage was formed, when Andrews, who had played a really good game all through, got hold, and dodging the half and three-quarter backs, got right behind the posts, for which he was heartily cheered by the spectators. Bate kicked a splendid goal from the place. Dropping out again and followed well up, the visitors looked as if they were going to score, but Larkin, who played a good game, with good judgment kicked into touch close to the half-way flag, thus clearing the danger again. The home team now got the ball on the loose and carried the leather into the visitors' 25, where Hoffiand looked very much like scoring, but the visitors got themselves together and cleared their territory past neutral ground. H. Hughes punted up again to Crewe 25, where play ensued for some time, the home team eventually compelling Harvey to touch down a fourth time. The ball was soon into play again, and play of the give-and-take nature took place. At this point Broady got the ball up into Crewe 25. when scrimmages lasted some time on the visitors' goal line, Andrews nearly scoring another try, the ball however, going into touch. From a line out Bate got hold, but was SOO3 held, with the ball on the visitors' line, no side was called, and a well-contested match ended in favour of Runcorn by two gaols, four touch- downs, to one try to Crewe. • The following were the teams: —Runcorn J. Pownall, full back; Larkin, Broady, and Roach, three-quarter backs ; Andrews and Hughes, half- backs; Bate (captain), Bennett, Wright, Cox, Hoffiand, Gatley, Lewis, C. Pownall, and Gleave, forwards. Crewe; Harvey, full-back; Walker and Talbot, three-quarter backs: Cowap and Hickton, half-backs; Critchley (captain), Fox, Lindrop, Garside, Webber, Day, Howell, Elliot, and Green- all, forwards.

div.head: PRESCOT LOCAL BOARD.
div.p: PRESCOT LOCAL BOARD.

The monthly meeting of the Present Local Board was held on Wednesday evening, in the Board-room, Derby- street, Prescot, Mr. C. Spencely presiding. There were also present :—Messrs. J. Wycherley, T. S. Preston, T. Dennett, J. Mawdsley, and A. T. Galloway; with Mr. H. Cross (clerk), and Mr. Wm. Goldsworth (surveyor).

div.head: GENERAL PURPOSES COMMITTEE.
div.p: GENERAL PURPOSES COMMITTEE.

At a meeting of this Committee, on Monday, the CLERK read a letter from Mr. Thomas Clark, of No. 17, High- street, applying to have his house registered as a lodging- house; also a report of Superintendent Barker thereon, to the effect that until improvements were made in the pre- mises they were unfit and unsanitary.—Resolved, that the same be referred to the medical officer and surveyor to report upon.—The SURVEYOR reported that Mr. Thomas Dennett was not building his house in Eccleston-street in accordance with the plan submitted at the last meeting of the Board. Resolved that the consideration of the same be referred to the meeting of the Board.—The ASSISTANT SUR• VEYOR reported that Mr. James Appleton was building a room over Mr. Coffey's workshop in the Market-place with- out having submitted a plan.—The Surveyor was directed to see Mr. Appleton thereon.—lt was resolved that the com- plaint about Mr. Dennett's house in Eccleston-street be referred back to the General Purposes Committee for Mr. Dennet to submit an amended plan. REGISTRAR'S REPORT. The REGISTRAR'S report showed that during the month of January there had been 15 births in the district as com- pared with 14 in the corresponding month of last year. The deaths numbered 18; corresponding month, last year, 14; death rate, per thousatd, 33.65, as compared with 28•04 in the corresponding month of last year. Two deaths had oc- curred from scarlet fever, and five from bronchitis.

A STRANGE CAUSE OF A FIRE.—Tbe Story goes that in ancient days, Archimedes, the famous mechanician 'of Syracuse, succeeded in destroying the ships of an enemy by directing the rays of the sun upon them through burning- glasses. A house in Massachusetts was nearly burnt down last summer in much the same way. On a very hot day smoke was observed to come from the sunny side of the house, and it was found that a hole had been burnt through the boarding of the dwelling, which would have been des- troyed but for the timely discovery'. A supply of water soon put an end to all danger, and on searcaing for the cause of the fire it was found a few feet distant in a pile of bright tin milk-pans, some of which were placed so as to concentrate the rays of the fierce sun upon a small part of the surface of the boards.—From Little Folks Jragazine for February.
