div.head: WIDNES POLICE COURT.
div.p: WIDNES POLICE COURT.

MONDAY :—Before Messrs. George Pilkington and Holbrook Gaskell, junr. A SHOP THIEF CAUGHT IN THE ACT.—HonOra. O'Neil, a middle-aged woman, was charged with stealing Sibs. of ham, the property of Mr. Samuel Sadler, grocer, Anne-street, West. Mr. John Holland, shop manager to the prosecutor, stated that about a quarter to ten on Saturday night, the prisoner entered the shop, and, after looking round, went out without purchasing anything; As she did so, he ob- served her pick up a piece of ham, which was worth ss. 4d. Be went after her, and charged her with the robbery, but she denied it, though she afterwards admitted her guilt.— The prisoner elected to be dealt with summarily, and, as she had been previously convicted of felony, she was sent to gaol for three months, with hard labour. WEDNESDAY—Before Mr. Holt (chairman) and Mr. E. K. Muspratt. SERIOUS CHARGE AGAINST A LANDLORD. Thomas Kearnan was summoned for having been drunk on the licensed premises known -as the Main Top Hotel, Mersey- road, and Mr. Thomas Littler, the landlord, for permitting drunkenness on his premises, and also for supplying drink to an intoxicated person. Mr. W. T. Husband appeared for the defence. P.C. Laing stated that on the 19th ult., he was on duty in Mersey-road with Sergeant Clarkson and P.C. Irving, when they saw the defendant going on the street drunk, and another man holding his arm to prevent him falling. Kearnan next walked into Main Top Hotel, and immediately afterwards they went into the house and found him standing at the counter, with a glass of hot whiskey before him. He called the attention of the land- lady to the state of the man, and she replied that she did not think he was drunk, or she would not have served him. Sergeant Clarkson and P.C. Irvin.. gave -evidence in sup- port of the case.—Mr. Husband then addressed the -Bench for the defence, and said that no one would suppose that if Kearaan were drunk, he became so through the liquor which he:had at the hotel. He pointed out that the two charges preferred again thc landlord were substantially the same; and it was provided by the Licensing Act that in order to constitute the offence, it must be proved that it was com- mitted with the privity, knowledge, assent, and connivance of defendant. In this case it was quite evident that there had been neither connivance nor privity on the part of Mr. Littler. The defendant and another man entered the bar hurriedly, whilst Mrs. Littler was in the parlour, and when she took their 'alders they were standing quietly, so that there was no sign made by Kearnan which wonld lead her to come to the conclusion that he was drunk.—Mrs. Littler was then called, and stated that she and her husband had kept the Main Top Hotel since 1866, and during the whole of that time had never had any trouble with the police. a She corroborated the statements made by her solicitor, and added that a sovereign was tendered her in payment for the Vrs liquor supplied, and she went upsiairs for the change. When she came down, she found the police officers in the re; house. On having her attention called particularly to Kearnan, she noticed that he had had something to drink, but did not consider him drunk. Had she known be was intoxicated, she should not have served him. In reply to Superintendent Barker, witness stated that on coming down stairs, the glass of whiskey was on the counter, and she allowed Kearnan to drink it, not being possessed of sufficient presence of mind to tell him not to do so.—Kearnan was also put in the box, and confirmed the landlady's statement. In reply to the Superintendent of Police, he said he was not drunk on the day in question, but he would not swear that he was quite sober.—fhe magistrates said the case against Kearnan was clearly proved, and he would be fined ss. and 7s. 6d. costs. They were also of opinion that the landlord had not exercised sufficient caution in serving a drunken man, and he v, oald be fined 20s. and costs for selling the drink to Kearnan. The other charge would be dismissed. WARRANT.—Martin Weir, who did not appear, was charged with assaulting Selina Keenahan, on the 22nd ult., and a warrant was issued for his apprehension. THE SCHOOL BOARD AT WORK.—The following were each ordered to pay 55., including costs, for not sending their children to school :—William Smith, Henry Burgess, Edward Scrutton, Daniel Brown, Mary Bower, Richard Glassey, John Murphy, aud Thomas Coffey. Mr. G. H. Danby, clerk, appeared on behalf of the School Board. WEAK CASES.—Dennis Dorman was summoned for caus- ing a breach of the peace of the peace in Travis-street, on the 21st ult.—The case was dismissed on defendant paying costs.--Elizabeth Checkett was charged with assaulting P.C. Anderson in the execution of his duty.—The officer stated that whilst he was taking a prisoner to the police station, the defendant got hold of his arm and made a slight attempt at rescue.—Superintendent Barker said he did not wish to press the case against defendant, and the summons was dismissed. THE RESULT OF A VISIT TO THE MARKET HOTEL.— Joseph Gerrard and William Gerrard were summoned for a breach of the Highway Act.—P.C. Skinner proved that on the 24th ult. the defendants left their carts in Catherine- street for upwards of 10 minutes, whilst they were "wetting their whistles" in the Market Hotel.—Each defendant was fined 2s. 6d., and ss. 6d. costs. Asa UNFEELING HonsE OWNElL—Edward Mulvey, owner, and Bernard McGee, carter, were charged with cruelty to a horse.—lnspector Allen, of the R.S.P.C.A., proved seeing the defendant McGee driving the animal, which was attached to a cart in Croft-street. The horse was in a very low condi- tion, and there was a wound four inches in length on its croup. The wound was covered with loose sacking. He afterwards saw Mulvey, who said he did uot know of the condition of the animal. He warned him that he must not work it again, but on the 24th ult. he saw McGee driving the horse, and the sore had been roughly covered with a composition resembling tar.—A fine of fs. 6d. and 13s. 6d. costs in each case was inflicted. AN OLD COAL STEALER CAUGHT IN THE ACT.—James Mullens was charged with stealing coal, value fourpence, the property of the London and North-Western Railway Company.—The evidence showed that the other evening P.C. Laing and a detective belonging to the Company, named Wilkinson, caught the prisoner taking the coal from beneath a wagon, the Marsh.—The Superintendent of Police said there were two previous convictions against the prisoner for similar offences, and, under these circumstances, the man was sent for trial at the Liverpool Quarter Sessions. A WARNING TO ANNOYERS OF THE LOCAL BOARD IN- sPEcToß.—Peter Fenney, labourer, was summoned for using defamatory language to Mr. John Dickson, nuisance inspector to the Widnes Local Board.—The Complainant said that on the 29th ult., he was passing on Victoria-road, and when near the police station, he heard some one calling him various filthy names. On turning round, he saw several young men, and defendant formed one of the csmpany. On seeing that he was watching them, they ran behind a wall, but only to emerge and call out in a most insulting manner, as soon as he had walked on. This conduct was repeated several times. He went into the police station and got a constable to .o with him, to see if they could find any of the rascals, but they had disappeared. The case should have come on for hearing at the Petty Sessions on the pre- vious Wednssday, but on the Tuesday night the defendant came to him, assured him that he was not guilty, and promised that if the proceedings against him were stayed, he would give up the name of the real offenders. He, there- fore, obtained an adjournment of the case. Subsequently the defendant gave up the name of a youth called Roscoe, who, in turn, accused Feeney. He (witness) felt perfectly sure that the defendant was the guilty man. For six years he had been annoyed in this most irritating manner. Young men and lads were the most guilty, but in low quarters of the town, young women and even little children bad taken up the cry. The prosecution was supported by the Local Board, and he thought it was only fair that the servants of that body should be protected in the discharge of their duties. One conviction had already been obtained.—ln reply to the Deputy Magistrates' Clerk (Mr. Lewin), complainant said the language used was such that he had at times thought that if he were stronger he should commit a breach of the Deace.—Thomas Roscoe was then called, and said he was in Victoria-road on the day, at the time in question, and he did not hear any bad language used. James Calligan stated that he heard abusive epithets bestowed on Mr. Dick- son by defendant, but he could not swear to the exact words. —After hearing some further evidence, the Chairman said the magistrates did not doubt that very disgraceful language had been used to complainant by defendant, and it was their duty to put a stop to such conduct. The defendant would be sent to gaol for one month, in default of finding sureties to keep the peace six months, himself in £lO and two sureties in £5 each.

div.head: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held this morning. Mr. Lea presided, in the absence of the Rev. Canon Barclay, and there were also present the Rev. W. Bennelly, and Messrs. Briscoe Norman, Pritchard, and Rigby (clerk.)—A bill was laid be fore the Board from Mr. George Yarwood, 59 Church-street, amounting to £3 3s. 711, for painting done at Mill Brow school.—Mr. Briscoe, Mr. Norman, and the Rev. W. Fennel ly made observations to the effect that the work was not executed so well as it might have been, and the charge made for it was considerably too much it was resolved that Mr. Yarwood should be asked to reconsider the charge, with the object of reducing it.—The Clerk read the certificate of the auditor as to the Board's yearly accounts —Mr. Bowyer, he school attendance officer, presented his monthly report, which was as follows :—Certified Government accommoda- tion, 2,323 ; number on the rolls 2.822; average attendance, 1972.4; average attendance for January, 1881, 1483.51; average attendance for the year 1874, 1,2:52; accommodation in excess of average attendance, 3506; number on the rolls in excess of accommodation, 499. These figures show an increase in the average attendance, as compared with the corresponding period of last year, of 488.8, and an increase, as compared with 1874, the year preceding the formation of the Board, of 7204.. The total number in attendance at private adventure schools under ninepence per week, is 61. At the usual attendance committee, held on the 18th ult., I reported 62 parents for the irregular and non-attendance of their children at school. 37 arents appeared before the com- mittee in answer to their notices, and two applications were nude for half time, and granted; seven parents applied for school fees, and, after enquiry by the committee, the fees of 12 children were recommended to be paid by the Board of Gaardians. Thirty parents were ordered to be served with cal notices, and the remaining cases were adjourned for a rtnight in order to be further dealt with at the discretion of Beard, These cases I again lay before you showing their eelance for the quarter ending December 23rd, 1881, and ..$o for the past month.—The ether business before the ioard was not of public interest.

div.head: RUNCORN POLICE COURT.
div.p: RUNCORN POLICE COURT.

MoisslT.—Before Mr. Charles Reynolds (chairman) and Mr. Thomas. CHARGE AGAINST A WESTON SCHOOLMASTER.-Mr. Frederick Morris, schoolmaster to the River Weaver Trus- tees at Weston, was summoned for assaulting Alfred Wil- liams, a lad aged nine years.—The complainant's mother said that on the 20th ult. the boy was sent to school, and when he started he was all right in health. He came home about a quarter to twelve for the purpose of taking his brother's dinner to the quarry. She found the lobe of his left ear was burst, and that it was bleeding very much, and discoloured. The ear had been bad ever since, and though kept clean, bad continued to fester. She thought it was not right for a schoolmaster to use his hand in striking scholars on the head; he ought to use a cane. This was not the first time defendant had abused both the boy and his sister.— Cross-examined by Mr. Burton, who appeared for the defence: —I believe you took your -son back to the school after- wards ? Yes.—Did you threaten, before all the scholars, to knock the master's neck out? Yes.—ln reply to further questions, witness said she had been with the lad to the Rev. Adam Ford and Mr. Bankes, J.P. The neighbours had urged her to summon defendant, "for he was nothing but a brute to the children." She bad not taken complainant to a medical man.—The lad was called, and said that defendant hit him on the ear twice with his open hand.—A girl named Susan Tinsley stated that she saw defendant hit the boy twice on the ear, and afterwards gave him a rag to wipe the blood from it.—Dr. McDougall said that on the previous Monday he saw the complainant in the court room, and examined his ear very carefully. There was not the slightest appearance of any assault having been committed upon him. If merely a blow had been given the complainant on the ear, with the open hand as described, it would have been utterly impossible to produce such a sore. The ap- pearance which the sore presented arose from the character- istic condition of the body of complainant. Such lacerated sores as that upon the lad's ear formed a peculiar kind of matter, and the scab frequently shelled off naturally. There was not the slightest bruise, or discolouration, to show that an assault had been committed. The slightest touch would cause such a scale to fall off—even a person rubbing against it with his clothes. In answer to the Bench, the witness , said a blow with the open hand could not possibly cause bleeding of the ear unless there had been a wound theie be- fore. He was of opinion that the sore was on the boy's ear at the time the blow was given.—Frederick G. Morris, about 14 years of age, said he assisted his father in the school, on the books of which there were about 120 scholars. He was about six yards from his father at the time of the alleged assault. He saw defendant go up to complainant, who was in the third class, and say, "My boy, your writing is very bad, and you don't improve." Defendant then hit him with two of the fingers of his right hand. The blow could not I fairly be called "a box on the ear." As soon as his father had hit complainant, his ear began to bleed, and he corn- mencld to crv. His father then observed the scale from the ear lying on the copy book, and remarked, "My boy, your ear has been sore before." Some time afterwards corn- , plainant's mother came to the school, said she would knoels I defendant's neck out, and used very vile language, on which I defendant said if she would come into the school he would tell her all about it.—A youth named Richard Clarke Rosenberg, aged eight years, said defendant merely hit the lad with 'his open hand.—Eliza Yarwood, aged nine years, also gave evidence for the defence. —Mr. Burton said the defendant had been a schoolmaster for twenty-one years, and for four of those be had been in charge of the school at Weston, belonging to the River Weaver truestees, which he had conducted to the entire satisfaction of his employers. He did not deny that on the day in question defendant found fault with the boy, and touched him on the ear, but he used no unnecessary violence. Never, under any circumstances, did defendant box the ears of any of the scholars. The only punishment he inflicted was with the cane. Mr. Morris had had to complain re- , peatedly of the complainant's conduct. He submitted that 1, the evidence he had called was entitled to the consideration, of the Bench, and that his client had not used any force beyond that which he was allowed to exercise to the chil- dren under his charge.—The Chairman said the summons would be dismissed.—Mr. Burton applied for costs, but the magistrates said they could not allow them.—Each party would, therefore, have his own costs to paw. ALLEGED ASSAULT ON AN OLD WOMAN. A powerful- looking man, named Patrick Haverty, was charged with a savage assault on Catherine Ford, about 70 years of age.— Complainant said that on the evening of the 14th ult. she was entering the Royal Hotel for the purpose of seeing whether her husband was there, when the defendant used most foul language to her, though she had not spoken a word to him, knocked her down, and kicked her on the side with his clogs. Haverty sent the onions and other things she was carrying into the street, and abused her so that she became insensible for some time, or, as she put it, " sant her into a trance." She had not been able to put down hc • head on a Pillow for a fortnight.—ln cross-examination complainant said her husband was not present," or defend- ant would not have had all the fun to himself."—The magis- trates said they would adjourn the CAS3 for a week, in order that the old woman might c ill a material witness, and Superintendent Williamson warned her that she would not be allowed to compromise the matter, which it was alleged defendant had been trying to do.—Haverty denied the charge, and said the old woman wrs drinking in the hotel at the time of the alleged assault.

div.head: GOLBORNE,
div.p: GOLBORNE,

- - FOOTBALL: EARLESTOWN 2ND. V. GOLBORNE 2ND.—The return match was played on Saturday last, between the above clubs, on the ground of the former. After a well. contested game, Golborne succeeded in again defeating their opponents by one gaol to none. MISSION SERMONS.—On Sunday, morning and evening, sermons were preached in the Congregational Church on behalf of the London Missionary Society by the Rev. P. Webster, of Preesail. The church was well attended at both services, and collections were made in aid of the mission fund.

----- . GOLBORNE AND DISTRICT LIBERAL ASSOCIATION.—On Friday evening week, the annual meeting was held in the Independent Methodist School, when officers for the ensuing year were elected. There was a good attendance. The president, Mr. John Unsworth, presided, and was re-elected, as were also the general secretary, the political secretary, and financial secretary. Votes of thanks were given to all for their past services. A committee was then elected for the ensuing year by ballot. Everything passed off in a most enjoyable manner, every one feeling pleased at the way in which the business was conducted. MAKERFIELD PLOUGHING SOCIETY..—The twenty-sixth annual meeting of the Makerfield Ploughing Society took place on Thursday in a field at Haydock Park, Newton, in the occupation of Mr. Hutton Wright. There were no entries in the double-furrow classes, while in the single- furrow classes twelve had entered and eleven put in an ap- pearance. In the second class there were 43 entries and 38 competitors, and the five who had sent in their names in the youths' event all turned up on the mark. The field is one that is fairly well adapted for the purpose for which it was used, and is something like 25 Cheshire acres in extent. At the close of the competition the members of the society and their friends adjourned to the Pied Bull Hotel, Newton, where a firs t-class dinner was served to upwards of 200 gentlemen. CONSERVATIVE LECTURE AT GOLBORNE.—On Tuesday evening, a public lecture was delivered in Mr. Brewis's school, In connection with the Conservative Club, by Mr. Byron Reed, of Darlington. The room was crowded very soon after the doors were opened. It was soon evident that the Liberals had assembled in great force, and the Conserva- tives, although they were joined by their Leigh friends, were evidently in a minority. Mr. Brewis president of the club, announced to preside, was absent, and the chair was taken by Mr. R. Y. Woollacott, who very briefly introduced the lecturer. Mr. Reed, on rising was heartily cheered‘ by all present. His subject was "A review of the policy of the Ipresent Government." He commenced with Mr. Gladstone's Midlothian campaign, which he condemned, and held LID Mr. Gladstone as a man whom the country had no conti-

den-ce in. The epithets he used were rather strong at this point, and brought up one of the Liberals, who objected to the epithets used. This caused a slight interruption. How- ever, the lecturer proceeded, and after a few remarks as to the interference by the Liberal gentlemen, began to speak of John Bright, and used some strong language with regard to that gentleman's policy. He said that Mr. Bright was no friend to the working classes, and would go down to the grave execrated by the workingmen. Afterwards he speke of Mr. Gladstone's letter of apology to Count Karolyi, of Austria, and the humiliation attendant thereupon. Austria was a country of progress while the surrounding nations were not so. He condemned the present Government on their policy in the Transvaal. He touched upon the Irish Land Act, and said it was an Act of spoliation. He praised Lord Beacons- field's manifesto on Ireland in 1880. He also criticised the conduct of the Government on the oaths question, and after- wards referred to the cloture, and condemned it most strongly. He next adverted to questions which would have to be dealt with next session. The Artizans' Dwellings Act and a few other measures he mentioned as being passed by the late Government, and said he hoped the Conservatives would soon be in power again —Mr. Hall, political secretary of the Liberal Association, challenged Mr. Reed, and offered to meet him en any public platform in Golborne, at his own time and place, and discuss point by point the assertions he had made.—Mr. Reed excused himself owing to engage- ments, but he would leave himself in the hands of his Con- servative friends.—A vote of thanks was given to the lecturer and chairman at the close of the meeting.

THE NORTHWIC2 GAS BILL, which is one to dissolve the present limited Company and re-incorporate it, came before Mr. Robinson, one of the examiners of the House of Commons, on Monday, for the purpose of complying with the standing orders of the House. The limits of the new Company are to include the townships of Northwich, Castle Northwich, Witton-cum-Twanbrooks, Rudheath Lordship, Wennington, Hartford, Anderton, Barnton, Lostock Gralam, Wincham, Daveoham, Leftwich, Shurlach- cum-Bradford, Shipbrook, Moulton, and Ealon, in the county of Cheshire. The capital of the Company is to be £50,000, whereof £24,000 is original capital. The promoters ask to l,orrow in respect of original capital £6,000, and of the additional capital £6,500. The number of directors is to be seven, the first directors being Messrs. Thomas Davis, Thomas Barlow, William Caldwell, John Moore, Wm. Starkey, Johnson Fletcher, and Thomas Caleb Hughes. The standing orders were complied with.

Well," the tenant said, "tell Mr. Birchall that when he will extend my contract and give me certain accommodations belonging to a dairy farm, such as I want, I will under- take to say that I will never sell another truss of ha ras long as I live." Now, Mr. Birchall understood what manufacturing was, and he understood the advantage of increased production in manufacture, and he increased the farmstead again and again as this man wanted him. When the man went to the farm his predecessor had kept eight head of cattle, and on this 160 acres at the present time this person was keeping 75 head of cattle. (Loud ap- plause.) There was another thing. There was one field on the farm that, when this gentleman went upon it, had never in the memory of any man living produced anything worth selling, and it had got a name—they knew the rude wit of Lancashire people—which signified bareness to the greatest extent they could imagine. A friend of Mr. Pearson's said to him, "Well, Thomas, do you know," mentioning the field which everybody knew by its rude appellation, "that is part of this farm? " "Yes, I do, and I am sorry for it." But he set to work on this field of 10 acres which had never produced anything, and he manured it and drained it in a satisfactory way, and last year this field paid the whole of his rent, £250. He raised 500 loads of potatoes upon it, and sold them at 103. a load. Knowing these things, and sup- posing they gave farmers a fair chance—which they did not—did not they think the fanners of this country were well able to take care of themselves, and to compete with all the world? (Hear, hear.) We had the best climate in the world, taking it all round, for farming. He should like people to get it into their heads that the farmer was a manu- facturer of food. In every other manufacture Englishmen were able to compete with foreigners. The manufacturer of cotton, iron, woollen, glass, or silk, licked the whole world into fits, and he feared no foe. So should the farmer. He would not take to their time further, but he hoped what he had said would have some good effect. (Applause). The motion was carried with acclamation. The remainder of the business was of a private character.
FRODSHAM.

div.p: ST. HELENS POLICE COURT,

DRUNK IN CHARGE OF A HORSE-AND CART.—WnI. Lloyd, of Frodsham Lordship, was summoned at the Eddisbury Petty Sessions, on Monday, for being drunk whilst in charge of a horse and cart at Frodsham Lordship, on December 27th, and was fined ss. and costs. TRESPASSING IN PURSUIT OF GA3lE.—William Stubbs, an old man, was charged at the Eddishury Petty Sessions, on Monday, with being found on a certain highway within the county, returning from land whereon he had been unlawfully in search of game; and Samuel Stubbs, his son, was charged with aiding and abetting—P.C. Wright stated that he was on duty on the highway at Kingsley, leading from the Frod- sham road to the Forest. He met the two defendants com- ing from land belonging to M. Horton and saw they had something in their pockets. They said they had been ferret- ing, but acknowledged that they had no permission to do so. They showed him the ferrets, and witness then asked if they had anything else about them. They said " No," but on being searched a gun stock and barrel, a ramrod, two snares with fresh soil on each, and also two nets were found. Flasks containing powder and shot were also found upon them, but no rabbits. Plaintiffs denied that they had used the articles for an unlawful purpose.—Wm. Stubbs was fined 20s. and costs, and the other defendant was discharged. FRODSHAM CRICKET CLUB.—ANNUAL GENERAL MEET- IN'G.—This meeting was :held in the Girls' School, Frod- sham, on Monday evening when Mr. Frank Hilditch, the retiring captain, presided, and there was a good representa- tive muster of upwards of 20 members. The hon. secretary, Mr. Samuel Davies, produced the statement of account for the past year, from which it appeared that the total receipts amounted to £76 14s. 50. and the payments to £72 17s. sp. leaving a balance in favour of the club of £3 16s. 11d. The following officers and committee were appointed for the season viz. :—Officers Rev. H. B. Blogg, M.A., president; Mr. Charles Reynolds, Mr. James Reynolds, Mr. Alfred Thomas, Mr. E. A. Wright, vice-presidents: captain, Mr. Henry Reynolds; sub-captain, Rev. A. P. Reynolds ; hon. sec. and treasurer, Mr. Samuel Davies ; committee, Charles E. Linaker, W. D. Jolliffe, R. E. Walford, Frank Hilditch, H. G. Linaker, Daniel Ashton and George Rigby ; auditors, Mr. Thomas Riley and Mr. Henry Tiley. FRODSHAM PRIMITIVE METHODIST CHAPEL.—SERVICE OF SONG.—On Tuesday eveming, a service of song, entitled, "The Pioneers of Primitive Methodism," with illustrative readings, and old hymns and tunes as sung by the early Primitive Methodists, was given in the above chapel, by the choir. The service is the compilation of the Rev. T. Mitchell, and the history of Primitive Methodism, from its commencement is admirably arranged, and interspersed with hymns set to tunes which doubtless carry the minds of early members of the church to scenes which have long been recorded in the past. The progress of Primitive Methodism must have been very rapid as it appears that the community was only formed a little over seventy years ago, and was helped on by the exertions of Messrs. Clowes and Bowine, names which will ever be remembered in the history of Primitive Methodism. We gather from the service that the Connexional statistics in 1851 were preachers 551 members 108,781, chapels 1,662, Sunday scholars 112,568, resnits which speak eloquently for the labour of forty years. The connective readings of the service were read by Mr. W. B. Gibson and Rev. D. Schofield; and the choir deserve all praise for the very efficient rendering of the music. Miss Thomas and Master Hough sang effectively in the piece "My heart is fixed, eternal God." Mr James Hough presided at the organ throughout. A vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Gibson, on the motion of the Rev. D. Scho- field, seconded by Mr. Ashley, of Runcorn, and Mr. Hinde, ef Norley, proposed, and Mr. John Rimmer, of Frodsham, seconded, a vote of thanks to the choir. s A FRODSHAM PUBLICAN CONVICTED OF PERJURY. On Saturday, at the Manchester Assizes, before Mr. Jnstice Chitty, William Youd, innkeeper, Frodsham' Cheshire. was indicted for having at Salford, in August last, committed wilful and corrupt perjury. On the sth of August the prisoner, who keeps the Bear's Paw Inn, Frodsham, appeared at the Salford Police Court in response to a summons, charg- ing him with being the father of the child of a young woman who had taken out the summons. The prisoner during the hearing of the case' denied the young woman's statement, I and said that he had never promised to marry her and settle £5OO upon her. An affiliation order was made against the prisoner, who gave notice of appeal. He, however, did not carry the case further, but made an arrangement with the woman, under which she released him from all obligation to her upon the payment of £l3O. Evidence was now given to show that the prisoner's evidence before the magistrates was untrue.—For the defence, it was shown that on the morning of the hearing of the case the prisoner had been drinking somewhat heavily, and when he entered the witness box he was not in a proper condition to give evidence. It I was argued that he was not prepared before hearing the woman's statement to admit that he was the father of the child, and with his mind clouded by drink he made assertions the effect of which he did not clearly see. Mr. Gully (for the defence) maintained that under these circumstances. , though his conduct in the police court was reprehensible, I the prisoner was not guilty of the offence of perjury.—The prisoner's solicitor, Mr. Linaker, junior, of Runcorn, stated , that he appeared for the prisoner at the hearing of the bastardy summons. He considered that when the prisoner I was examined he was under the influence of drink, and not fit to give evidence, although his condition might not have been apparent to the people in the court generally. After asking the prisoner two or three questions, he (Mr. Linaker) gave up the examination. —ln cross- examination. Mr. Linaker said he did not tell any one in court that 'in his opinion Youd was under the influence of drink.—Several witnesses gave the prisoner an excellent character.—His Lordship, in summing up the case, said there was a general rule of law that drunkenness was no defence; but, 67 course, the condition in regard to drunken- ness of a man when he was giving evidence might have some bearing on the point of whether what he said be said deliberately and intentionally. For the benefit of persons engaged in litigation, he might state that if they were aware that a witness was not in a fit state to give evidence, they ought to give some information to the Court of the fact, in order that the trial might be adjourned. A practitioner find- ing his own client in this condition might perhaps scarcely know what course to take. It was certainly in Mr. Linaker.'s favour that when he perceived the state of the prisoner he dropped his examination. It would be a most dangerous thing to allow a man to get off in a case of this kind on the ground of drunkenness; but if the jury were satisfied the prisoner was in such a state of mind at the time in question, that substantially he was not intending to deceive, they might take a merciful view of the case.—The prisoner was fcund guilty. Sentence was deferred. On Monday Youd was put up for sentence. His Lordship said the crime was a serious one in any person, and it was most serious in a man like the prisoner, who had until the present time stood before the world as of high character. His defence was that he was drunk when he was examined in Court; but the jury, who had taken all the circumstances into consideration' had in substance negatived that, and it was quite plain that all those who heard him at the time treated him as if he was not a drunken man. He should be very sorry that such a defence should be admitted in a case unless proved most conclusively—in fact, that a man did not know what he was doing. Looking at the nature of the per- jury—it was not one answer as to the paternity of the child; it was a detailed statement—he felt, too, compelled to, call attention to this, that in fact the prisoner charged the unfor- tunate young woman who was the mother of the child with committing deliberate perjury, both she and her sister. He bore in mind the good character the prisoner had, although the high reputation of a man made the crime in one sense more dangerous to society, because his character made him more readily believed when he was on his oath. He bore in mind, also, the ruin which the verdict would perhaps entail upon the prisoner; and would endeavour, in dealing with the case, to temper justice with mercy. The sentence was that he be imprisoned and kept to hard labour for six months.

GRAND CONCERT.—A great treat is in store for lovers of music in the St. Helens district, in the concert promoted by Mr. Geo. Barton, and arranged for Monday next, in the Town Hall. It is always delightful to bear Madame Patey, and with such vocalists, in addition, as Miss Maggie Juanita Jones, Mr. Geo. Barton, Mr. F. Gordon, and the choir of Mr. W. H. Jude, of Liverpool, an entertainment of a thoroughly enjoyable character may be expected. Mr. Jude will also give two solos ou the harmonium.

FRlDAY.—Before Messrs. H. S. Hall and T. Pilkington. SELLING DURING PROHIBITED HOURS.—Wm. Thompson was charged with selling drink during prohibited hours.— P.C. Rhymer stated that at 20 minutes past 11 on the night of the 16th January he was passing defendant's beerhouse, in Ashcroft-street, when he saw defendant's daughter stand- _ _

, . log just within the door. He got about five yards past, when she bolted the door. Hearing voices of men inside, he went to the door and demanded admittance. Some one inside asked who he was, and he replied that he was a policeman, and wanted the door opening. After a considet- able time had elapsed he got in, and stopped a Alan in the lobby named John McHugh, who resided at 4, Bolton-st. Three men were sitting in the kitchen with their coats off.

Thy said they were lodgers. Witness spoke to the land- lord about the matter, and the landlord replied he was under the impression it was not 11 o'clock.—ln answer to Supt. Johnston, witness said there was sufficient time to move any drink while he was at the door.—Defendant said his clock was rather late; it was quite a mistake, but there was no drink stirring at all.—Superintendent Johnston said there was nothing against the defendant, but there were three convictions against the house.—Fined £2 125., and the license to be endorsed. WHEELING A BARROW ON THE FOOTPATH.—John Rim- mer, a lad, was fined is. and costs for wheeling a barrow on the footpath in Higher Parr-street on the previous Saturday. ASLEEP IN CART.—Michael Tansey was fined 2s. 6d. and costs for being asleep in his cart whilst driving along Rainford-road, Windle, on Thursday afternoon. ASSAULT ON A WOMAN.—James McCormick was charged with assaulting and beating Ann McGhee on the 21st Jan.— Complainant said that on the day in question she went into High-street to see a person there on a matter of business. Defendant came out of a house in that street, and said, "What are you going about this place for ?" and followed up those remarks by kicking her very much. If she had not taken refuge in a house defendant would have given her an awful kick on the back.—Defendant said the com- plainant came in the street and commenced to make a row, and when he spoke to her she began an altercation with him, and said she would fetch her husband, who was every inch a man, to give him a good thrashing.—Defendant was fined 40s. and costs, or one month's imprisonment.—lt was stated that defendant had been previously convicted of similar offences.

SELLING ARTIFICIAL FLOWERS.—John McKenna was charged with hawking artificial flowers without having a certificate authorising him so to do.—Defendant said he had sold artificial flowers 14 years without having a certifi- cate.—He was fined ss. and costs, or seven days in default. BEGGING.—John Lea was charged with wandering abroad in Union-street to beg.—P.C. Cottam saw prisoner go to two doors in that street and receive two pieces of coin. There were four men in the street attempting to sing, but who made a hideous noise. Three of the men decamped.— Prisoner, who said he was called by the neighbours, who

gave him bread, was sent to gaol for 14 days. CHARGE OF THEFT.—Peter Fairclough, one of Messrs. Greenall's lurry drivers, was charged with stealing two Venetian blinds from an unoccupied house at Eccleston at half-past four o'clock on Friday, the 6th January.—Joseph Finney, keeper of the Soldier's Inn, St. Helens-rcad, Pres- cot, said that in November last he kept the Sportsman's Arms, and when he lef tthe window blinds there. On the 7th January he saw they had gone, and he gave that informa- tion to the police.—John Ashall (10) said his parents lived ' near the empty beerhouse in question, and on the 6th Jan. he saw the prisoner, whose horse and lurry were standing in the road, break in the door of the tap-room and enter. He then saw prisoner up at the window taking down the blinds. Prisoner came out, placed them on the brewer's cart, and drove on.—P.C. Millington apprehended prisoner on the 24th January and charged him with the thef t.— Prisoner replied, " I know nothing about it."—Mr. J. 0. Swift appeared on behalf of the prisoner, whose character, he said, was irreproachable. It was utterly impossible to conceive that a man in his senses would go into a house, and in the presence of a boy, with neighbours near, take down the blinds, and drive away with them. Prisoner was certainly on the road, and so were other drivers of brewery carts, aud one of them had a horse similar to that which ' was under the control of the prisoner.—Evidence was given by John Taylor, who has management of the carts at the brewery, and he said that no blinds were on the lurry when it reached the yard. Prisoner had been with Messrs. Green- all eleven years, and had never been found guilty of dis- honesty.—Two drivers said they were in the road and saw prisoner after the time of the alleged theft, but they saw nothing on the lurry but barrels.—The Bench dismissed the case.
MONDAY.—Before Messrs. H. S. Hall and T. Pilkington.

A WOUNDING CASE—Elizabeth Moore, a young woman, was charged with wounding a young woman named Polly Turner.—Superintendent Johnston said the prosecutrix was unable to be present in court, and after sufficient evidence had been given he would ask for a remand for eight days.-- Ann Swift, wife of Thomas Swift, who keeps a beerhouse in Bridge-street, said that between nine and ten o'clock on Saturday night she was in attendance there. She served five persons, amongst whom was the prisoner, with porter and lemonade. Witness went back into the vaults, and im- mediately after prisoner followed and said in a very loud tone "What have you brought this rotten stuff for." Witness said it was not rotten and that she had already served several people with it; and that perhaps prisoner's mouth was out of order. Prisoner said her mouth was better than witness's. After some further language between them witness went out, and prisoner threw the porter on the hearth and fire-grate. Witness went back and asked her why she had done that. An altercation ensued between them, and witness threatened to have her put out. Prisoner said she would do what she liked and threatened to throw a glass of something in witness's face. Witness then called Polly Turner, at whom prisoner threw a glass, and with another glass thumped her on the 1124 and broke the glass in the operation. The head was wounded in many places, and had been stiched in two places by Dr. Reid, who had seen prosecutrix twice since the affair, and was of opinion that she was unable to go out for four or five days, or, probably, a week.—Prisoner said that "three of them" had her on the floor, and the glass was broken by being knocked off the table. She never took a glass in her hand.—Remanded till Monday. AN OBSTINATEFELLOW.—John Connelly was charged with being drunk on licensed premises and refusing to quit when requested to do so. A police constable said that at ten minutes to seven on Saturday night he went to the Lord Nelson Inn, occupied by "John Whalley, Oldfield-street, Windle. The landlord, in witness's presence, requested prisoner to leave the premises twice, but the prisoner re- fused to do so. Witness then requested him to leave two or three times, but he still refused, and witness was obliged to eject him. With the assistance of a sergeant he took the prisoner in custody.—Fined 10s. and costs or 14 days. A CAUTION TO BEERHOUSE KEEPERS. Alice Rimmer, beerhouse keeper at Parr, was charged with having, on the 22nd January, unlawfully permitted drunkenness to take place on her licensed premises at Parr; also with selling intoxicating liquors to Francis Bromilow, who was drunk, and further with unlawfully opening her house, for the sale of intoxicating liquors, at a time when it ought to have been closed.—Sergeant Banks said the defendant was a beerseller, and kept "The three pigeons" at Parr Village. At eight minutes past ten o'clock he was in the company of P.C. Bryne watching the beerhouse, which was open. They went in and saw the landlady under the influence of drink. Francis Bromilow was sitting in a chair with a glass con- taining beer in front of him. Witness asked her what she was doing with her house open at that time, and defendant referred to a clock on the rnantlepiece, which she said was a little too fast. The man Bromilow, who was drunk, swore that he would drink his beer before he left, and he did so.— P.C. Bryne corroborated the evidence of last witness, adding that there was a drop of beer left in Bromilow'a glass. H tasted this and found it was beer.—Defendant said that the drink supplied was not beer but ginger ale.—The Bench said they would not take the case of selling intoxicating liquors, but in the two other charges they would inflict a penalty of .£1 and costs in each case, or, in default, one month's imprisonment in each case. Bromilow would be fined 10s. and costs. UNJUST WEIGHTS: A HEAVY PENALTY.—John Tomlinson, butcher, was summoned by Superintendent Johnston for having unstamped weights in his possession on the 21st January.—Superintendent Johnston said he visited the shop kept by the defendant's agent in Church-street. The shop was a butcher's shop. He found three weights which were not stamped.—Fined 20s. and costs.—John Hilton Chisnall, painter, &c., was summoned under the same Act.—Superirf- tendent Johnston said that on the same day he visited the defendant's shop in the old market place and found a two pound weight three drachms light; and a half pound weight half a drachm light. There was a second charge against Chisnall for having three weights unstamped. Defendant admitted that he had not been to him (Superintendent Joh- nston to have the weights examined, although be had been in that division three years. The weights were old ones, so that he could not stamp them. Defendant said that he was not aware that there was anything wrong with the weights, which were used in his workshop for weighing by his mer. —Mr. Pilkington : Not for sale.—Defendant said that the stuff weighed was certainly for sale, as most of his work was done by contract, and the material was charged to his cus- tomers.—The Bench did not think this was a very serious case, but the weights, nevertheless, ought to be properly looked after. A fine of 10s. and costs in each case would be imposed—£l 2s. in each case.—Henry Fishwick, butcher, Church-street, was charged with having unjust weights in his shop; also with having unstamped weights in his posses- sion.—Superintendent Johnston said there was a 4/b weight two drachms light; three 2th weights one and a half drachms light; three 2M, two 111 a, a 1-lb, and a Th weights one drachm light. There were 10 weights that were light and unjust.—Defendant was up for a similar offence and con- victed in 1876.—The Bench considered this a bad case and they would inflict the full penalty of £5 and costs on the Ifirst charge, and £1 and costs on the other, altogether £7 45., or one month in each case. REFUSING TO ADMIT AND ASSAULTING THE POLICE.— James Parr was charged with refusing to admit P.C. Cottam into his house whilst in the execution of his duty, on being requested to do so by him, on the 23rd January.—William Parr, son of James, was charged with unlawfully assaulting P.S. Canister whilst in the execution of his duty.—Mr. J. 0. Swift appeared for the defendants, who pleaded not guilty.—P.C. Cottam said that at five minutes to twelve on Sunday night, the 22nd January, his attention was drawn to a beer-house in College-street, occupied by the elder defen- dant, by hearing people talking very loudly inside. He went to the kitchen window, and heard three women and two men talking. He saw Sergeant Callister, and told him what he had beard. They both went to the kitchen window, and he (witness) again heard the voices arguing as to who should

1 PRESCOT UNION SCHOOL ATTEN- DANCE COMMITTEE. The monthly meeting of the Prescot Union School Atten- dance Committee was held on Thursday, at the Workhouse. Whiston, the Rev. T. Chambers presiding. There were also present—The Rev. J. Barnacle, Mr. H. S. Hall (ex-officio), Messrs. Paris, Leatherbarrow, J. T. Hall, Leigh, Ranson, Dobell, and Rowe; with Mr. Hartley (clerk), and Mr. H. S. Welch (school attendance officer).—The minutes of the last meeting were read and confirmed. THE ATTENDANCE AT THE HIrYTON SCHOOLS. At a meeting of the Huvton Local Committee, held on the 25th January, Mr. Edward. Banner, J.P., presidin2, the atten- dance officer reported that the average attendance at the schools in the township was as follows :—Huyton-with-Roby school, 190; Congregational, 153; infants, 52; Huyton Quarry, 64; Catholic, 34; Roby infants, 40; total, 533.—1 t was suggested that the teachers of the private schools should be asked to supply the committee with the names audl addresses of the children attending their schools, and the officer was directed to obtain the information.— The officer also reported that he had made a house to house visitation of the township of Huyton-with-Roby, and found that there were 840 children, 427 boys and 413 girls; 326 were children under five years of age and 514 were over five years of age. The houses visited numbered 442.—The minutes of the committee were passed. MR. WELCH OVERWORKED.—RECOMMENDATION THAT AN ADDITIONAL OFFICER BE APPOINTED. The CHAIRMAN read letters which he had received from Mr. Edward Banner, J.P., of Roby, Mr. Walter Glynn and the Rev. George Beaumont, of Woolton, the Rev. John Barton, of Rainlaill, and the Rev. R. B. Stewart, of Hale, relative to the duties of the school attendance officer (Mr. IL S. Welch). The writers complained that they believed the duties of the officer were more than one man could efficiently discharge, and suggested that a second officer be appointed. Considering what Mr. IVelch had to do, he (the chairman) thought it was impossi- ble for him to carry out the work to the satisfaction of the various local committees, and for the benefit of the children in the different townships. The officer had 16 townships to visit, comprising 43,000 acres, and containing a population of about 29,000 people. In the township of Widnes there were three attendance officers to a population of about 29,000, but the acreage was considerably less than the com- mittee's district.—After a long discussion, it was resolved, on the motion of Mr. PARIS, seconded by Mr. DonELL, that an additional attendance officer be appointed for 12 months at 'a salary of £BO, his duties to be defined by the com- mittee.
